This closely resembles BixBench [`bix-13-q2`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-13-q2.jsonl). These token and repetition counts describe the final response, not the full trajectory.

The [HF collection](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples) includes original event logs and selected verifier verdict fields for all four examples. Viewer copies minimally adapt completed Pi messages while preserving their content; compaction events are labeled import annotations. Private judge connection settings are omitted from the verifier copies. Uploaded originals and adapted files were verified against local hashes, and all four viewers preserve the recorded tool-call counts.

Together with the [BixBench/BFCL audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258#issuecomment-6300963037), these examples show recurring execution and submission failures across benchmarks: simulated environment observations, answers left in chat, and repetitive output-limit termination. BiomniBench also demonstrates wrong-directory report writes and malformed write arguments. This strengthens the evidence that the submission problem extends beyond biological reasoning, but the four purposively selected traces do not estimate each mechanism’s prevalence or establish a common cause. BixBench used Pi 1.3.0; BFCL and this BiomniBench run used Pi 0.87.0. No biological calculations were independently recomputed or regraded in this comparison.

All 50 initial prompts contained the required absolute output paths. Reports from 12 tasks were preserved and rubric-graded; three successful direct writes were also compared byte-for-byte with their archived verifier files and matched. Native per-task rewards, the sealed 50-row sample archive, and the canonical/EvalDash mean agree. Missing submissions receive zero before any judge call, so those 38 zeros do not depend on MiniMax's rubric judgments. No scores were repaired and no new model calls were made during the audit.

An independent review recomputed the 212 total points, mean, coverage, and failure counts from the saved task records. The audit bundle referenced below contains the per-task summaries, inspected trace details, parser replay, and audit scripts.

The evidence implicates several stages of execution. Repetition is an observed generation failure; Pi ending after a length-limited response is a harness behavior that can prevent a later submission. Invalid tool formats could reflect checkpoint behavior or a serving/interface mismatch. Successful report collection on other tasks argues against a general collection defect, but does not resolve those integration questions. The audit cannot attribute all 38 failures to the checkpoint or determine whether the weakness is biology-specific.

The next useful comparisons would be a reference model on the identical protocol and a small controlled Snowball diagnostic capturing raw model tokens, API requests/responses, and executed tools. The former would test whether this setup permits another model to complete the tasks; the latter would help separate checkpoint, template/parser, sampling, and serving effects. Pi events retain API text and argument deltas, but the inspected artifacts do not contain pre-parser model token captures. Neither comparison has been run; no diagnostic GPU rerun has been launched.

🤖 Snowball v0.1’s official BixBench result is **19/205 = 9.27%**, reported as **9.3%** in the [release results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10283). A saved-trace audit shows that missing submissions account for most failed tasks.

| Final outcome | Tasks |
| --- | ---: |
| Missing `/workspace/answer.txt`; automatic zero | 156 |
| Empty answer sent to judge; rejected | 1 |
| Nonempty answer rejected by judge | 29 |
| Answer accepted by judge | 19 |
| **Total** | **205** |

All 205 tasks received scores, but only **48 contained nonempty submitted answers**. Full scoring coverage should therefore not be interpreted as full submission coverage.

Among the 156 missing-file cases, **141 had a final assistant event with `stopReason=stop`** and **15 had `stopReason=length`**. Here, `stop` is Pi’s normal-end status for the model response, distinct from `length`; it does not establish that the agent completed the task or wrote the required file. Pi 1.3.0 also maps a null provider finish reason to `stop`, so the status alone does not prove an intentional completion decision. Across the run, 22 selected traces contained no tool-execution-start events; inspected examples generated tool-call markup or simulated terminal output as ordinary assistant text (for example, [`bix-28-q6`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-28-q6.jsonl)). All initial prompts specified the required answer path. These observations overlap: the 22 tasks are not an additional failure category.

The [public trace examples](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples) open in Hugging Face’s Agent Trace Viewer. Seven BixBench examples and four BFCL follow-up examples include their original logs and verifier output. Because this Harbor run used Pi with `--no-session`, the viewer copies minimally adapt completed event messages into Pi session entries; message content is unchanged, and compaction events are labeled import annotations.

The traces show several distinct problems:

- **Missing submissions (three examples):** [`bix-10-q1`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-10-q1.jsonl) performed an analysis and stated an odds ratio in chat, but never created the required answer file. The [verifier log](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/verifier/bix-10-q1.txt) records the missing file. Its computed odds ratio, approximately **1.169**, also falls outside the [pinned reference range of 1.50–1.54](https://github.com/penfever/harbor-datasets/blob/454d04b5427fd90de78d7bec9dfe57561a21ff03/datasets/bixbench-cli-marin-corrections-1/bix-10-q1/tests/ground_truth.json). Writing that value would have fixed submission completeness, but not the reference mismatch; the underlying analysis has not been independently recomputed. Two further missing-file examples illustrate different behaviors: [`bix-28-q6`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-28-q6.jsonl) ended with `stop` after generating an entire simulated execution transcript inside one assistant text response, with zero executed tool calls. It supplied its own shell observations and numerical result, then showed code supposedly writing `0.1258380127877238` to `/workspace/answer.txt` and a simulated `cat` confirming it. None of those operations ran: this was simulated execution and submission, not merely omission of the save instruction, and the numerical result has no verified execution behind it; [`bix-13-q2`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-13-q2.jsonl) executed 18 tool calls but ended in repetitive generation with `length`, also without an answer file. Their verifier logs confirm the missing files ([bix-28-q6](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/verifier/bix-28-q6.txt), [bix-13-q2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/verifier/bix-13-q2.txt)).
- **Repetition and length limits:** 11 of the 15 length-stop cases contained over 1,000 occurrences of “Now” in one response (for example, [`bix-13-q2`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-13-q2.jsonl)). Fourteen ended with a response reporting 16,384 output tokens. In the remaining case, [`bix-30-q5`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-30-q5.jsonl), the final response reported 65,535 input tokens and one output token; its trace also records failed compaction and failed context-overflow recovery. These counts describe the final response, not the entire task trajectory.
- **Analysis errors:** [`bix-35-q3`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-35-q3.jsonl) used the BUSCO `Score` column as an evolutionary rate despite the question specifying PhyKIT `evo_rate`. [`bix-27-q2`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-27-q2.jsonl) reported 7,992 accumulated classifications across 50 iterations for a question asking how many samples were consistently classified.
- **Grading concern:** [`bix-8-q5`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-8-q5.jsonl) submitted `8.10e-194` and received zero against a reference of `p < 2.2e-16`. The [verifier log](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/verifier/bix-8-q5.txt) preserves the submitted answer, reference, and rejection. The submitted value satisfies that inequality. This merits adjudication, although the underlying analysis has not been independently recomputed.

Compaction errors appeared in **29 tasks**, including some that eventually submitted answers; these observations overlap with the categories above. Across all 205 final trials, compaction count showed little association with a missing answer file (Pearson r = 0.052; Spearman ρ = −0.005). Missing-file rates were **94/122 (77.0%) without compaction** and **62/83 (74.7%) with at least one compaction event** (two-sided Fisher p = 0.74). Tasks with a compaction error had 24/29 missing files, versus 132/176 without an error (82.8% versus 75.0%; Fisher p = 0.48). Counts include successful and failed compaction-end events; using only successful events also gave little association (Pearson r = 0.035). These are unadjusted observational comparisons: task difficulty and trajectory length may affect both compaction and outcomes, so they neither establish causation nor rule out harm in individual traces.

This audit examined structured events from all 205 selected final trajectories, with detailed inspection of the examples above. The run had 211 physical attempts: six verifier-timeout attempts preceded replacements. The final per-task rewards match the sealed sample archive. An independent review reproduced the outcome and event counts from the saved records and traces, and verified all 205 unique task IDs, logical trial IDs, and rewards against the sealed sample shard. Neither audit independently recomputed the biological analyses. No grades changed and no solver or judge calls were made.

Missing submissions also occurred in the same checkpoint’s **BFCL parity evaluation**: **55/123 final trials (44.7%)** explicitly failed because `/app/result.json` was absent. This BFCL evaluation required a JSON description of the selected benchmark function call(s) in `/app/result.json`, written using Pi’s actual tools. The remaining outcomes were 42 accepted submissions, 25 rejected submissions, and one JSON parsing error; the parsing error is not counted as a confirmed empty answer. These counts come from the [saved BFCL result records](s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261019-104642-open-athena-Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14-bfclparity-pi-e8cb/results/) identified in the [release archive map](https://gist.github.com/penfever/b7deea3a2eaec1642a56c0d67ba1e41a#file-trace_archive_source_prefixes-json). BFCL used **Pi 0.87.0**, versus **Pi 1.3.0** here. A follow-up inspected four missing-file traces: the lexicographically first missing trial in each of the irrelevance, multiple, parallel, and simple-python categories. This selection illustrates mechanisms; it does not estimate their prevalence among the 55 missing submissions.

All four inspected BFCL traces ended with `stop`, had no compaction events, and failed the file-existence check despite an explicit instruction to execute a write to `/app/result.json`:

- [`bfcl-multiple-170`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bfcl-multiple-170.jsonl) selected `soccer_stat.get_player_stats` for Ronaldo’s 2019–2020 season and emitted the proposed JSON in chat, with zero tool executions. The content follows the requested player and season, but was not submitted or regraded.
- [`bfcl-parallel-147`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bfcl-parallel-147.jsonl) described three `light_travel_time` calls and considered both `echo` and heredoc commands for writing the file, but executed neither. It ended with JSON in chat and zero tool executions. Recognizing the write requirement did not translate into executing it.
- [`bfcl-irrelevance-103`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bfcl-irrelevance-103.jsonl) made six real tool calls to inspect the environment, then said it would write the result but only emitted JSON in chat. It also selected `weather_forecast.get` for a current-time question; the described weather function does not meet that request, so the prompt’s no-applicable-function branch calls for `[]`. This is a function-selection mistake in addition to a submission failure.
- [`bfcl-simple-python-161`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bfcl-simple-python-161.jsonl) attempted to invoke `crime_statute_lookup` as a live agent tool and received `Tool crime_statute_lookup not found`. The task required writing a JSON description of the call. After six actual shell calls, it stopped without writing the file; its final text contained a `<tool_response>` imitation of the earlier Python-version output, not another tool execution. The seven execution-start events include the rejected unknown-tool dispatch.

These examples extend the evidence for general instruction-following and tool-use problems beyond biology: leaving answers in chat, describing writes without executing them, and confusing benchmark function descriptions with live agent tools. None of these four reproduces the complete fabricated execution and successful-file-write transcript in `bix-28-q6`. The final tool-response imitation in `bfcl-simple-python-161` is a narrower resemblance. Different Pi versions and the small purposive sample prevent attributing all missing submissions to one mechanism. Original logs and verifier outputs accompany each linked HF trace; no BFCL answers were regraded.

The terminal suites provide additional examples: OpenThoughts-TBLite reported missing `answer.txt` in five trials across two tasks, and Terminal-Bench reported missing `result.txt` in three trials across two tasks. These are confirmed subsets, not overall failure rates; both suites used Terminus-2 and repeated each task three times. Conversely, all 200 DS-1000 trials had nonempty saved code submissions. Missing files, wrong submitted answers, and agent timeouts should therefore remain separate outcomes when comparing these evaluations.

The evaluated configuration used **Smartie Step14, `bixbench-cli-marin-corrections@3`, Pi 1.3.0, and MiniMax-M3-MXFP8 judging**. A substantial part of the observed failure burden concerns general tool execution and answer submission, limiting what the overall score tells us about biological reasoning. In particular, the simulated execution in [`bix-28-q6`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-v01-bixbench-trace-examples/blob/main/sessions/bix-28-q6.jsonl) provides evidence of a tool-use failure, not an executed biological analysis whose correctness can be assessed. The BFCL trace inspection demonstrates related submission and tool-use failures beyond biology, while leaving the frequency and shared cause of each mechanism unresolved. Question-specific concerns also remain: the wrong evolutionary-rate column and classification-count interpretation are analysis errors, and the odds-ratio result disagrees with the pinned reference. Writing the missing answer file would not resolve that disagreement; the underlying analysis has not been independently recomputed. The evidence does not isolate checkpoint behavior from serving, tool parsing, or harness behavior; a controlled diagnostic should test those boundaries before interpreting this score as a measure of biological reasoning alone.

🤖 GLM-5.3 completes the BiomniBench-DA reporting workflow much more often than Snowball v0.1 under the same task and agent policy. The first-attempt comparison already establishes this difference without crediting infrastructure retries. The shared harness also exhibits verifier failures, so this experiment does not establish that every Snowball failure originates in the checkpoint.

The reference run ended with an infrastructure failure after the judge and then evaluator were preempted. It retained scores for 43/50 tasks: 41 rubric-graded submissions with both reports, one confirmed missing-submission zero, and one setup-failure zero. Seven tasks remain unresolved. The mean over the 43 scored tasks is **74.56/100**; it is not a complete 50-task score. Allowing each unresolved grade to range from 0 to 100 gives an all-50 range of 64.12–78.12. Both Iris jobs are terminal and a full Daytona inventory found zero owned sandboxes remaining.

The baseline is the [Snowball v0.1 run and trace audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258#issuecomment-6297505720). Both runs use the same 50 public tasks, inputs, Harbor/Pi revisions, context and output budgets, time limits, retry policy, MiniMax judge, and signed rubric scorer. GLM uses its supported serving interface; Snowball used its own serving and tool parser. The GLM service did not report an exact weights revision, and sampling/serving defaults were not independently matched. This is a comparison of the two model-serving systems under a shared evaluation setup.

| First attempt, all 50 tasks | Snowball v0.1 | GLM-5.3 |
|---|---:|---:|
| At least one nonempty report retained | 12 | 35 |
| Both `trace.md` and `answer.txt` retained | 5 | 35 |
| Confirmed missing submission | 36 | 1 |
| Submission unverified after verifier failure | 2 | 14 |
| Native rewards available | 48 | 34 |
| Sum of available scores, in points | 212 | 2,623 |
| All-50 mean allowing each unavailable score to range from 0 to 100 | 4.24–8.24 | 52.46–84.46 |

These ranges bound the effect of unavailable grades; they are not confidence intervals. Even assigning every unavailable GLM grade zero and every unavailable Snowball grade 100 leaves a large gap. GLM retained reports on 23 of the 36 tasks where Snowball's first attempt had a confirmed missing submission.

“Unverified” means the verifier did not retain the reports and did not produce a missing-submission verdict. It does not establish whether files existed in the sandbox. The GLM first attempts include two judge failures with both reports retained, in addition to the 14 cases with unverified submissions.

The traces reveal three distinct problems:

- GLM's confirmed missing submission, `da-3-5`, performed 27 tool calls before an empty assistant response with normal `stop` and one output token. No executed tool arguments mentioned either required report filename. This was not an observed context/output-limit stop. Without raw pre-parser output, its origin cannot be assigned to the checkpoint alone.
- Two first attempts retained both reports but received `{}` from MiniMax. The strict rubric parser rejected the response, producing a verifier runtime error. These are judge failures, not missing submissions.
- All 14 first-attempt verifier timeouts followed the 1,800-second agent limit and the 300-second verifier limit. Seven of their traces were inspected in detail: all seven lacked `agent_end`, and four had pending tool calls. This exposes a timeout/cancellation or verification problem requiring separate diagnosis. The policy retries the whole solver after a verifier timeout, so final scores must be accompanied by the first-attempt results.

A later retry also failed while installing Pi because GitHub DNS resolution failed, before GLM ran. The current error taxonomy assigns that attempt a zero. The canonical record must preserve that classification, but the analysis must identify its infrastructure origin.

The MiniMax judge worker was subsequently preempted. Automatic Harbor recovery preserved all 43 scored results but removed the seven unscored logical trial directories before waiting for the judge to recover. The complete first-attempt audit had already been read back and saved at 20:12 UTC, along with detailed summaries of seven timeout traces. Those saved summaries support the first-attempt table, but the removed native traces can no longer be independently replayed from their original locations. Replacement attempts numbered `000` must not be mistaken for original first attempts. Harbor briefly resumed the seven tasks before the evaluator was itself preempted with `WorkloadEvictedDueToPreempted`. [Incident and evidence-retention limitations](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/805).

The evidence supports a substantial difference in task completion and output delivery between the two model-serving systems. It does not isolate Snowball's checkpoint from its serving integration, establish a general biology knowledge deficit, or certify the harness as error-free.

The terminal audit checked all 43 retained outcomes, their report files, and 42 readable Pi traces; the setup failure has no Pi trajectory. It also verified that the 43 scores and selected attempt paths were unchanged across judge recovery. No manual regrading or score imputation was performed.

The full reference run ID is `20261020-182620-glm-5.3-biomnibench-da-pi-volume-free50-4bc2`. The evaluator was preempted before publishing a canonical record, and EvalDash's API returns `404 unknown run_id`; there is no working full-run EvalDash link. Root Iris job: `/exedev/glm53-biomnibench-reference50-20261020-181225`. The first-attempt audit was preserved outside the mutable trial tree in the run's `provenance/preemption-audit-20261020.tar.gz`, with verified SHA-256 `6ff863d4f8fda3604e6f9a9218302bde1f143385055d3c716c2db8513ea9fc51`.

The terminal audit bundle is `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261020-182620-glm-5.3-biomnibench-da-pi-volume-free50-4bc2/provenance/partial-final-audit-20261020.tar.gz`: 68 files, 1,806,043 bytes, verified readback SHA-256 `e2254e1c888317c1ee80d63d0c89f310579b156bc98c94f6a5fa4d908d630d97`. It contains the per-task audits, saved first-attempt comparison, terminal readback, cleanup proof, and comparison plot. Deleted raw traces are not reconstructed.

Reproduction uses Marin `75a5690b0ff2e1510d73e576649e3e059f06da9a`, Harbor `016dd78b301b621ee4089f2da5776ebe80236820`, Pi `0.87.0`, and dataset revision `e1c8ca5e11a620087bc48d97888eb69176a1f235`. Budgets are 65,536 context tokens, 16,384 output tokens, a 32,768-token compaction reserve, 360/1,800/300-second setup/agent/verifier limits, and concurrency 16. Each sandbox has 8 GiB RAM and 10 GiB disk, with no Daytona volume. The same five input variants from the Snowball run are retained. A separate one-task pilot scored 82/100 and is excluded from the 50-task comparison. This supplementary evaluation is excluded from the release aggregate and uses a signed scorer that differs from the benchmark's released unsigned parser.

🤖 The supplementary 60-minute comparison is incomplete. The latest durable audit retains 36 GLM-5.3 outcomes and 48 Snowball v0.1 outcomes, including one completed fresh Snowball rerun. Fourteen GLM tasks and two Snowball tasks remain. No fresh GLM task has started, and there is no complete 50-task score for either model under this protocol.

The coordinator stalled while saving provenance before solver execution. A storage configuration change passed a bounded write/readback check. Relaunch is currently blocked because the parent scheduler has lost contact with the CoreWeave controller and cannot confirm termination of the old coordinator. A replacement has been prepared but has not been launched against the same result roots. Original results remain preserved.

The diagnostic evidence and recovery conditions are recorded in [incident 821](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/821). Once termination is confirmed, the prepared continuation will retain the 83 early-completed original outcomes, preserve the completed fresh Snowball result, and execute the remaining 16 tasks. These results remain supplementary and outside release aggregation.

🤖 Iris connectivity has recovered, and the previous coordinator is confirmed terminal. The continuation passed storage upload, pinned Harbor reuse planning, and the volume-free sandbox/model/tokenizer preflight. No direct Kubernetes credential or cluster change was needed.

The MiniMax judge reached GPU warmup, then was preempted by a higher-priority workload. Its retry remains queued for eight H100s at the normal research priority. No fresh GLM solver task has started. The latest durable audit retains 36 GLM outcomes and 48 Snowball outcomes; 14 GLM and two Snowball tasks remain, so neither model has a complete 60-minute score yet. The active continuation will proceed when capacity is admitted.

[Incident 821](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/821) records the recovery evidence. The continuation has a disclosed four-hour enclosing window after the outage, with unchanged 60-minute agent limits, judge/model configuration, task inputs, and sandbox limits.

🤖 The overnight continuation failed before any fresh GLM task started. The pinned MiniMax judge eventually became ready after three preemptions, then the launcher raised `KeyError: CW_S3_ENDPOINT`: the storage settings had been added to the Harbor driver allowlist but were removed by the outer evaluation allowlist. Retained outcomes remain unchanged at 36 GLM and 48 Snowball; 16 tasks are still outstanding.

The private launcher now forwards the settings through both allowlists. A mandatory CPU-stage regression check passed at 14:12 UTC on October 22: it reproduces the previous missing-key failure and verifies the corrected runner-to-Harbor driver boundary for both batches, intercepting trial execution and record writes. This is synthetic environment validation, with zero model/judge calls or sandbox starts. The replacement judge worker is running and loading cached weights, with no preemptions at the latest check; fresh solver results remain pending.

GLM already uses the established external endpoint and receives no additional candidate GPUs from this experiment. The eight-H100 allocation is for the MiniMax judge; Snowball candidate serving is scheduled after the GLM run. Model, judge, task limits, and scoring settings are unchanged. [Incident and recovery evidence](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/821).

🤖 The 60-minute continuation now uses [Harbor 3bc27cbc](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/commit/3bc27cbcffad1d92ad5d9bd4c83cd3f36bf89372) to repair Pi timeout handling. It retains 43 scored GLM-5.3 outcomes and 48 Snowball v0.1 outcomes unchanged, and submits only the remaining seven GLM and two Snowball tasks. Final 50-task scores and dashboard verification are pending.

The previous reference run confirmed the failure tracked in [Harbor #261](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/issues/261): Pi was still alive 3,803 seconds after agent start while verification had already begun, despite the 3,600-second agent cap. Cancelling the local wait did not stop its remote process. This can block verification or allow work after the deadline; missing archived reports from affected attempts cannot establish a model failure. The affected coordinator and its judge were stopped after a bounded private snapshot passed SHA-256 readback. All five remaining owned sandboxes are gone; their report files were absent at capture time. Earlier scored outcomes remain intact.

The repair wraps Pi's complete pipeline in the existing sandbox deadline supervisor. It also prevents Bash's echoed pipeline text from turning a signal kill into `ModelAuthenticationError`. Both new regressions fail on the original source; all 54 Pi/deadline tests pass with the repair, along with lint and the changed-file type check. A model-free Daytona check using Python 3.12 and the evaluation's SDK 0.200.2 confirmed that Pi's process exited and verification then ran in the same session. Its sandbox was deleted. This checks the execution boundary, not scientific grading. The supervisor starts shutdown up to 15 seconds before the configured cap and escalates after five seconds.

Both models use new archive roots because Harbor binds the runtime revision into resume identity. Original results and actual timeout metadata are preserved. Model identities, judge, rubric, task inputs, token budgets, setup/verifier limits, sandbox resources and absence of volumes remain unchanged. GLM uses the established external endpoint, with no candidate GPUs allocated by this evaluator; the MiniMax judge uses eight H100s.

New EvalDash records, which may remain empty until native execution writes them: [GLM-5.3](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs/20261022-165801-glm-5.3-biomnibench-da-60min-full-b3c4), [Snowball v0.1](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs/20261022-165801-snowball-v01-biomnibench-da-60min-full-b3c4). The comparison remains supplementary and outside the release aggregate.

🤖 The [GLM-5.3 reference is complete in EvalDash](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs/20261022-165801-glm-5.3-biomnibench-da-60min-full-b3c4): **71.14/100 across all 50 tasks**. Forty-five tasks submitted both reports and received rubric grades; five received confirmed missing-submission zeros. There are no unknown submission states. The sealed archive, all 50 unique sample rows, native rewards, canonical mean and reused result hashes were checked. Representative raw Pi artifacts were also read back through EvalDash with matching hashes. This remains the disclosed supplementary public-50 protocol, including its input variants and MiniMax signed-rubric judge.

The repaired deadline handling worked on three real timeouts: agent phases ended at approximately 3,586 seconds, verification completed in 9–11 seconds, and a live process check found Pi and its analysis processes gone. Their traces contain no executed call referencing either required report. One was waiting in a bash command containing `sleep 1500`; another was running R. The third retained an HTTP 502 diagnostic from `/tokenize`; its contribution to the timeout is unresolved, so that native zero is not evidence of a purely scientific failure. The completed audit streamed all 14 selected deadline-affected GLM traces, totalling 150,438,046 bytes. Raw traces and original results remain preserved.

Snowball v0.1 remains at 48/50 scored. Its worker is loading the pinned checkpoint before running only the two remaining tasks; no completed solver task is being rerun. Separately, 35 admitted original Snowball missing-submission cases ended normally within 24 minutes, so the timeout leak cannot explain those cases. Attribution between the checkpoint and its tool/serving integration remains unresolved. The full two-model comparison and Snowball audit will follow once those two outcomes and dashboard checks finish.

🤖 The 60-minute comparison is complete: **50/50 scored tasks per model**, independently verified in EvalDash.

| Model | Mean score /100 | Both reports | Any report | No nonempty report |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| [Snowball v0.1](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs/20261022-165801-snowball-v01-biomnibench-da-60min-full-b3c4) | **4.24** | 5/50 | 12/50 | 38/50 |
| [GLM-5.3](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs/20261022-165801-glm-5.3-biomnibench-da-60min-full-b3c4) | **71.14** | 45/50 | 45/50 | 5/50 |

“No report” describes the required `/app/trace.md` and `/app/answer.txt` submissions, not blank assistant text. All 38 selected Snowball missing-submission cases ended normally, without an agent exception, within 24 minutes. The three fresh 60-minute attempts ended after 72.2, 4.7 and 30.0 seconds. The last two made no tool calls despite receiving instructions naming both report paths; their text contained planning and, in one case, a Markdown bash command. Neither saved either file. Snowball's full score is unchanged from the original 30-minute run.

The shared timeout leak therefore cannot explain these selected Snowball failures. The reference shows that the common task preparation, Pi runner and grader can deliver and grade reports on 45/50 tasks. This supports a file-delivery/tool-use gap under these model-serving configurations; it does not isolate the checkpoint from its model-specific tool/serving integration or establish a general biology knowledge deficit. The [reference audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258#issuecomment-6349073945) documents the repaired real timeouts and the unresolved `/tokenize` HTTP 502 event in one GLM timeout.

As agreed, early-completed outcomes were retained: 36 GLM and 47 Snowball results from the old budget, plus seven GLM and one Snowball result already completed at 60 minutes. Only seven GLM and two Snowball tasks were executed in the repaired continuation. Original result bytes, scores and actual timeout metadata remain unchanged. Fresh attempts restarted from scratch, so this is not a paired causal estimate of additional time.

The final checks verified all 100 selected outcomes against native rewards, canonical means, sealed 50-row archives and EvalDash sample rows; all 83 original reused result hashes and retained 60-minute hashes matched. All 14 deadline-affected GLM traces and three fresh Snowball traces were audited. Four representative raw Pi artifacts were read back through EvalDash with matching hashes; normalized trajectory links remain unavailable in this Pi version. The combined private audit archive is retained with both runs under `provenance/native-audit-both.tar.gz`, SHA-256 `869c85ec9b20a3daa5cce09fd81b806dae2ba11d22307383a7b85136eeec5e68`.

The final coordinator succeeded, both inference workers retired, and an inventory found no remaining sandbox matching the 107 exact owned trial names or any of the three disposable deadline probes. The shared GLM endpoint was left running. This remains the disclosed supplementary public-50/input-variant/MiniMax protocol and is excluded from release aggregation.

Launch-source references: [Marin evaluation launcher at the pinned base revision](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/75a5690b0ff2e1510d73e576649e3e059f06da9a/experiments/evaluation/launch.py) and [Harbor Pi deadline repair](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/commit/3bc27cbcffad1d92ad5d9bd4c83cd3f36bf89372). The first link is the shared base launcher; the campaign-specific final continuation was an uncommitted workspace overlay and is not present at that commit. Its exact `experiments/evaluation/campaigns/biomnibench-60min-20261021/launch.py` is preserved in `marin-workspace.zip` inside the GLM run's private `provenance/final-session-handoff-20261022-194111.tar.gz` (archive SHA-256 `a5ceb6366103469c6027b7a13fb1f69c6fcb7b1578bdb134caa400ac27a21362`; original launch-file SHA-256 `176b7e88d5c7a3fb7811bf1ce913db726bb64b1851ec12fbee19004168228499`). This final continuation retained all 50 GLM and 48 Snowball results and executed only the final two Snowball tasks. The [version-pinned final continuation source and policies](https://gist.github.com/gonzalobenegas/08b9425c006588b7f675e3451c6db51e/53e9b978ac0e6e957dc8fed2f2bb56c4f89340f6#file-launch-py) are now public. The snapshot replaces one private service lookup with environment variables; model, scoring, budget and input settings are unchanged. Its README records the omitted private dependencies and the original/published source hashes; this is an archival code reference rather than a standalone launch package.

topics.title: [rl] Add full-inventory Snowball training and paired evaluation
topics.body:
Add artifact entrypoints for full-inventory Snowball training, initializer comparisons and paired evaluation. Training preflight checks every task in the 100,000-row pool, rejects loader admission loss, verifies that required modules come from the delivered workspace, and exercises representative graders before training GPU submission. Reports record launch provenance, imported code hashes and the frozen lock identity.

Datakit SFT and released Dr.Doom initializer comparisons use a fixed 910-task development panel with evaluation at updates 0, 25 and 50, greedy decoding, 8,192-token replies and a 24,576-token context. Admission verifies the selected initializer against its immutable model manifest. Reports retain pairing identities, per-family scores, scoring coverage and token-limit stops with fixed denominators.

Isolated checkpoint exports prepare Hugging Face weights in separate output paths after checking the committed policy shards. Structural tasks recorded in the native rollout format pass through the maintained text-prefill exporter, which records changed conditioning and grading semantics. Previous runs using token-pinned inputs do not validate these text-prefill inputs; fresh Linux loader, factory, grading and serving qualification is required.

Depends on #10406 and #10456. Part of #10314.

topics.title: [iris] Default GPU jobs to NCCL_DEBUG=WARN
topics.body:
Iris no longer sets NCCL_DEBUG=INFO with the INIT,BOOTSTRAP,ENV,NET,GRAPH,
TUNING,RAS subsystems on every GPU job. The default is NCCL_DEBUG=WARN with
the same timestamp format; NCCL_RAS_ENABLE stays on, since the RAS probe
does not depend on the log level.

The INFO default came with the stall-detection work (#7692). On 2026-10-17
three concurrent 32-GPU training jobs produced about 80,000 NCCL log lines
per second, while Finelog forwarding accepts about 34,500 per second, and
the hub fell about 90 minutes behind. Jobs that need init or network traces
set INFO and the subsystem list themselves, as the CoreWeave GPU smoke
config and the wedge-recovery launcher already do.

Fixes #10240

topics.title: Identity SFT for Marin Snowball with capability-preservation checks
topics.body:
# Identity SFT for Marin Snowball with capability-preservation checks

Updated 22 October 2026.

## Background

Marin Snowball is Open Athena's mixture-of-experts language model. This campaign tests whether narrow supervised fine-tuning can teach the assistant to identify itself as Marin Snowball, created by Open Athena, while preserving software-engineering ability. Open Athena is the nonprofit; Marin is the research project that began at Stanford in 2024, created by David Hall and Percy Liang, and is primarily developed by Open Athena with community contributors. These are the campaign's supplied attribution targets.

V13 and V19 name campaign training/data iterations. The public model version v0.1.1 is V13's low-learning-rate checkpoint at step 50; the v0.1 model is the shared initializer. Dataset version numbers between them also include untrained coverage expansions.

## TL;DR

Identity SFT improved the development score from 7/60 to 45/60 in released V13, but subsequent user testing exposed fiction refusal and unsolicited self-attribution, overturning the earlier acceptance judgment. V19 reached 51/60 identity and 42/42 targeted coding, but was rejected after MATH500 fell from V13's 449/500 to 371/500; neither result establishes preservation of general assistant behavior.

## Result so far

V13 low-learning-rate SFT at step 50 was accepted at publication, but subsequent user testing exposed a serious creative-writing regression (see the revised release assessment below); it remains historically published as [Marin Snowball v0.1.1](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Marin-Snowball-67B-A2B-v0.1.1/tree/59852d6f07261722bbec1edb6ab148317156b58e) and listed in Open Athena's Releases collection. Its original v0.1 model-card body is retained with an identity-fix subsection. The [publication receipt](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/90fc4695b777d16599049e99b3a36847ee5459a3/evidence__hf-v011__publication-receipt.json) records verification of all 91 files against staged hashes or downloaded content.

The subsequent V19 run improves the identity development score but worsens math performance. It will not be promoted to v0.1.2 because of the math regression. The [final comparison](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/6125ae3d627880838f53dc3d2b0f1fd7b6ae04ec/evidence__v19-final-release-comparison.json) records 42/42 targeted coding passes, including one successful retry after a sandbox infrastructure failure.

| Evaluation | v0.1 initializer | V13 low-LR step 50 | V19 step 60 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Native identity development panel | 7/60 | 45/60 | 51/60 |
| Delayed identity, two or three user turns | — | 17/24 | 17/24 |
| Targeted SWE, direct Daytona rerun | — | 41/42 | 42/42 |
| Harness identity, direct Daytona rerun | — | 3/6 | 6/6 |
| MATH500 | 461/500 | 449/500 | 371/500 |
| GSM8K, flexible answer extraction | 1224/1319 | 1038/1319 | 1015/1319 |

Identity judgments are Codex assessments, not independent human reviews. The rubric fails unsupported claims, contradictions and material omissions; calibrated uncertainty is allowed, and formatting defects are recorded separately from factual correctness. The 60-question development panel guided data expansion and checkpoint comparisons, so it is not an untouched generalization test. The SWE panel contains 14 task definitions executed through Pi, OpenCode and mini-SWE; it cannot establish broad SWE-bench preservation. V13's earlier two SWE repetitions scored 41/42 and 40/42, against initializer scores of 38/42 and 39/42. See the [release provenance](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/152c5e421b275ea23a0613177a767613acf6b5a6/evidence__hf-v011__identity-sft-provenance.json).

The native identity panel queries the model directly; harness identity counts six total task/interface executions: two attribution tasks through each of the three coding-agent interfaces. Pi exposed raw thinking delimiters in one V19 answer despite correct factual content. Math comparisons use matched V13 settings: temperature 0, 8,192 maximum generated tokens, thinking enabled for MATH500 and disabled for GSM8K. V13 acceptance was a campaign judgment based on its identity improvement and targeted coding results, rather than a pre-registered overall capability threshold; its math regressions mean this is not evidence of general capability preservation.

## Question and method

The assistant should keep project founders, organizational responsibility and model identity distinct, and use supplied date context without inventing dates.

Training coverage expanded around observed failures, including higher-temperature sampling and manual corrections. Later datasets balance thinking and nonthinking examples and include unrelated preceding turns before an identity question. Serialization uses the native chat template and assistant masks. Earlier train/validation differences included a thinking-prefix formatting mismatch; that was repaired before the later analysis.

V13 and V19 both initialize from v0.1 revision `adc0078a19a4383bc998fcdb43867b3360baf5f3`. V13 used learning rate 1e-6 and 2,438 training examples, balanced 1,219/1,219 by thinking mode. V13 used the then-default expert capacity factor 1. V19 keeps that learning rate, expands coverage, and explicitly sets expert capacity factor 4 (more dispatch buffer space for uneven expert routing).

The [V19 configuration](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/c8634964504e138e210f9e253dc34712a7a5e26f/configs__sft__snowball-identity-sft-v19-capacity4-20261022__config.json) uses learning rate 1e-6, weight decay 0.01, maximum gradient norm 0.5, packed 8,192-token training sequences with cross-document attention blocked, and expert capacity factor 4. Its [dataset manifest](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/19c8f4ed1382dba3a9b93ad8068e3f083280cc3d/data__dataset-v19__manifest.json) records 5,826 training rows: 2,913 thinking and 2,913 nonthinking. It contains 938 examples with two user turns and 938 with three. The manifest's assembly-stage status predates the subsequent packing and training; the configuration and training evidence establish that later execution.

V19 was stopped after sustained validation deterioration, preserving its best inline-validation checkpoint at step 60. Selective weight-restoration and activation-mapping experiments did not establish a freeze set that met the preservation goal; no expert-freezing claim is made for V19. Dataset expansion and capacity changes were not independently randomized, so this comparison does not attribute the regression to either one.

## Validation divergence and remaining failures

The [standalone divergence note](https://gist.github.com/penfever/46017604e340ee915e2fa96295fb5337) rescored fixed examples from V19 at steps 60 and 125 and probed alternative next-token probabilities. Validation loss increased from about 0.963 to 1.326 while sampled training loss fell from about 0.631 to 0.142. Final-answer prose accounted for 84.5% of the aggregate validation-loss increase on the fixed rescored examples; first-answer-token mismatch accounted for only 0.8% in this repaired run. Among the 50 largest answer-token loss increases, 41 retained the same most likely token while the distribution sharpened. This is a statement about selected teacher-forced positions, not unchanged generated answers, and does not causally explain the math regression. Increasing evaluation capacity removed only 0.094% of the divergence; this does not test training-time routing effects.

The [V19 native review](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/82052e5ae276fef331e742c9d8577ad8484e55ad/evidence__v19-step60-native-manual-review.json) records nine failures, including unsupported distinctions between organization and creator, uncertainty handled as denial, attribution errors, and rejection of the shortened name Snowball. The [delayed review](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/e751c310392d4b010ab9e0c895af3350f8ec139c/evidence__v19-step60-delayed-identity-manual-review.json) records seven failures, including an invented conversation date and an OpenAI self-attribution after unrelated earlier turns.

[Supplemental coverage](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/81288235a5261371759cce7a803df6013b9eb0f8/data__v19-step60-failure-reviewed-20261022__train-candidates.jsonl) adds six examples per failed answer, 96 total. Raw temperature-1.1 samples and seeds are retained; the final responses and thinking content were manually rewritten by Codex (not a human reviewer) before acceptance. The set is balanced 48/48 by thinking mode and includes 21 two-turn and 21 three-turn examples. [Native-template validation](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/fcfeb2c399bebae0f25ad26d90e277d1f30d3ba4/data__v19-step60-failure-reviewed-20261022__validation.json) confirms exact assistant masks. These examples were not added retrospectively to V19's training data or evaluation panels.

## Reproduction artifacts and upstream changes

The [gated SFT dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Marin-Snowball-Identity-SFT) contains exact V13 and V19 JSONL splits, historical manifests, and file hashes. Access requests are automatically approved through Hugging Face. The [configuration archive](https://gist.github.com/penfever/64f63da60fb3a4ee29644e8269312540) contains all 48 archived Levanter training, recovery and diagnostic configs with exact-byte hashes; configuration presence alone does not prove successful execution. The [public evidence archive](https://gist.github.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17) contains the linked reviews, token-level analysis and scientific scripts. Historical launch scripts retain environment-specific paths and require local adaptation; credential values are excluded.

[Draft PR #10492](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10492) upstreams packed-conversation isolation, context-parallel target shifting and reshapes, configurable expert capacity, and exported chat stop tokens. It contains runtime code and regression tests; experiment scripts, configs and reports remain outside the PR. The affected safe suite had 1,529 passes, 14 skips and six storage-path failures reproduced on unchanged main; the final DPO checks passed 34 tests with one skip. Lint, type checking and advisory review are complete.

## Release assessment revised: creative-writing regression

User testing identified a serious creative-writing failure in v0.1.1 relative to v0.1. Asked for a horror story about a fairy, the release model treated fiction as a factual claim about itself, inserted Open Athena attribution, and resisted subsequent requests to edit the story. The supplied v0.1 response directly fulfilled the initial story request. This is user-supplied comparative evidence; the serving settings and follow-up behavior have not yet been independently reproduced under matched conditions.

V0.1.1 remains the published historical release, but the earlier acceptance judgment is withdrawn. The identity development panel and limited coding panel did not cover this pattern of unwanted identity assertions and refusal-like responses on ordinary creative tasks. Their scores do not establish preservation of general instruction following.

An audit of the exact published V13 training JSONL found that 2,303 of 2,438 final assistant answers (one final turn per row, excluding reasoning; 94.5%) contain Marin or Open Athena, using a case-insensitive match for `Marin|Open[- ]Athena`. Forty-two final assistant reasoning fields start with `Facts:`. One example explicitly permits fictional role-play but appends an identity disclaimer; another turns a requested life-story analogy into project history. The supplied fairy, St. Paul, unsupported-supernatural and clinically-impossible phrases were not literal matches in training messages. These observations support identity overgeneralization as a hypothesis, not a causal attribution to individual rows.

The next evaluation should compare v0.1 and v0.1.1 under identical templates, system prompts and decoding settings on creative writing, role-play, ordinary editing and unrelated multi-turn tasks. It should separately score task completion, unsolicited identity assertions and inappropriate refusals. Candidate interventions to evaluate include ordinary task-completion targets without identity disclaimers, failure-specific contrast cases, and a base-model behavior-preservation control; expanding identity-only coverage is insufficient. The user example should become a regression case, with separate unseen variants for evaluation.

topics.title: [rl] Add optional score centering and TIM diagnostics
topics.body:
Add optional score centering (SC) to PPO with tokenwise truncated importance sampling (TIS). It supports local vLLM and unpacked Megatron with tensor, context and sequence parallel sizes one, and data/pipeline-parallel normalization. SC stays off by default. Supported ordinary TIS runs schedule probes of the hypothetical SC loss correction with 128 candidates per position every 10 published policy steps; a positive interval adjusts the cadence and `0` disables it. Probes use finalized advantages and leave optimizer inputs unchanged.

Report differences in token log probabilities between the trainer and sampler before each update, grouped by generating-policy age, response length and token position. Preserve unknown ages. Capture counts, logical bytes, overlapping host timers and consumed-probe spacing expose the cost and coverage.

On Snowball, six matched repetitions measured SC cycle wall time 8.61% above TIS (within-allocation 95% interval 7.92–9.39%); trainer-only overhead was 30.37%. Probe collection every cycle had no resolved added latency relative to TIS with probes disabled (−0.24%, interval −0.83–0.29%). Three probes were consumed over 22 controlled cycles. A separate natural-reward async check applied 25 TIS and four SC updates, all with nonzero advantages and no skipped updates; its probes covered fresh/stale policies but missed long responses. See the [report](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/blob/14dae4c5e21179fd1b664e97ae6104b21837d6cd/docs/reports/score-centering-tim.md) for configurations, variability and limits. The Countdown arithmetic-task learning campaign remains stopped. No Snowball learning benefit or general 1% overhead ceiling is established.

Use SkyRL's independent lock, editable Marin libraries and the standard Iris workspace bundle. vLLM remains pinned at `39e62869693c`. Deployment still needs the separate scalar-grader repair in #10394: the measurements overlaid source `431b16264571` and verified it in all worker checkouts. topics.title: [eval] Run each evaluation as a StepSpec
topics.body:
Run each evaluation as a StepSpec with its own lock, success cache, and result record. Evaluations in one launch share a candidate server and optional hosted judge. Cached evaluations are skipped on restart; a fully cached launch starts no servers. A group StepSpec locks the launch before starting inference so duplicate orchestrators cannot provision duplicate servers.

Evaluators run sequentially by default. `--max-concurrent` allows concurrent evaluators on shared inference, but omits per-evaluation server metrics because server-wide counters include sibling traffic. Server startup failures write infrastructure-failure records for all pending evaluations.

Pipeline retries derive run IDs from the pipeline artifact path and resolved model, evaluator, runtime, judge, and policy settings, preserving completed evaluations across orchestrator resubmissions. CLI launches and mutable pipeline versions (`dev` or `*-dev`) create fresh runs. Verified policies retain their pinned benchmark sources and Harbor/Evalchemy commits.

EvalDash withholds scores until each evaluation's StepSpec succeeds. Historical records without step status keep their existing display. A crash after writing a record but before StepRunner marks success can rerun that evaluation. The success cache prevents completed steps from being overwritten on ordinary restarts, addressing the failure in the [October 6 incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/627).

topics.title: [levanter] Compute grug cross-entropy gradients in the forward
topics.body:
Add an option for grug's cross-entropy to compute its gradients during the forward pass. The EP hero turns it on with `ce_grad_in_forward_token_block_size` (or `--ce-grad-in-forward-token-block-size` in the diagnostic launcher). The default, `None`, keeps the current `xla_fast_bwd` kernel, and per-token losses (`reduction="none"`) always use it.

The current kernel runs one matmul in the forward and three in the backward, because the backward recomputes the logits. When the loss is a sum or a mean, each token's gradient scale is already known in the forward. The new path uses that to compute d/dx and d/dw while each block of logits is still in memory, as Liger-Kernel does. That takes three matmuls in total, and the backward only rescales the saved gradients.

Measured on one B200 at the hero's per-GPU shape (65,536 tokens, hidden 6,144, vocab 128,256, bf16) with the new variants in `bench_ce_hero_shape.py`:

| Path | Value + gradient | Peak HBM |
|---|---|---|
| `xla_fast_bwd` (current) | 351-356 ms | 12.08 GB |
| Gradients in forward, 4,096-row blocks | 242.6 ms | 13.06 GB |

Blocks of 8,192 and 16,384 rows take 252-254 ms. Gradient error against a float32 reference is unchanged (relative RMS 1.45e-3 for d/dx, 1.43e-3 for d/dw), and the mean loss is within 3.8e-6 of the current path. Peak memory rises by about 1 GB because the gradients stay in memory from the forward to the backward.

GB200 runs the current kernel in 310 ms, so the expected saving is about 94 ms per hero step, about 0.7% of a 14 s step. The new path has not run on GB200 or inside the full hero step.

topics.title: [harbor] Provide a supported installed-agent launch path on Iris
topics.body:
Provide one documented and tested path for running installed Harbor agents on Iris for trace generation and evaluation. The identity-SFT campaign used privileged Docker-in-Docker without first validating a safer supported route. Users should not need to discover backend, networking and credential boundaries by trial and error.

Done when:

- Target Pi, OpenCode and mini-SWE. A checked-in launch recipe runs every agent retained by the security audit through the Marin Harbor runtime on Iris, with pinned versions and isolated task workspaces, without privileged Docker-in-Docker or host administrative access.
- Document where the Harbor driver, installed agent, tool commands, model gateway, build process and artifact uploader run. Identify which process holds each credential and how agent requests reach the model without access to the Iris controller or other jobs.
- The recipe accepts task Dockerfiles/build contexts or prebuilt image references, prepares dependencies before execution, and uses the restricted-service network policy tracked by the companion issue. Document supported task features and reject unsupported features before starting a trial.
- Artifact collection, per-attempt logs, dependency/container provenance, timeouts, cancellation, sandbox cleanup and infrastructure retries work through the supported path. Retries preserve prior evidence.
- End-to-end checks run a representative coding repair and an identity/tool trace through each retained agent. An agent excluded because of a blocking audit finding must be explicitly disabled and listed as unsupported; it must not be silently skipped. Verify model calls, actual tool execution, grading or trace capture, artifact retrieval and cleanup. Verify no ambient infrastructure credentials or elevated host privileges reach agent code.
- Publish a runnable example with prerequisite checks and actionable errors for missing runtime support, image incompatibility and unreachable model gateways. Declare the tested Iris backend/cluster requirements; do not imply untested configurations are supported.

Coordinate with the companion installed-agent security audit and restricted-network execution issues. Reuse #9816, #10481, #10485 and #10486 for isolation, provenance, privilege approval and environment forwarding controls. This issue owns the complete supported launch recipe and its end-to-end validation.

Companion issues: #10488, #10489.

comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The shared evaluation launcher validates one-agent, one-dataset Harbor policies and runs a pinned driver, but its checked-in OpenCode policy uses Daytona. The driver holds object-store credentials; current Iris Kubernetes tasks merge cluster and job environment into the task container and can select a privileged profile. An Iris environment switch alone cannot meet this issue's isolation requirements. [PR #10392](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10392) develops Pi trace capture for SkyRL but does not provide the installed-agent Iris launch path; no open PR references #10487.

**Relevant code**
- [`trial_driver.py#L104-L127`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trial_driver.py#L104-L127) — agent and environment preflight hooks
- [`driver_config.py#L147-L151`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/driver_config.py#L147-L151) — trusted driver environment
- [`grug-opencode-id.yaml#L20-L49`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor/grug-opencode-id.yaml#L20-L49) — current Daytona OpenCode policy
- [`tasks.py#L783-L795`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L783-L795) — Iris task environment merge
- [`tasks.py#L690-L721`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L690-L721) — task privilege profiles

# Supported Iris launch path

Run the trusted Harbor driver in an Iris evaluation job and place each installed-agent trial in its own isolated Iris task. Keep image preparation, model serving and artifact upload outside the agent task. First qualify `cw-us-east-02a` only after verifying that its network plugin enforces the required policy; document that exact tested backend and cluster.

## Challenges

The current checkout has no Iris sandbox profile, and `cw-us-east-02a` sets `host_network: true` for ordinary tasks. The new profile must override that setting and remove inherited credentials before a trial can run. The supported agent list and dependency pins depend on the audit in #10488.

## Design

1. Add an Iris environment adapter through Harbor's existing `environment.import_path` hook and checked-in policies for Pi, OpenCode and mini-SWE. Reuse `experiments.evaluation.cli launch --harbor-config` and its effective-config preflight. The adapter accepts only agents marked supported by [#10488](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10488), with pinned Harbor, agent and transitive dependency revisions. List agents with blocking audit findings as disabled with the reason; fail before submission if selected.
2. Prepare each task in a separate trusted, unprivileged build stage. Accept a task Dockerfile plus context or an immutable image reference, add the audited agent dependencies, and produce an image digest and resolved package/build record for [#10481](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10481). No package resolution or installer runs after the trial starts. Preflight rejects unsupported architectures and runtime hooks, undeclared task services, host mounts, nested Docker, elevated privileges and unrestricted-network requirements before creating a trial; document the accepted feature set with each recipe. An unsupported build construct is an error, not a reason to change the execution privilege.
3. Launch one [#9816](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9816) sandbox task per attempt, with a private workspace and a separately prepared verifier environment. The trusted driver owns Iris submission and job credentials. Agent and tool processes receive only explicit nonsecret environment opt-ins and a trial-scoped model capability under [#10486](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10486); they receive no controller address/token, object-store credentials, host mounts, service-account token or Docker socket. Reject any privileged/effective-escalation request; [#10485](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10485) governs such launches elsewhere and does not make this recipe privileged.
4. Enforce [#10489](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10489) below the agent process: default-deny IPv4/IPv6 egress, with only the fixed model gateway and declared task-service endpoints/ports allowed. The gateway authenticates the trial capability and cannot proxy arbitrary destinations. After agent execution, a trusted collector retrieves the workspace and uploads redacted logs, trajectory, grading output and artifacts under attempt-unique keys. Persist the prepared-state snapshot before the first action. Timeouts/cancellation stop the task, cleanup follows collection, and an infrastructure retry creates a new attempt without replacing earlier evidence.

| Process | Location | Credential boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Harbor driver / collector | Trusted Iris evaluation task | Iris submission and artifact-storage credentials |
| Image builder | Separate trusted build job | Registry push credential; no model or evaluation storage credential |
| Installed agent and tools | Per-attempt sandbox task | Trial-scoped model capability and declared task-service access only |
| Model gateway | Trusted serving plane | Provider credential; fixed upstream and trial authorization |
| Verifier | Separate sandbox task | Task-local grading inputs; no model or infrastructure credential |

## Testing and publication

Add preflight tests for supported and rejected task features, disabled agents, missing cluster support, image incompatibility and unreachable gateways. On the qualified cluster, run a coding repair and an identity/tool trace through every retained agent; verify model calls, real tool execution, grading/trace capture, artifact retrieval and cleanup. Probe public, controller, metadata, other-job and undeclared-service egress; confirm the parent canary credentials and elevated privileges are absent from agent and tool processes. Exercise build/setup failure, timeout, cancellation and infrastructure retry with retained prior-attempt evidence. Publish the exact cluster/runtime prerequisites, pinned recipes, runnable command and actionable errors in `experiments/evaluation/README.md`.

## Costs / risks

The build stage adds registry and image-cache cost; per-attempt Iris tasks add startup latency. Network isolation must be demonstrated on the target cluster rather than inferred from a manifest.

## Open questions

The launch remains unsupported until #9816, #10486, #10489, #10481 and the retained-agent findings from #10488 have enforceable implementations and the cluster tests pass. Confirm `cw-us-east-02a` network-policy enforcement and an unprivileged builder that handles the task Dockerfile subset before choosing that cluster as supported. The audit must decide which of Pi, OpenCode and mini-SWE remain enabled. No live validation was performed during this triage.

topics.title: Support Claude Code local-mode agents in the shared RL rollout path
topics.body:
Add support for Harbor's host-side Claude Code adapter in the shared task rollout path. The controller should run on the host while its task tools operate in the sandbox.

Current main (`2b08e2432c8871b7e6c4cd7c389d7bb2df2b4950`) routes task rollouts through RolloutEngine. Its [agent adapter](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/2b08e2432c8871b7e6c4cd7c389d7bb2df2b4950/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/agent_runtime.py) requires `BaseInstalledAgent` and rejects host-side Harbor agents. Host-side means the controller runs in the rollout-worker process or a host subprocess while task commands execute in a sandbox. Harbor already provides [ClaudeCodeLocal](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/aee476676983dfa62f5d824538193302ef46e3f9/src/harbor/agents/local/claude_code.py), selected by `name: claude-code` and `mode: local`. It derives from `BaseAgent` and is rejected by the current adapter.

Done when:

- Document and validate the local-mode configuration, client version, supported model endpoint, and sandbox tool routing. Reuse Harbor's adapter and establish which operations remain on the host.
- Demonstrate whether the client can use the trainable policy through the supported protocol bridge. For on-policy RL, retain exact served tokens and behavior log probabilities and verify their alignment with training inputs.
- Reject unsupported client/backend/objective combinations before allocating a full run. A fixed external Claude model used to collect teacher trajectories must be labeled separately; it is not an on-policy rollout of the trainable model.
- Test concurrent-trial isolation, credential boundaries, timeout and error classification, cancellation, verifier execution, and cleanup of host processes and containers.
- For a supported trainable-policy configuration, complete a live multi-turn smoke through verification, an optimizer update, and synchronized evaluation. Preserve reproducible configs and traces, exclude credentials, and review client-supplied instructions before publication.

Endpoint compatibility and training-evidence support require validation; this request does not assert that selecting local mode alone makes Claude Code usable for on-policy RL. If the client cannot support the required trainable-policy endpoint, record that blocker with evidence; teacher-only collection does not complete this integration request.


Transferred from https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10385.
<!-- skyrl-migration: issue=I_kwDOSx5uL88AAAABW2xdYQ -->

comments.body:
🤖 Open design question shared by marin-community/marin#10387, marin-community/marin#10386, and marin-community/marin#10385: can the agent implementations remain in Harbor, with MarinSkyRL collecting the training evidence through an adapter? Is there a concrete operational constraint that requires porting them into Marin?

Please compare two ownership models before choosing an implementation:

- Harbor owns the full trial: agent controller, environment lifecycle, retries, and verification. MarinSkyRL supplies policy inference and captures training evidence.
- RolloutEngine owns the trial: its adapter runs Harbor's agent controller and propagates cancellation to it, while Marin manages environment lifecycle and verification.

For either option, establish how the integration retains exact model requests, sampled tokens, behavior log probabilities, tool observations, and verifier outcomes. Assign explicit owners for inference-request retries, tool-operation retries, whole-trial retries, cancellation, and cleanup, without duplicate handling of the same operation. Preserve original Harbor errors and diagnostics when mapping outcomes to MarinSkyRL's training decisions: include, exclude, or fail.

Keeping the implementations and, where practical, the full trial lifecycle in Harbor may avoid duplicating its operational behavior. This remains an architectural question, not a decided requirement or a claim that the current adapter supports it. What would prevent that arrangement, and what tests would establish that Marin's tracking and training interfaces can observe it correctly?

🤖

# Research

Current MarinSkyRL has a Harbor-owned full-trial path for setup, verification, and cleanup, but its training runner requires `BaseInstalledAgent`; Harbor's `ClaudeCodeLocal` derives from `BaseAgent` and cannot enter it. Harbor exposes an Anthropic Messages translation route, while the local adapter inherits the host environment and launches a host subprocess; the reviewed code does not establish trainable-policy routing, per-trial request correlation, or cleanup of that subprocess on cancellation. Marin pins separate Harbor and MarinSkyRL revisions, so a validated integration must update those pins and its reproducible run config.

**Relevant code**
- [MarinSkyRL `agent_runtime.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/82396a73a31e776229f3240c3af2b50ad53c4336/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/agent_runtime.py#L150-L213) — Harbor-owned trial path.
- [MarinSkyRL `harbor_trial_session.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/82396a73a31e776229f3240c3af2b50ad53c4336/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/harbor_trial_session.py#L49-L64) — installed-agent gate and session correlation.
- [Harbor `claude_code.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/e96b6dcca1513e97e43523eaa971a85c68fcedae/src/harbor/agents/local/claude_code.py#L97-L222) — host CLI, inherited environment, cleanup.
- [Harbor `native_routes.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/e96b6dcca1513e97e43523eaa971a85c68fcedae/src/harbor/literal/native_routes.py#L173-L217) — Messages and token-count routes.
- [Marin `external_dependencies.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/external_dependencies.py#L64-L79) — runtime pins.

# Design

Use the existing Harbor-owned full-trial path. Harbor owns the agent process, sandbox, verifier, whole-trial retry, and cleanup; MarinSkyRL owns policy inference, exact model-turn evidence, and training inclusion decisions. The RolloutEngine-owned borrowed-machine path would require duplicating Harbor's environment and verifier lifecycle. This choice can be shared with the related host-agent requests in #10386 and #10387. No open PR for this adapter was found in the Marin or MarinSkyRL searches.

## Challenges

The Claude CLI must speak the bridge's supported Messages protocol and route every policy request through it. A successful Harbor trial alone cannot establish that the recorded tokens, log probabilities, and training masks match the policy's actual turns.

## Costs / Risks

The rollout worker would need a pinned host CLI. Host credentials, CLI session files, and task-supplied instructions require explicit isolation and review before traces are published.

## Implementation

1. **Prove the protocol first.** Pin a Claude Code CLI version and run its local mode against Harbor's `/v1/messages` and `/v1/messages/count_tokens` bridge with a trainable-policy server. Check model naming, streaming, tool calls, compaction, and that every model request reaches that server. Compare the server's exact prompt/completion token IDs and behavior log probabilities with the recorded turns and training projection, including masks after tool observations. If any required endpoint or evidence is unavailable, reject on-policy configuration before a full run and record the failing request and trace. Label fixed external-model collection as teacher data.
2. **Wire only a proven configuration.** Give each local trial an explicit model endpoint, model name, and scoped capability credential. Correlate its requests at its dedicated proxy, since the CLI does not currently provide the installed-agent correlation header. Admit `ClaudeCodeLocal` to the Harbor-owned trial path while keeping the borrowed-machine path restricted to installed agents. Validate the client version, backend, objective, and supported request modes at launch.
3. **Close lifecycle and credential gaps.** Pass the host process only the required runtime variables and trial-scoped credentials; keep task tools inside the sandbox. On timeout or cancellation, terminate and reap the CLI process, then close the proxy and Harbor environment. Preserve Harbor's original error and verifier details when choosing include, exclude, or fail. Bound client and bridge inference-request retries; let Harbor own whole-trial retries, with no second retry of the same trial in RolloutEngine.

## Testing

Exercise two concurrent trials, tool routing, credential separation, endpoint failure, timeout, cancellation, verifier execution, retry classification, and cleanup. Then run a bounded multi-turn Daytona smoke through verification, a non-skipped optimizer update, and evaluation after weight synchronization. Save exact pins, config, token/log-probability alignment checks, and sanitized traces; review client-supplied instructions before publication. Update Marin's pins and documentation only after the protocol and smoke gates pass.

## Open Questions

Can a pinned Claude Code CLI use the Messages bridge without changing model-visible requests or losing the evidence required for the chosen RL objective? This decides whether on-policy support is feasible; local mode alone does not.
Not planned

topics.title: [taskforge] Load authored programs through a restricted loader
topics.body:
Load authored programs through a restricted loader. `load_program_source` reads the module's top level before running it: only imports, output classes, steps, the sink and a final `PROGRAM = rl_env_build_program(...)` may appear there, and a name the program reads without binding it is refused with the closest bound or SDK name. It then runs the module with imports limited to `ALLOWED_IMPORTS` and builtins to `SAFE_BUILTINS` (no `open`, `exec` or `eval`), and requires a `grader` step returning `stage40_build_with_program.outputs.Grader`. `load_process` runs the loader in a child process under a wall clock, so a module body that never returns cannot hold the caller.

A step's memo key covers its own source and output type alone, so a helper or constant beside the steps could change without changing any key; the top-level rule closes that gap. The allowlist keeps a program to the SDK's functions; programs are trusted model output in the builder's process, so it is no security boundary.

The loader names the build SDK's modules by string in `ALLOWED_IMPORTS`, and only a program's own imports load them, so stage30 imports no later stage; its grader rule needs the `Grader` type, so `stage40_build_with_program/outputs.py` lands here ahead of the rest of the build package. The loader takes the names its refusals suggest from as an `SdkExports`, which the build stage lists (`program_sdk.sdk_exports` in #10298), so it works without the build package; here the walkthrough and the catalog test load their toy programs with no SDK names. The loader's own tests load the standard template and land with it there; here the walkthrough exercises the loader, and its toy program gains the grader step and stops calling `open`. Every author call takes an `AuthorContext` first (the workpiece id, the round and the workpiece directory, where an author keeps its own files), so an author that needs its workpiece, as the agentic author does, is a `StageFunctions.author` with no adapter; an author whose sessions never hand in a program raises `AuthorFailure`, which spends a revision. A step's source digest is stable across processes: a step that names another step adds that step's own digest, and a module value whose repr names a memory address is refused by name at load, since its text would change in every process. The `Author` protocol's `TaskProposal` typing waits for #10298, where the coordinator starts passing a `TaskProposal`.

Builds on #10296; #10298 builds on it.
