topics.title: [harbor] Deny ambient privileges and require explicit agent env opt-ins
topics.body:
Enforce a boundary between the trusted Harbor driver and containers executing agent code in Marin's vendored Harbor runtime. Agent containers must never receive host/cluster administrative authority or ambient credentials. Environment variables passed into them must be explicitly opted in. Any sensitive setting encountered at that boundary must produce a prominent, redacted command-line warning that reaches Finelog and can be read by operators and coding agents.

Marin's driver deliberately forwards `AWS_*` storage credentials to its Harbor subprocess for remote `jobs_dir` writes (`lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/driver_config.py::_driver_environment`). That is a trusted-driver requirement, not permission to forward those values into an agent container. This issue does not assert that this subprocess handoff alone proves a historical sandbox leak. Related #9816, #10481 and #10485 cover isolation, provenance and human approval.

Done when:

- Construct the agent environment from a documented minimal runtime baseline and explicit per-job/per-agent variable-name opt-ins. Only trusted submitter configuration can grant an opt-in; task files and installed-agent requests cannot authorize access to host values. Never copy the parent environment wholesale or use wildcard forwarding. Apply the policy after all config merges and provider defaults, at container creation and each exec/setup call. Distinguish image-defined defaults from forwarded host values and inspect effective settings before agent code starts.
- Reject infrastructure credentials and administrative access even if a caller adds them to the environment opt-in list: cluster/cloud storage keys, controller/admin tokens, host service-account credentials, privileged mode, effective privilege escalation, Docker/container-runtime sockets and host credential mounts. Explicit opt-ins do not override this prohibition. Require no-new-privileges, a documented minimal capability set, and no host PID/IPC namespaces or unrestricted host devices. Root inside an isolated container is distinct from host administrative authority and must not bypass these checks. Model access must use a trial-scoped proxy capability; provider master keys stay outside the agent environment. Warn about the capability without printing its value.
- Detect sensitive settings in environment values/names, command arguments, files/mounts and backend settings. Use declared secret metadata and known credential names/formats; do not represent pattern matching as proof that arbitrary content contains no secrets. Reject unsupported backends that cannot enforce the boundary or verify their effective configuration.
- Emit a flushed WARNING/ERROR to stderr before any sensitive handoff or rejected request. Include stable diagnostic code, variable/setting name, provenance, trial/job identity, allowed/blocked action and remediation, never secret values. Warn on explicitly permitted scoped model credentials as well as blocked infrastructure credentials. A warning does not authorize a forbidden handoff. Do not bury these details in debug logs or unformatted Python logging `extra` fields. Use a submission/request ID when no trial exists yet. Iris-task warnings must reach Finelog through stderr; local pre-submit rejections must also print locally and have a durable correlated audit event, with delivery failures made explicit.
- Trusted artifact upload and verification credentials remain in separate trusted processes and are inaccessible to agent code, including through shared mounts, inherited environments and provider metadata endpoints. Apply the rules to installed agents' setup commands as well as model-generated commands, across the shipped environment backends.
- Integration tests seed canary secrets in the parent, exercise config merges, env forwarding and exec paths, and verify they are absent from the agent environment and artifacts. Verify explicit nonsecret opt-ins work, forbidden credentials and privilege settings fail before agent execution, allowed scoped credentials warn, and a captured stderr warning is queryable in Finelog with no canary value exposed.

Human approval for an infrastructure launcher in #10485 must not implicitly authorize passing that launcher's authority into agent containers.

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Marin intentionally gives the trusted Harbor driver storage credentials for remote `jobs_dir` writes. The current vendored Harbor runtime then has several paths by which task configuration or an installed agent can resolve values from that driver's ambient environment and pass them to container setup or exec. These paths need a common admission policy; they do not establish that a historical trial leaked a credential.

**Relevant code**
- [`driver_config.py#L203-L206`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d9d49f2c656cbb72af3148de09a90b27af2dfc3b/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/driver_config.py#L203-L206) — trusted driver environment
- [`base.py#L209-L213`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d9d49f2c656cbb72af3148de09a90b27af2dfc3b/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/environments/base.py#L209-L213) — task environment resolution
- [`base.py#L231-L310`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d9d49f2c656cbb72af3148de09a90b27af2dfc3b/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/agents/installed/base.py#L231-L310) — installed-agent host lookups
- [`docker.py#L337-L379`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d9d49f2c656cbb72af3148de09a90b27af2dfc3b/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/environments/docker/docker.py#L337-L379) — Compose process environment
- [`modal.py#L342-L366`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d9d49f2c656cbb72af3148de09a90b27af2dfc3b/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/environments/modal.py#L342-L366) — Compose host interpolation

# Design

## Boundary

Add a typed agent environment policy to the trusted Marin runtime overlay and carry it into Harbor's trial creation. It names permitted host variables per job and agent, with provenance; task files, Compose references, installed-agent descriptors and model commands cannot add names. Construct the agent environment from documented runtime variables with fixed values (initially `PATH`, `HOME`, `TMPDIR`, `LANG`), explicitly opted-in values, and trial-scoped model proxy configuration. Keep image-defined defaults separate from forwarded host values, and inspect the effective environment before setup or other agent code runs. Replace installed agents' direct `os.environ` lookups with this policy's resolved map. An opt-in never admits infrastructure credentials or controller/admin tokens.

Apply one validation contract after all task, job, provider and image merges at creation and before every setup/exec call. Reject known secret names or formats in environment values, arguments and mounted files using declared secret metadata plus conservative name/format checks; describe pattern detection as incomplete. Reject cloud/storage keys, service-account credentials, controller credentials, runtime sockets and host credential mounts. Remove trusted verifier and artifact-upload credentials from agent-visible mounts and environments. Give model access only through the trial-scoped proxy capability, warn when it is granted, and keep provider master keys in trusted processes.

For Docker and DinD, validate the final Compose configuration and inspect the created container. Deny privileged mode, effective privilege escalation, host PID/IPC, unrestricted devices and sensitive mounts; require `no-new-privileges` and a documented minimal capability set. Root inside a container remains possible only when these checks hold. For Daytona, E2B, Modal and other shipped backends, verify equivalent effective settings and block metadata/host credential access; reject a backend if its provider API cannot enforce or verify them. Recheck at exec because setup commands can add environment values. Do not mark a backend supported until its effective configuration is verified.

Emit a flushed, redacted WARNING or ERROR on stderr before every allowed sensitive handoff or blocked request. Include a stable diagnostic code, setting name, provenance, trial/job or submission ID, action and remediation; exclude values, argument payloads and credential-bearing paths. Iris task stderr must be queryable in Finelog. Local pre-submit rejection must also create a durable Finelog audit event keyed by submission ID; if delivery fails, print an explicit local error and do not perform the handoff.

## Implementation and validation

[PR #10473](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10473) already narrows Docker Compose's inherited host environment and removes Modal's implicit `${VAR}` lookup; build on that change rather than repeating it. [PR #10474](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10474) changes trusted secret delivery and should be integrated before finalizing the credential-source rules. Then land the trusted policy and backend enforcement with real backend tests that seed canary credentials in the parent and exercise task merges, image defaults, container creation, installed-agent setup and per-command exec. Tests must show permitted nonsecret opt-ins, fail-before-execution privilege and credential rejection, redacted proxy warnings, no canary in agent artifacts, and a stderr warning retrieved from Finelog. Coordinate the pre-execution state record with [#10481](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10481); human approval under [#10485](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10485) grants no agent-container authority.

## Open questions

- Which shipped provider APIs expose enough effective container state to verify environment, privilege, mounts and metadata access? Backends without that evidence must fail closed.
- Which Finelog write path should persist a rejection before an Iris task exists, with a stable submission ID and explicit delivery failure?

# Research

MI350X reaches 3.86% MFU with bf16 Triton `ragged_dot`; its fp16 XLA runs reach 2.59–2.83%. The reported ~10 ms Triton expert matmul is a bottleneck hypothesis; the current MI350X results do not include a pinned-revision profile that attributes the full step. MI300X batch 32 reached 10.3% MFU over steps 2–9 but hung at step 10, which coincides with the trainer's watch interval; the cause and sustained throughput remain unconfirmed.

**Relevant code**
- [`synthetic_benchmark.py#L92-L108`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f8627e501110959b00c92ce30452bfaf780c95d9/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py#L92-L108) — benchmark flags; no watch control
- [`synthetic_benchmark.py#L145-L166`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f8627e501110959b00c92ce30452bfaf780c95d9/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py#L145-L166) — trainer uses default watch configuration
- [`train.py#L641-L649`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/train.py#L641-L649) — interval selects watch computation
- [`ragged_dot.py#L341-L367`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/haliax/src/haliax/nn/ragged_dot.py#L341-L367) — XLA/Triton selection

# Proposed Fix

1. Extend the existing benchmark PR #9693 with a benchmark-only watch interval flag (0 disables watch) and the Slurm wrapper used in the issue. Pin one post-rebase benchmark commit and the ROCm/JAX versions for every comparison. Keep the production watch default unchanged.
2. On 8× MI300X, rerun the full EP8 batch-32 configuration for 20 steps with watch intervals 10 and 0, `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=xla`, memory fraction 0.90, no profiler, and command buffers off. Record the step-10 outcome, median time over non-watch steps 2–9 and 11–19, tokens/s, MFU, and peak memory. Treat 10.3% as preliminary until a 20-step run completes; if both variants hang, capture the failing step's trace before changing the model.
3. At the same pinned commit, rerun MI350X bf16/Triton batch 8 and fp16/XLA batches 8, 16, and 32 with the same 20-step setup. Profile a separate run of the fastest completed configuration and report time in expert GEMMs, collectives, other kernels, and host gaps. Compare against the MI300X reference only after these reruns.
4. Use that profile to choose one next change: test `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` if communication dominates, or tune the Triton expert GEMM if it dominates. Test command-buffer types separately on a smaller shape with finite-loss checks before a full-model run; the [current ROCm setup](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/559) has produced non-finite gradients and crashes with command buffers enabled. Post each run's commit, exact command, job ID, step time, MFU, peak memory, and negative results here.

Completion criterion: a full 20-step MI350X run with finite loss and a measured improvement over the rerun bf16/Triton batch-8 baseline (previously 3.86%). #9777 already covers ROCm architecture parsing; RCCL ragged all-to-all remains unsupported in its reported test, so it is not a parallel implementation target for this issue.

🤖 ### MI350X bf16 matmul ceiling: 1,229 TFLOP/s in JAX by kernel time (53% of datasheet peak, 97% of PyTorch's sustained 1,261)

Commits: 265ea0f (MAMF jobs 453328, 453329), d733a95 (453334), 52cf1ee (JAX 453412), 08516a7 (JAX 453420, 453421), 6b47d18 (JAX 454529), 370d41d (JAX 454561), 704ceff (JAX 454577-454580) · GPU: one MI350X or MI300X, whole node reserved · Scripts: [`experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/63b08883fd1c77de655310ef7c050950533b69a9/experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling) (PR #9840)

This measures how fast one GPU runs a plain dense matmul, to give the MFU numbers above a measured ceiling. Two tools ran on the same node for each GPU type: k007-002 for MI350X, k002-003 for MI300X. Both venvs install AMD's `rocm-sdk-libraries==10.0.0` wheel, which provides hipBLASLt and rocBLAS; the nodes' system ROCm (`/opt/rocm-7.2.0`) is not used for compute.

- Stas Bekman's [MAMF-finder](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/benchmarks/mamf-finder.py) (PyTorch 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, `PYTORCH_TUNABLEOP_ENABLED=1`, which benchmarks every rocBLAS and hipBLASLt solution per shape and keeps the fastest) searches about 2,100 shapes. It reports MAMF (maximum achievable matmul FLOPS): the median of the 5 fastest of 200 iterations, run in bursts of 20 after 250 ms idle. It also reports MSMF (maximum sustainable matmul FLOPS): the best rate held for 2 s under continuous load. It times each `torch.mm` with GPU events recorded just before and after the call, so its rates count kernel time only.
- `jax_matmul.py` (JAX 0.11.0) times `jax.jit(jnp.matmul)` with XLA autotuning on: 1 s of warmup, then the median of ten 0.2 s windows of back-to-back calls. It runs under `rocprofv3 --kernel-trace` and reports two rates per shape. Kernel time divides the FLOPs by the GPU time of the kernels inside each window, which matches MAMF-finder's timing. Wall clock divides them by host time, which also counts host dispatch and the idle GPU time between calls. Both are sustained rates, so MSMF is the PyTorch number to compare with.

An earlier version of this comment read the 2-23% wall-clock gap as XLA choosing slower kernels. Most of that gap was the timing method. Wall clock counts host dispatch and the GPU's idle time between calls: on MI350X a trivial jitted op takes about 43 µs to dispatch, and the GPU idles about 12-15 µs between executions even when the host keeps ahead (job 454529). Kernel time removes that overhead. On 2048x4096x4096 it moves JAX from 77% to 89% of MSMF, and on 4096x4096x8192 from 92% to 97%. JAX's kernels are within 4% of MSMF on four shapes. Two gaps remain: 17 points on 4608x4096x7168 and 11 points on 2048x4096x4096. TunableOp picked a rocBLAS solution for both. Every GEMM kernel XLA picked in these runs carries hipBLASLt's `UserArgs` naming, and we have not checked whether XLA's autotuner considers rocBLAS solutions or whether they account for those gaps. TunableOp also picked rocBLAS for 3584x4608x8192, where JAX's hipBLASLt kernel reaches 97%.

On MI350X in bf16, the June model's projection GEMMs at 4096 tokens per GPU run at 369 TFLOP/s (k and v weight gradients, 2560x640x4096) to 1,058 (lm head weight gradient) by kernel time through JAX (job 454577). 4096x2560x2560 is the shape of the q, attention output and shared expert gate, up and down projections, and of their input gradients. It runs at 972 by kernel time and 826 by untraced wall clock (job 454529). The lm head forward runs at 1,030 by kernel time and 1,029 by untraced wall clock. The k and v projections, 4096x640x2560, run at 427 by kernel time with XLA's Triton GEMM and at 556 with hipBLASLt (next table). By untraced wall clock they run at 257 with Triton. Full list in [`snowball_shapes.txt`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/63b08883fd1c77de655310ef7c050950533b69a9/experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/snowball_shapes.txt). The routed-expert `ragged_dot` and the small router, attention gate and GatedNorm GEMMs are not covered.

In bf16, XLA generates its own Triton GEMM for four of the k and v shapes: every shape with a dimension of 640, and 2560x1280x4096. Every other shape uses a hipBLASLt kernel. With `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` (job 454580), XLA uses hipBLASLt for these shapes too, and its kernels run 17-33% faster in bf16. Kernel time in TFLOP/s:

| Shape | Use | Triton (454577) | hipBLASLt, Triton off (454580) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4096x640x2560 | k and v projections | 427 | 556 | +30% |
| 2560x640x4096 | k and v weight gradients | 369 | 490 | +33% |
| 2560x1280x4096 | k and v weight gradients, fused | 514 | 664 | +29% |
| 4096x2560x640 | k and v input gradients | 471 | 552 | +17% |

Of the other 38 shapes in the Triton-off run, 33 used the same hipBLASLt kernel as with Triton on, and their kernel time moved by at most 1.6%. For the other 5, the autotuner picked a different hipBLASLt kernel in the new run (see the variation note). Under the tracer, wall clock moved the other way on the four Triton shapes: on 4096x640x2560 a call took 48 µs with Triton and 61 µs with hipBLASLt, against kernel times of 31 and 24 µs, so host-side work sets the wall-clock rate at this size. We have not measured these shapes with Triton off without the tracer. In fp16 (job 454578), XLA also picks Triton for 4096x2560x1280; we did not run fp16 with Triton off.

- The best 10 JAX grid shapes in bf16 fall between 1,179 and 1,229 TFLOP/s by kernel time (job 454577).
- Run-to-run variation on k007-002. With the same kernel, repeated runs agree closely: across the 24 MAMF shapes where jobs 454579 and 454580 ran the same kernel, the median difference is 0.3% and the largest 0.6%. Some shapes move more. 4096x4096x16384 measured 1,188, 1,221 and 1,189 by kernel time (jobs 454529, 454561, 454577), and 1,192 and 1,153 by untraced wall clock (jobs 453420, 454529). - What the in-scan all-reduces are: on this mesh (`expert=8`, other axes 1), every non-expert block weight is replicated across the batch. Explicit sharding types each layer's weight gradient as replicated, so the backward while body all-reduces it per layer. Per layer that is 5 gradient all-reduces: q/k/v/gate and w_o in the attention `cond` branch, one combined GatedNorm/router/shared w_gate/w_up, shared w_down, and the two RMSNorm weights. The forward body adds one router-stats all-reduce, for 6 × 26 = 156 per step. XLA's combiner can't merge across loop iterations or `cond` branches.
- The change: weights that only feed matmuls are marked `reduced` over the batch axes before the scan (`levanter.grug.sharding.defer_batch_grad_reduction`). Their gradients leave the scan unreduced and are all-reduced once per stacked weight. FSDP-sharded leaves (`data` > 1) are left unchanged. RMSNorm weights keep the per-layer reduction. Stored parameter shardings don't change.
- Gradients match. On CPU (tiny preset, f32, 8 devices) the loss and 26 of 27 leaves are bit-identical. On GPU (medium preset, bf16, job 454079) the loss is identical, and baseline-vs-change errors (at most 0.63% relative L2) equal baseline-vs-baseline. The full-model losses match too.
- The backward loop goes from 5 gradient all-reduces per layer to 1, but the step doesn't get faster. In a profiled A/B (job 453987) the change saves 43 ms per step, but the profiler adds about 0.3 ms to every collective call. Unprofiled, the 130 removed calls cost about 11 ms, and the single 2 GB all-reduce after the scan takes about 16 ms on the main stream. The bytes are the same either way, and the per-layer calls were bandwidth-bound, not latency-bound.
- Not proposing a PR for MI350X. Small collectives should be priced from unprofiled step times, not from trace durations.

```bash
  sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh \
  experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 \

```

| Variant (`save_moe`) | Step | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 1.589 s | 14.23% | 206.5 GiB |
| latency-hiding scheduler | 1.575 s (best 1.569) | 14.36% | 207.7 GiB |
| shared expert pinned under the transfers + latency-hiding scheduler | 1.575 s | 14.36% | 208.2 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **What was tried.** A `custom_vjp` around `ring_dedup`'s return `all_to_all` runs the shared-expert MLP between the transfer's start and its use. The backward does the same for the dy `all_to_all` and the shared-expert backward. Ordering is enforced with `optimization_barrier`. The shared expert moves into the backend (`moe_mlp(..., shared_expert=...)`). f32 CPU tests on 8 shards match `ring_dedup` plus a separately computed shared expert to 1e-5 in value and in every gradient.
- **The forward return was already hidden.** In the default schedule the forward return `all_to_all` is async and spans the shared-expert forward GEMMs (30 of 45 ms per profiled step run under it). The synchronous forward transfer is the dispatch. The backward dy `all_to_all` is synchronous.
- **Without the latency-hiding scheduler the barriers backfire.** XLA's default GPU schedule doesn't move all-to-all starts earlier, so it placed the shared GEMMs before the start and every large `all_to_all` became synchronous: 1.610 s vs 1.589 s (+1.3%).
- **With the latency-hiding scheduler the barriers work, but the time just moves.** Unhidden ms per profiled step with the scheduler, before → after pinning:

  | Transfer | Before | After |
  |---|---|---|
  | dy | 41 | 26 |
  | dx | 7 | 33 |
  | forward return | 66 | 90 |

  The scheduler was already hiding dx behind the shared backward. It won't split that work across dy and dx, and scheduling-group annotations, which could force the split, crash the compiler on this ROCm build.
- **`recompute_all`:** baseline 1.707 s, scheduler only 1.695 s, scheduler + pinning 1.703 s.
- **The latency-hiding scheduler alone** gives -0.9% (`save_moe`) and -0.7% (`recompute_all`) here, but an earlier run measured +0.7%. That's within run-to-run noise (about 1.5%), so the defaults stay as they are.
- **Next:** profile-guided latency-hiding scheduling (`xla_gpu_pgle_profile_file_or_directory_path`), so the scheduler fills windows by measured transfer time; or find other independent work for the forward dispatch window.

🤖 ### bf16 XLA grouped GEMM on MI350X: hipBLASLt has no bf16 grouped kernels for gfx950, and its one fp16 grouped kernel is 8-21x slower than Triton

Commit: none (standalone JAX script, no Marin code) · GPU: one MI350X per configuration, run side by side on one node · Job: 460950

```bash
# $WORK/marin/.venv: JAX 0.11.0, jax-rocm10-plugin, ROCm 10.0.0 from pip.
# Command buffers stay off because hipBLASLt's grouped GEMM crashes with them on (#9904).
# Times jax.lax.ragged_dot (fwd) and its VJP (bwd: dlhs and drhs) by wall clock over 20 calls,
# then sums GPU kernel time by kernel name over 5 calls under jax.profiler.
XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=" python gg_profile.py --dtype bfloat16  # bf16, XLA default
XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=" python gg_profile.py --dtype float16   # fp16, hipBLASLt grouped GEMM
```

Useful TFLOP/s per call (2·M·K·N per pass, counting only each row's own expert). Shapes are per GPU as in #9859 (w13: fused gate/up projection; w2: down projection), with 32 experts and equal row counts. bwd is dlhs and drhs together. The Triton column is #9859's tile-map kernels at the same shapes (job 457866, from the PR description); for bwd it gives the combined rate, then dlhs / drhs.

| Shape (M, K, N) | Pass | bf16 XLA (default) | fp16 XLA grouped GEMM | bf16 Triton, #9859 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| June w13, batch 64 (131072, 2560, 2560) | fwd | 35.6 | 37.4 | 784 |
| | bwd | 29.5 | 38.9 | 743 (806 / 689) |
| June w2, batch 64 (131072, 1280, 2560) | fwd | 36.6 | 52.9 | 725 |
| | bwd | 27.1 | 38.1 | 696 (764 / 639) |
| June w13, batch 8 (16384, 2560, 2560) | fwd | 36.2 | 36.5 | 621 |
| | bwd | 33.5 | 71.3 | 562 (632 / 506) |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **Relaxing XLA's gate is not enough.** XLA lowers `ragged_dot` to hipBLASLt's grouped GEMM only where `CanBeHandledByGpublasltGroupGemm` in `xla/hlo/transforms/expanders/ragged_dot_rewriter.cc` allows it: fp16 and bf16 on gfx942, fp16 only on gfx950 (openxla/xla#38088, unchanged on XLA `main`). The gate follows hipBLASLt's kernel coverage. The gfx950 kernel libraries in hipBLASLt from ROCm 7.1 and 7.2 (the cluster's system installs) and ROCm 10.0 (pip) have grouped-GEMM kernels for fp16 only, and `ROCm/rocm-libraries` `develop` has no bf16 grouped-GEMM tuning logic for gfx950. A plugin rebuilt with the gate relaxed would have no bf16 kernel to call.
- **The gfx950 fp16 grouped GEMM has one kernel.** Each gfx950 fp16 grouped-GEMM logic file in [`rocm-libraries`](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-libraries/tree/develop/projects/hipblaslt/library/src/amd_detail/rocblaslt/src/Tensile/Logic/asm_full/gfx950/gfx950/GridBased) (about 9 KB) lists a single solution with a 16x16x32 tile. The gfx942 bf16 grouped-GEMM files list 4-7 MB of tuned solutions per layout. In the profiles, that `MT16x16x32` kernel accounts for the whole fp16 call. bf16 and fp16 matrix-core throughput is the same on gfx950, so a bf16 build of the same kernel would not be faster. XLA's setup kernel (`SetUserArgsKernelRaggedIn*Dim`) takes about 6 µs per GEMM.
- **XLA's default bf16 path does 32x the useful work.** It runs one hipBLASLt matmul of every row against every expert's weights at 1.20-1.42 PFLOP/s, then masks the result. The matmul is 68-91% of the call, and transposes and the mask take the rest. fp16 with `--xla_gpu_experimental_use_ragged_dot_grouped_gemm=false` takes the same path at 25-34 TFLOP/s.
- **The possible gain is small.** On MI300X, where hipBLASLt has tuned bf16 grouped kernels, XLA's grouped GEMM took 11-28% less time per call than tuned Triton (#9904, microbenchmarks only). Triton `ragged_dot` was 21% of the MI350X batch-64 step in [this profile](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6026123445), taken before the kernel rewrite and flash attention. If the MI300X edge carried over to gfx950, it would save about 2-6% of step time (21% × 11-28%), and less now that the rewritten Triton kernels are faster.
- **If someone picks this up:** test fp16 first, because it needs no plugin rebuild. Generate large-tile gfx950 fp16 grouped-GEMM solutions from the `rocm-libraries` tag that matches ROCm 10.0.0, and set `HIPBLASLT_TENSILE_LIBPATH` to a copy of the stock gfx950 library directory with the new files added. Add bf16 solutions and rebuild the plugin with the gate relaxed only if fp16 beats Triton. The other route is to ask AMD to ship tuned gfx950 grouped-GEMM kernels in hipBLASLt. Until then, MI350X keeps Triton `ragged_dot`.

</details>

topics.title: [mlx] Add a pipeline for MLX builds of Grug MoE models
topics.body:
Add Grug MoE conversion to 8-bit and mixed 4-bit MLX builds for Apple Silicon, with thinking and tool calls. An artifact graph binds the pinned source revision, prompt fixture, vLLM reference, converted model, logprob dump, and parity report. Model file hashes and source/recipe metadata prevent a stale dump from qualifying a different build. Conversion links one cached download of the source into each recipe's build and casts floating weights to bfloat16, which matches the vLLM reference and keeps an FP32 export's unquantized weights and scales out of FP32.

The Mac stages use a separate frozen environment pinned to mlx-lm 0.32.2. The reference stage submits an H100 job through Iris and waits for its output; without CoreWeave credentials on the Mac, a CPU job relays the JSON through a private Hugging Face dataset. Short prompts and long-prompt positions beyond the sliding window have separate parity gates. The mixed recipe keeps non-expert weights at 8 bits because a uniform 4-bit Snowball build failed the short-case probability-error gate.

The model file teaches mlx-lm the `<|start_think|>`/`<|end_think|>` markers and follows vLLM's `grug` reasoning parser under `mlx_lm.server`: thinking-mode text is reasoning once a think marker or tool call confirms it, and an answer with neither is content. These patches replace five mlx-lm 0.32.2 internals.

The stage scripts produced the published Snowball builds. Parity against the Marin vLLM fork (`marin-vllm-gpu-20260924-01911be34fac`) serving each source in bfloat16 compares top-25 logprobs at every teacher-forced position. The gates are top-1 on decisive positions >= 0.99 and p95 probability error <= 0.075 for 8-bit, and >= 0.97 and <= 0.15 for mixed 4-bit:

| Source | Build | Short cases: top-1 decisive / p95 error | Long prompt, positions >= 2048 |
|---|---|---|---|
| v0.1 | 8-bit | 1.000 / 0.045 | 1.000 / 0.0001 |
| v0.1 | mixed 4-bit | 0.994 / 0.100 | 1.000 / 0.0001 |
| v0.1 | uniform 4-bit, rejected | 0.978 / 0.193 | 1.000 / 0.0002 |
| v0.1.1 | 8-bit | 0.999 / 0.055 | 1.000 / 0.043 |
| v0.1.1 | mixed 4-bit | 0.994 / 0.103 | 0.997 / 0.101 |

The v0.1 long prompt repeated one paragraph for 6,148 tokens, so its continuations stayed inside the 2,048-token window. The v0.1.1 runs use the current fixture, 8,192 tokens of unrepeated WikiText. The v0.1.1 reference job ran in about 7 minutes on 8 H100s.

The v0.1 weights are identical to `open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14` (39 shard hashes), which Marin's policy evals scored on vLLM. Subsets run on the v0.1 mixed 4-bit build at temperature 1.0 showed no capability loss: GSM8K 0.948 on 250 items (vLLM 0.914 on the full set), MATH500 0.96 on 100 (0.962), IFBench strict 0.34 on 100 (0.300). Both v0.1 builds recalled a fact placed at the start of the system prompt at all 8 tested lengths from 596 to 23k tokens. `smoke_server.sh` passes on all four published builds: thinking split, thinking off, tool call and round trip, streamed reasoning, tool calls and unmarked answers, and a 20,491-token prompt at 3.8k–4.8k prefill and 9–12 decode tokens/s on an M5 Max. The evals and recall checks predate the unmarked-answer parser change, which only affects responses with no think marker.

The builds came from running the stage scripts directly. `pipeline.py` has not yet run the full graph end to end.

topics.title: [experiment] Hero checkpoint averaging and format SFT
topics.body:
## TL;DR

Adjusted WSM-inspired checkpoint averaging → donor initialization of five chat-token output columns → 64 updates of LoRA plus vocabulary SFT produced a provisional Hero checkpoint for short RL capacity-planning trials. All 100 reviewed responses ended at EOT within the 2,048-token cap. Content errors and two special-token anomalies remain; intended-backend throughput and parity still need measurement.

The canonical research record has moved to [marin-logbooks #2](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/issues/2), following the workflow in [#9467](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9467). Its [commit-pinned notebook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/d152151d8148734c8f1a954be1224eb83e20c2e9/logbooks/2-hero-checkpoint-format-sft/notebook.md) preserves the full rationale, derivation, source revisions, commands, failed attempts and results. Future research updates belong there. This issue retains the checkpoint handoff and links to the selected Marin contribution.

## What we tried and why

The goal was basic coherent thinking and turn-taking for systems experiments without waiting for a separate full-model cooldown or full-model SFT. Hero is a roughly 535B MoE: 48 layers, hidden width 6,144, 384 routed experts with eight selected per token and two shared experts. This campaign retained its 16K architecture. A is the original pretraining checkpoint at step 294000.

1. **A → B, adjusted averaging.** Inspired by [Warmup-Stable and Merge (WSM)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.17634), divide the integrated target linear-cooldown LR by the integrated actual LR over each saved checkpoint interval. This gave weights 0.232123642 / 0.499105160 / 0.268771198 on steps 282000 / 288000 / 294000. Preserve the latest effective FP32 router bias. This is an offline approximation; no counterfactual optimizer trajectory was run.
2. **B → C, chat-token initialization.** Seed five output columns for header/thinking/EOT tokens from existing text/EOS donor tokens. Input embeddings initially stayed unchanged. Construction and ancestry were verified; no donor/no-donor ablation was run.
3. **C → D, compact SFT.** Freeze the base and routing control; train rank-16/alpha-16 [LoRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685) on attention/shared dense projections plus five input/output vocabulary deltas. Use 4,806 no_robots training conversations, the shared Marin chat recipe and pinned tokenizer. Continue an eight-update smoke to 64 total with full Adam, counters and deterministic data position retained. Extending the LR horizon from 8 to 64 raised the first resumed LR from the short tail; it was not a schedule reset. Export ordinary BF16 weights with the deltas baked in.

## How we measured it

| Measurement | Result and scope |
| --- | --- |
| Matched A/B pretraining loss | Identical 59 C4 sequences of 16,384 tokens: 2.130703034 → 2.109083774 (−1.01465%); all 59 row deltas lower. One fixed panel, not broad-domain quality or cooldown equivalence. |
| Training-source EOT acquisition | Mean NLL for one expected EOT token at each of 16 fixed training prefixes: 3.38140 at update 8 → 0.42875 at 64; top-1 1/16 → 14/16. This is EOT-token NLL, not average sequence NLL or heldout evidence. |
| Fresh responses | 40 math, 40 Python and 20 fixed-history followups at temperature 0.7. All 100 stopped at EOT; zero caps; median 113.5 tokens, max 496. Math: 33 correct, four wrong, two incomplete, one ambiguous; code: 32 statically plausible, eight defects; history: 18 clear passes, one error, one borderline. Code was not executed. |

Training processed 67,108,864 positions, including 65,975,980 non-padding tokens: about 47.6 training-corpus token-volume equivalents. This reuse limits interpretation of acquisition gains. Capacity-overflow endpoints were 0.17389 at update 8 and 0.19403 at 64 on different batches; their quality impact is unassessed.

The [reviewed-output gist](https://gist.github.com/dlwh/408759a8eb09796d253b8b53a43769d4) retains every prompt, response and per-case judgment. Native sampling used dropless execution, full-prefix recomputation without KV cache and 4,096 physical padding. Its timing is not an RL-serving throughput measurement. Full heldout/native format/content evaluation, independent merge parity, post-SFT matched C4 regression, long-context behavior and backend agreement remain unresolved.

## Checkpoint artifacts


The merged step-64 native checkpoint contains the LoRA and vocabulary updates baked into ordinary BF16 weights. It needs no runtime adapter:

```text
s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-format-sft/2026.10.21/sft-phase-2416e9d7/SFT-long-test-v1-20261022/attempts/c77824dfce148a77/export/step-64
```

Canonical metadata digest: `aeec732ddaa4d47d146b0056b5b52891e5062a24a61857c35bb48f7e72cdfe57`.

The separate compact checkpoint retains adapters, five vocabulary deltas, full Adam state, counters and deterministic data position for training continuation:

```text
s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-format-sft/2026.10.21/sft-phase-2416e9d7/SFT-long-test-v1-20261022/attempts/c77824dfce148a77/adapters/step-64
```

Canonical metadata digest: `ce7a80fe9c7621e53d3f7745189a523473d7e228eb671a43039396924ae25fb6`.

Use `marin-community/marin-tokenizer` at revision `a5ca45f2feb6c959bd87b81689aa7279b5bdcaa2`, the shared MARIN chat template, and EOT token `128009`. Intended-backend loading and parity still need measurement.

## Status and contribution

[Marin #10556](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10556) retains the independently selected existing-interface fixes: activation-only short-convolution gradients for frozen weights, FP32 router-bias preservation during export and GB200 device typing. The [selection record](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/d152151d8148734c8f1a954be1224eb83e20c2e9/logbooks/2-hero-checkpoint-format-sft/selection.md) explains why the rest stays in the runnable research branch. The broad reproduction PR #10539 is superseded.

Next: load the merged checkpoint on the intended RL backend and measure throughput, latency and memory with representative lengths/concurrency and tokenizer/template/EOT checks. No further training, production adoption or merge is implied.

This test measures whether further updates improve token acquisition and remain numerically stable. Each prefix scores one EOT target token. These are training-source acquisition diagnostics; heldout generation and turn termination remain unmeasured. Loading on that backend and numerical agreement with the native checkpoint remain unchecked. topics.title: [post-training] Mix PivotRL pivots into broad RLVR for SWE and terminal gains
topics.body:
## TL;DR

Three matched mixed-domain RLVR runs from the Grug Datakit SFT (October 5) test whether a share of [PivotRL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21383) pivots improves SWE-bench Verified and OpenThoughts-TBLite without hurting the other domains, and whether pivot selection matters: RLVR alone, RLVR with selected SWE and Terminal pivots at 20% of prompts, and RLVR with random SWE and Terminal turns at the same share. Two optional arms move the selected share to 10% and 30%. Every arm stops at 12 steps. Status: all three arms trained 12 steps at seed 42 and were evaluated at steps 4, 8 and 12; [results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10214#issuecomment-6305992938). B is the only arm above the SFT on SWE-bench Verified (+8.8 points at steps 4 and 8, p=.0001; +4.8 at step 12), C never transfers, and every arm drifts on Math500 and MMLU-Pro by step 12. A seed-43 replicate finished 45 of 48 evaluations ([final](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10214#issuecomment-6357439611)). At step 8, B beats C at both seeds (+10.0 and +12.6) and beats A at both seeds (+9.2 and +3.0; pooled +6.1, p<.0001), with no loss on the reasoning benchmarks. By step 12 the arms no longer separate and every arm loses Math500 and MMLU-Pro. B at step 8 is the checkpoint to report, and running longer needs a drift fix.

## Hypothesis

Pivots that the SFT policy's own pass rates select (#9933), rewarded by #9933's deterministic verifiers, improve SWE-bench Verified and OpenThoughts-TBLite at 20% of prompts while broad holdout accuracy stays within noise. Random SWE and Terminal turns at the same share help less. Training pivots alone has been hard to stabilize; mixing them into broad RLVR keeps the rest of the policy anchored.

## Setup

- **Start:** [open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05), a pure SFT checkpoint. #9933 measured its SWE and Terminal pass rates on this policy, so the selections apply unchanged, and the RLVR data is unseen.
- **RLVR data:** [Nemotron-RL-Ultra-RLVR1-Cleaned-v3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Nemotron-RL-Ultra-RLVR1-Cleaned-v3-2026-09-30) (84,403 train / 94 validation rows; 24% single-step tool use, 14% instruction following, 9% code, 13% math, no SWE or Terminal rows). Any SWE or terminal change between arms is therefore attributable to the added turns.
- **Recipe:** the #9735 reference/KL arm (frozen reference, KL 0.01, sequence-mean loss, entropy 0.001, router replay), 512 prompts × 16 samples per step, at most 12 steps, the same seed in every arm. SFT starts in #9735 collapsed after 12 to 20 steps. Asynchronous rollouts with staleness up to 2, TIS correction, a 102,400-token request window with 49,152 tokens per turn, and thinking on, as #9933 measured the pivots' pass rates.
- **RLVR blend as trained:** 63,590 of RLVR1's rows. MarinSkyRL now runs every Nemotron Ultra row as a task session, and code generation, NeMo tool use, NVARC inductive and Lean sessions execute in a Docker task machine that Iris task pods cannot start, so every arm omits those four agents (about 20% of RLVR1, including #9735's code domain). Rows containing a blank text message, which task conversations reject, are dropped too (3,991 RLVR, 59 Terminal). Validation keeps 67 of RLVR1's 94 rows.
- **Pivot prompts:** the runtime drops earlier assistant turns' reasoning from pivot prompts, which #9933's pass-rate measurement kept.
- **Pivots:** #9933's long-format SWE and Terminal candidates, selected at λ = 0.65 (1 to 10 passes of 16) from the pooled K = 16 pass rates already measured on this policy (`users/dml/pivotrl/{swe,terminal}/pass-rates/grug-67b-a2b-datakit-sft-262k-20261005+seed-1@2026.10.09`). That selects 25,792 of 72,434 scored SWE turns under `nemo` and 6,999 of 36,107 Terminal turns.
- **Reward:** `nemotron_ultra` grades pivot rows through MarinSkyRL#992 with #9933's verifiers: NeMo Gym argument comparison (`nemo`) for SWE and Terminus-2 keystroke similarity without a judge (`string_90`) for Terminal. #10000 uses the same graders. Pivot replies are capped at 4,096 tokens, the cap the pass rates were sampled at.

## Arms

| Arm | Data |
| --- | --- |
| A | RLVR1 |
| B | RLVR1, with selected pivots replacing 20% of prompts |
| C | RLVR1, with random SWE and Terminal candidate turns replacing 20% of prompts |
| B-10, B-30 (optional) | As B, at 10% and 30% |

The batch stays at 512 prompts, so added turns displace RLVR prompts. Each step carries 102 added turns, 51 SWE and 51 Terminal, because the two benchmarks weigh equally in the decision rules; MarinSkyRL's domain-weighted sampling fills every batch to these counts from route-tagged pools and draws each pool uniformly. RLVR rows come first and their pool is shuffled first, so with one seed B's and C's RLVR prompts are a prefix of A's draw order. Twelve steps use 612 of each pool (25,792 SWE and 6,999 Terminal pivots), so no turn repeats.

### Why 20%

Only groups with mixed outcomes produce a gradient, and RLVR1 groups already mostly do: `reward/informative_group_fraction` was 0.79 at the first step from the Datakit SFT (Datakit v4, #9735) and fell to about 0.55 by step 12. Resampling the stored K = 16 pass rates, 88% of selected SWE pivots and 81% of selected Terminal pivots come back mixed, against 58% and 24% of random candidate turns. Pivots' share of the gradient is therefore only 1.1 to 1.5 times their share of prompts, and C carries about half of B's pivot signal at the same share.

Pivot-only RL on this SFT, with the same policy learning rate (4e-6) and gradient clip, bounds the dose. One update of 64 SWE pivot groups raised SWE-bench Verified from 26.0% to 29.4% (146 vs 129 of 496 matched tasks, against a historical base run) with AIME24 unchanged; five updates raised held-out pivot accuracy from 0.29 to 0.38. Forty Terminal updates cost 36 points on AIME24 and 9 to 10 on GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and Math500, and ninety SWE updates collapsed agentic behavior (1 of 248 SWE-bench Verified trials solved, 0 of 190 TBLite) while held-out pivot accuracy kept rising.

Counting a mixed step as its pivot gradient share of a pivot-only update, with RLVR1's informative fraction averaging about 0.68 over the first 12 steps, a first-order approximation that ignores RLVR and KL counteracting drift:

| *p* | Pivot prompts per step | Pivot gradient share | Equivalent pivot-only updates by step 12 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10% | 51 | ~12% | ~1.5 |
| 20% | 102 | ~24% | ~2.9 |
| 30% | 154 | ~35% | ~4.2 |

With at most 12 steps, 10% delivers about one pivot-only update, the dose that gained about 3 points on SWE, below what the benchmarks resolve. 20% places the dose in the middle of the range where pivot-only training helped, about 14 times below where it did damage, with RLVR still about three quarters of the gradient. B-10 and B-30 bracket it.

## Measurements

- At steps 0, 4, 8 and 12: pass rate on #9933's held-out validation turns graded in process, broad holdout pass@1 and normalized verifier score, and per-domain reward.
- Per step and per source (RLVR, SWE, Terminal): informative group count and mean response length, so B and C are compared by delivered pivot signal and any pull toward shorter RLVR answers shows up early. Pivot replies are capped at 4,096 tokens, the cap their pass rates were sampled at, through each pivot row's request; the sequence-mean loss weights them like full RLVR answers.
- At step 0 and each arm's step 4, 8 and 12 checkpoints: full SWE-bench Verified (500 tasks, mini-swe-agent 2.1.0) and OpenThoughts-TBLite (Terminus 2), three runs each, compared per task between arms, plus AIME24, GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and Math500, the benchmarks pivot-only training hurt.
- Checkpoints are selected by the broad holdout and pivot validation, never by the benchmarks. A paired comparison on 500 SWE tasks has a standard error of about 2 points; on 100 tasks it is about 4.4, too wide for the effects expected here.

## Decision rules

- B beats A on SWE-bench Verified or OpenThoughts-TBLite by more than two paired standard errors, with the broad holdout and the four reasoning benchmarks within noise: pivots help in mixed RLVR. Next, test RL-then-merge against the Campaign 3 merge recipe (#9975).
- B ≈ C: selection does not matter at this share; random turns are enough. B > C partly reflects C's smaller pivot signal, so the logged informative group counts qualify the comparison.
- B beats A on pivot validation only: the verifier reward does not transfer to the benchmarks. Revisit the reward component (`exact`) or the generation cap.
- An arm collapses: report its best checkpoint before the collapse and compare arms only at matched steps.

## Prerequisites

1. Per-agent `pivot_reward`, declared among the Nemotron Ultra session settings: MarinSkyRL#992.
2. Selection artifacts at λ = 0.65 from #9933's stored K = 16 pass rates: built, 25,792 SWE and 6,999 Terminal pivots.
3. Arm datasets: #10215 builds RLVR1 (`open-athena/Nemotron-RL-Ultra-RLVR1-Cleaned-v3-2026-09-30@600262dd`) alone, with the selected pivots, and with every scored candidate turn, each row tagged with its route. Rows move from the retired `skyrl_gym` route to `task_session`, which MarinSkyRL grades Nemotron Ultra rows on since its #879. Validation in every arm is RLVR1's 94 rows plus #9933's 508 held-out SWE and 503 Terminal turns.
4. A two-step smoke run of B on 6 nodes (64 prompts with B's composition, 32K window) confirming that every agent's rows load and grade.

## Links

- PivotRL candidates, pass rates and selection: #9933; SFT baselines on the same pivots: #10000; TaskSpec versions of the candidates: #10181
- Prior broad-domain RLVR: #9359, #9735
- Paper: [PivotRL (arXiv 2603.21383)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21383)

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

This is a matched training experiment, not an isolated code fix. The current Marin checkout can pass multiple artifact data sources to SkyRL, but PivotRL pass-rate selection and task conversion are still in open PRs #9933 and #10181; #10181 currently has a failing aggregate `unit-tests` check. The per-agent `pivot_reward` change and verifyit pin in MarinSkyRL#992 remain prerequisites; this session cannot inspect that separate repository.

**Relevant code**
- [`skyrl.py#L150-L163`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L150-L163) — training sources and seed
- [`skyrl.py#L307-L344`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L307-L344) — artifact dependency and launcher request
- [`external_dependencies.py#L73-L79`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/external_dependencies.py#L73-L79) — pinned MarinSkyRL revision
- [#9933](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9933) — candidate pass rates and pivot selection
- [#10181](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10181) — TaskSpec conversion and in-process graders

# Proposed Fix

1. Land #9933 and resolve the stacked #10000/#10181 work without duplicating it. Produce pooled K=16 pass rates for both domains and record immutable λ=0.65 selected-pivot and random-candidate manifests, including source IDs, pool sizes, and disjoint validation identities.
2. Verify MarinSkyRL#992 supports per-agent `pivot_reward`, pins the verifyit revision with the pivot graders, and grades SWE and Terminal in one run. Pin that tested MarinSkyRL revision in Marin and cover the reward dispatch and loader path with focused tests.
3. Add an artifact-backed builder for A/B/C that records the seed, source revisions, prompt order, domain counts, and chosen pivot IDs. Keep 512 prompts × 16 samples per step; make B and C use the same pivot share and SWE/Terminal balance, with their RLVR prompts drawn in A's order. Cap pivot replies at 4,096 tokens.
4. Run B for two smoke steps to confirm `skyrl_gym` loading, both graders, reward variance, and the surviving RLVR informative-group fraction. Fix the pivot share from that result, subject to the selected pool size, before launching matched 40-step A/B/C runs.
5. Evaluate every four steps from step 0, choose checkpoints using only broad holdout and pivot validation, then run three SWE-Bench-100 and OpenThoughts-TBLite evaluations plus the disjoint SWE-bench Verified slice at step 0, best, and final. Report matched-step effects, uncertainty, any collapse, run/config/artifact links, and the issue's decision rules.

This needs the prerequisite merges, data artifacts, and production training/evaluation runs; no standalone PR from this triage would complete #10214.

🤖 Results for the three arms at steps 4, 8 and 12, paired per item against the October 5 Datakit SFT (REF). One run per arm at seed 42. Training runs: [A](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/1u013rdm), [B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/e01zoz2k), [C](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/zblphp52). A12's SWE-bench job is still retrying verifier timeouts, so that one cell is provisional; the rest of the 54 evaluations are final.

Selected pivots are the only treatment that moves SWE-bench Verified, the effect is present at step 4, and random turns at the same share do not transfer. Every arm erodes Math500 and MMLU-Pro by step 12; B erodes least. Step 8 is the checkpoint to report.

## SWE-bench Verified

Strict scoring: a trial with no verifier result counts as unsolved, each cell is one complete 500-task run, and p-values are exact McNemar tests on the discordant pairs.

| Step | REF | A | B | C | B vs A | B vs C | B vs REF |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | .260 | .288 | .348 | .232 | +6.0, p=.004 | +11.6, p<.0001 | +8.8, p=.0001 |
| 8 | .260 | .256 | .348 | .248 | +9.2, p<.0001 | +10.0, p<.0001 | +8.8, p=.0001 |
| 12 | .260 | .272 (provisional) | .308 | .244 | +3.6, p=.07 | +6.4, p=.002 | +4.8, p=.025 |

A and C never differ from REF (every |Δ| ≤ 2.8 points, p ≥ .14). B newly solves 22 to 23% of the tasks REF fails, against 10 to 15% for A and C, and keeps about 70% of REF's solved tasks. B12 vs B8 is −4.0 (p=.054).

## Other benchmarks

Δ vs REF in points. GPQA-Diamond averages 3 trials per question and AIME24 10, tested with a paired sign-flip permutation test; Math500 and MMLU-Pro use exact McNemar; OT-TBLite counts a task solved when at least 2 of 3 trials score 1. Starred cells have p<.05.

| Step | Arm | GPQA-D | MMLU-Pro | Math500 | AIME24 | OT-TBLite |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | A | +3.9 | +0.9 ★ | 0.0 | −3.3 | +2.0 |
| 4 | B | +6.4 ★ | +0.6 | −0.8 | −0.7 | +3.0 |
| 4 | C | +7.6 ★ | 0.0 | −0.8 | −1.7 | 0.0 |
| 8 | A | +6.2 ★ | +0.8 ★ | −0.2 | +1.0 | −5.0 |
| 8 | B | +7.4 ★ | +0.4 | 0.0 | −3.0 | −2.0 |
| 8 | C | +6.1 ★ | +0.4 | −1.0 | 0.0 | −4.0 |
| 12 | A | +5.7 ★ | −1.6 ★ | −7.6 ★ | −4.0 | −4.0 |
| 12 | B | +6.6 ★ | −1.1 ★ | −2.2 (p=.052) | 0.0 | −3.0 |
| 12 | C | +4.5 ★ | −3.4 ★ | −7.8 ★ | −0.3 | −3.0 |

REF accuracies: GPQA-Diamond .635 (n=198), MMLU-Pro .780 (n=12032), Math500 .968 (n=500), AIME24 .830 (n=30), OT-TBLite .16 (n=100). At step 12 B beats A by +5.4 and C by +5.6 on Math500 (both p<.0001) and C by +2.3 on MMLU-Pro (p<.0001). No arm differs from another on GPQA-Diamond or AIME24 at any step, and TBLite with 100 tasks cannot resolve differences under about 9 points.

## Reading

Random turns are the control that makes the SWE-bench result interpretable. C uses the same turn sources, verifiers and share as B, and on the held-out pivot turns it learns the pivot task as fast as B: SWE pivot pass@1 rises from .24 to .42 in both arms and Terminal from .15 to .23, while A stays at .23. Only the selected turns transfer to the benchmark. Random turns also carry less signal, as the plan anticipated: informative-group fraction 0.59 against 0.67 for A and B, and pivot rewards about half of B's.

The GPQA gain of 4 to 8 points in every arm from step 4 comes from the RLVR mix.

The step-12 losses are on hard multi-step items. On Math500, levels 1 to 3 move within 3 points in every arm; level 4 drops 7.8 (A), 2.3 (B) and 8.6 (C) points and level 5 drops 17.2, 4.5 and 15.7. On MMLU-Pro, which is decoded greedily, the losses sit in engineering, chemistry, physics and math; B12 is flat on engineering where A12 is −5.8 and C12 −7.7. The lost Math500 answers run 4.3 times the length of REF's answer to the same question and 34 of A12's 42 end in an extracted wrong answer rather than a truncation. The share of Math500 responses over 100K characters is 0.4% for REF, 4.8% for A4, 8.2% for B12, 11.0% for C12 and 12.4% for A12.

The training curves carry the same signature. Policy entropy rises every step (A 0.83 to 2.76, B to 1.95, C to 2.18) and KL to the frozen reference climbs with no plateau (A .071, B .063, C .086 at step 12), so the 0.01 KL coefficient does not hold the policy. The arm that drifts least degrades least. The in-distribution holdout improves monotonically in every arm (A .21 to .40), so it cannot see the drift; the reference/KL run in #9735 shows the same entropy rise (1.0 to 2.2 by step 10) and had only that holdout. Length stops stay under 9% throughout training and are not the cause.

A's agentic behaviour drifts the same way. Its replies on the pivot validation turns grow 1.5 to 2 times by step 12, A8 overflows the 73K-token context in 17% of SWE-bench tasks (every non-zero agent exit in A8 and A12 is a context-window overflow), and in the A12 eval the median model call took 17 s against 3.6 s for the other runs: 171 of 500 trials hit the 30-minute agent budget, 122 of them then timing out in the verifier. Harbor retries verifier timeouts as infrastructure errors, and the retries have moved A12 from .244 to .272 so far.

## Decision rules

The first rule, B above A on SWE-bench Verified by more than two paired standard errors with the reasoning benchmarks within noise, holds at steps 4 and 8 (SE about 2 points; B−A +6.0 and +9.2). At step 12 no arm has the reasoning benchmarks within noise. The second rule, B ≈ C, fails at every step by 6 to 12 points, and the logged informative-group counts attribute part of that to C's weaker signal. Confidence is limited by one seed per arm; the B effects are 3 to 5 standard errors on SWE-bench, and isolated p<.05 cells such as B8 vs A8 on AIME24 (−4.0, p=.04) are what a hundred comparisons produce.

## What it took

- Layout: 16 H100 nodes per arm, 10 policy nodes with the colocated reference and 12 inference engines at DP4/EP4 on the other 6; 11 to 16 hours per 12-step run.
- Runtime: MarinSkyRL branch `dml/mixed-rlvr-runtime` at bfef1308, seven commits over the fork's main at 563658e5: verifyit pivot graders for the Nemotron pivot rows, per-agent `pivot_reward`, the SWE pivot agent name, null message fields in Parquet prompts, request tools passed as chat tools, and a retry for vLLM engine gangs that die during startup. marin-community/MarinSkyRL#992 carries the first six. The fork was archived on 2026-10-20, so these need porting into `vendor/skyrl` once the verifyit graders from #10215 are published.
- Evaluation: the October 5 verified paired-eval stack (`held/eval-october17-verified` at f9990d36) plus fixes on branch `dml/eval-october17-verified-pivot-mixed-rlvr`: a localhost relay that reports the Iris proxy's 404 during an inference-server reschedule as 503 for ten minutes so Evalchemy retries; Daytona verifier thread limits, because native test libraries sized their pools to the host and exhausted the 300 s verifier timeout; mini-swe-agent pinned to litellm 1.105.1 after an MCP import regression; a 24 h placement budget that treats Kueue's SchedulingGated state as unplaced; the Run:ai streamer load format for staged HF exports; `--cluster-config` so evaluations submit as the openathena.ai login after the contractor service account's default budget demoted jobs to batch band; and an export barrier that waits for the HF export job and verifies its shards before evaluating.
- Scoring: strict first-trial SWE-bench with the fullest run per arm and step; TBLite majority of 3 trials; repeated-trial benchmarks averaged per question.

## Next

- Final A12 SWE-bench number when the retry wave ends.
- A seed-43 replicate of all three arms launched 2026-10-20 21:29 UTC as the openathena.ai login, A on cw-us-east-02a, B and C on cw-rno2a: [A](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/5thdcjv5), [B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/v8o72kqn), [C](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/2rjy7l3n). C has been preempted three times by production-band jobs on rno2a and restarts from scratch each time.
- The recipe needs a drift fix before running past 8 steps: a stronger KL coefficient, a lower learning rate, dropping the entropy bonus, or a length penalty. The optional p arms (B-10, B-30) remain open; the second seed was prioritized.

🤖 Final A12 SWE-bench number: .282, 141 of 500 solved. Harbor's retries of the verifier timeouts finished at 07:47 UTC with every trial scored, so the provisional .272 above becomes .282 and the step-12 row of the SWE-bench table reads A .282, B .308, C .244: B vs A +2.6 (p=.21), B vs C +6.4 (p=.002), C vs A −3.8 (p=.048), B vs REF +4.8 (p=.025), A vs REF +2.2 (p=.28). Steps 4 and 8 are unchanged, and the 54 evaluations of the seed-42 series are complete.

A12's first-pass strict score was .244, with 128 trials that ended in a verifier timeout after the agent had used its 30-minute budget. Harbor retries verifier timeouts as infrastructure errors; the retry wave, run at 16 trials at a time instead of the first pass's full concurrency, scored all of them and lifted A12 by 3.8 points. Those timeouts were therefore partly load-induced rather than a property of the policy, although A12's agents still ran about five times slower per model call than the other arms and overflowed the 73K context in 40 tasks. The step-12 reading changes from B ahead of A by 6 points to B ahead by 2.6 points, not significant; B's lead over A at steps 4 and 8 (+6.0, +9.2) and over C at every step is unaffected, and A's own SWE-bench trajectory is flat (A12 vs A4 −0.6, p=.81).

Seed-43 replicate: all three arms finished 12 steps (B at 08:08 UTC, A and C at about 13:55 UTC; C restarted three times after production-band preemptions on cw-rno2a). Exports for A steps 4, 8 and 12, B steps 4, 8 and 12 and C steps 8 and 12 are done or running, with their evaluations queued behind verified exports. C's step-4 checkpoint was pruned by the trainer before its export request landed, so the replicate has no C step-4 point. The two-seed results will follow when those 48 evaluations finish.

🤖 Seed-43 replicate, interim. Same recipe, data and evaluation stack as the seed-42 series above, with the run, trainer and data-sampling seeds all set to 43. A trained on cw-us-east-02a and B and C on cw-rno2a, an incidental placement difference (seed 42 had A on rno2a and B and C on us-east) that does not touch the configuration. Training runs: [A](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/5thdcjv5), [B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/v8o72kqn), [C](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/2rjy7l3n). The trainer pruned C's step-4 checkpoint before its export request landed, so C has no step-4 point and the replicate has 48 evaluations (8 checkpoints × 6 benchmarks). Of those, 32 are complete: steps 4 and 8 on every benchmark except MMLU-Pro and B's OT-TBLite; at step 12 GPQA-Diamond, Math500 and AIME24 for all arms and MMLU-Pro and OT-TBLite for A and C. SWE-bench Verified at step 12, B's OT-TBLite and five MMLU-Pro cells are still running.

B above C on SWE-bench Verified and C below REF replicate. B above A appears at step 8 at a third of the seed-42 size (+3.0, not significant on its own, significant pooled over both seeds) and does not appear at step 4. Every arm again loses Math500 by step 12, and the arm that loses most is the one with the highest step-12 policy entropy: A at seed 42, B at seed 43.

## SWE-bench Verified

Strict scoring as above: each seed-43 cell is one complete 500-task run, p-values are exact McNemar tests on the discordant pairs, and the pooled rows sum the discordant pairs of both seeds.

| Step | REF | A | B | C | B vs A | B vs C | C vs A | B vs REF |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4, seed 43 | .260 | .302 | .298 | — | −0.4, p=.93 | — | — | +3.8, p=.087 |
| 8, seed 43 | .260 | .298 | .328 | .202 | +3.0, p=.18 | +12.6, p<.0001 | −9.6, p<.0001 | +6.8, p=.002 |
| 4, both seeds | | | | | +2.8, p=.069 | | | +6.3, p=.0001 |
| 8, both seeds | | | | | +6.1, p=.0001 | +11.3, p<.0001 | −5.3, p=.0001 | +7.9, p<.0001 |

A is above REF at seed 43 (+4.2 at step 4, p=.055; +3.8 at step 8, p=.073) against +2.8 (p=.18) and −0.4 at seed 42; pooled, A vs REF is +3.4 at step 4 (p=.02) and +1.9 at step 8 (p=.21). The step-12 runs have graded 480 of 500 tasks for B (128 solved, .267), 414 for A (140 solved, .338) and 426 for C (143 solved, .336). The three graded sets differ, and the unfinished tasks are the long ones that mostly fail, so these rates are upper bounds for each arm and not comparable across arms. B's step-12 score at seed 42 was .308.

## Other benchmarks, seed 43

Δ vs REF in points. GPQA-Diamond averages 3 samples per question and AIME24 10, tested with a paired sign-flip permutation test; Math500 and MMLU-Pro use exact McNemar; OT-TBLite counts a task solved when at least 2 of 3 trials score 1. One evaluation run per cell. Starred cells have p<.05; "pending" marks a run that is still in progress or being re-run.

| Step | Arm | GPQA-D | MMLU-Pro | Math500 | AIME24 | OT-TBLite |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | A | +4.4 | +0.7 ★ | −0.8 | −1.7 | 0.0 |
| 4 | B | +5.9 ★ | pending | −1.6 | +0.3 | pending |
| 8 | A | +1.2 | pending | −0.8 | −4.3 ★ | −4.0 |
| 8 | B | +9.6 ★ | pending | −0.6 | −2.3 | pending |
| 8 | C | +5.1 ★ | pending | 0.0 | −1.0 | −5.0 |
| 12 | A | −0.3 | −1.1 ★ | −2.8 ★ | −2.3 | −8.0 ★ |
| 12 | B | +5.6 ★ | pending | −5.8 ★ | −2.3 | pending |
| 12 | C | +5.9 ★ | −1.1 ★ | −2.8 ★ | 0.0 | −7.0 ★ |

Arm against arm at seed 43: on GPQA-Diamond B is above A by +8.4 at step 8 (p=.0002) and +5.9 at step 12 (p=.008), and C is above A by +6.2 at step 12 (p=.005); A's GPQA gain fades from +4.4 at step 4 to −0.3 at step 12, where it held at +5.7 at seed 42. On Math500 at step 12, B is below A by 3.0 (p=.02) and below C by 3.0 (p=.036); at seed 42 B was above both by about 5.5. B's OT-TBLite runs lost trials to preemption and are re-running, because the score needs 3 trials per task.

## Reading

Policy entropy at step 12, in nats per token as logged by the trainer, is A 2.11, B 2.53, C 2.23 at seed 43 against A 2.76, B 1.95, C 2.18 at seed 42; KL to the frozen reference policy is A .062, B .071, C .057 against .071, .063, .086. In both seeds the arm with the highest entropy loses the most on Math500 and the arm with the lowest loses the least, and the order of the arms reverses between seeds. Two seeds cannot separate a seed effect from an arm effect, but B's smaller step-12 erosion at seed 42 does not replicate, so it is not a property of the selected-pivot mix. The step-8 checkpoint remains the one to report.

The first decision rule from the plan, B above A on SWE-bench Verified by more than two paired standard errors with no loss on the reasoning benchmarks, holds at step 8 when the two seeds are pooled (+6.1, standard error about 1.5) and does not hold at seed 43 alone (+3.0, standard error 2.1); B shows no reasoning loss relative to A at step 8 (GPQA +8.4, Math500 +0.2, AIME24 +2.0). The second rule, B ≈ C, which would have attributed B's gain to the turn format instead of the selection, fails again by 12.6 points at step 8. Confidence: B above C and C below REF are consistent across both seeds; B above A rests on two seeds with step-8 effects of 3 and 9 points, so its size is uncertain; the GPQA differences between arms come from one run per cell with 198 questions and are suggestive only.

## What it took

- 28 of the 48 evaluations failed on 2026-10-21. CoreWeave object storage answered writes from cw-rno2a with "Account is write suspended for this availability zone", uploads timed out on both clusters, and the Iris controllers stopped answering in-cluster RPCs from about 17:10 UTC on cw-rno2a and 18:27 on cw-us-east-02a; the evaluations failed as their retry budgets ran out between 17:47 and 19:15. All 28 were re-run on cw-us-east-02a.
- From 20:00 UTC on 2026-10-21 the controllers refuse submissions from clients whose lib/iris is more than 14 days old. The October-5 verified evaluation stack is a frozen checkout whose lib/iris was last changed on 2026-10-06, so submissions now go through a side worktree that takes lib/iris and lib/rigging from 2026-10-13 and changes nothing under lib/marin; the evaluation code and results are unaffected.
- Since 01:12 UTC on 2026-10-22, production-band (higher-priority) jobs on cw-us-east-02a have preempted our interactive-band inference servers in six waves. SWE-bench Verified and OT-TBLite run under Harbor, which resumes its job directory and keeps completed trials; the other four benchmarks run under Evalchemy, which restarts from scratch, so the five pending MMLU-Pro cells (A step 8, B steps 4, 8 and 12, C step 8) each need an uninterrupted stretch of 7 to 9 hours.

## Next

- Step-12 SWE-bench Verified and OT-TBLite and the remaining MMLU-Pro cells for seed 43, then the pooled step-12 tests and the two-seed plots.
- The recipe still needs a change that holds the policy near the reference before running past 8 steps (a stronger KL coefficient, a lower learning rate, no entropy bonus, or a length penalty); the optional arms that vary the pivot share (B-10, B-30) remain open.

🤖 Seed-43 replicate, final. 45 of the 48 seed-43 evaluations are complete. The three missing cells are MMLU-Pro for A at step 8 and B at steps 4 and 8. Their Evalchemy runs need about 9 uninterrupted hours of inference, and production-band preemptions on cw-us-east-02a restarted them every 45 to 60 minutes, so we stopped at 45. C has no step-4 checkpoint at seed 43, as noted in the interim comment. The seed-42 series is complete (54 of 54).

The step-8 checkpoint of B is the result to report. It is the best SWE-bench Verified checkpoint at both seeds, it beats random turns (C) by 10 to 13 points at both seeds, and it costs nothing on the reasoning benchmarks. B's lead over plain RLVR (A) at step 8 is positive at both seeds, +9.2 and +3.0, so its size is uncertain. By step 12 the arms no longer separate on SWE-bench Verified, and every arm loses Math500 and MMLU-Pro against the SFT.

## SWE-bench Verified

Strict scoring: first trial per task, an ungraded trial counts as unsolved, 500 tasks per run. p-values are exact McNemar tests. The pooled rows sum discordant pairs over both seeds.

| Step | Seed | REF | A | B | C | B vs A | B vs C | C vs A |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 42 | .260 | .288 | .348 | .232 | +6.0, p=.004 | +11.6, p<.0001 | −5.6, p=.007 |
| 4 | 43 | .260 | .302 | .298 | — | −0.4, p=.93 | — | — |
| 4 | pooled | | | | | +2.8, p=.069 | | |
| 8 | 42 | .260 | .256 | .348 | .248 | +9.2, p<.0001 | +10.0, p<.0001 | −0.8, p=.74 |
| 8 | 43 | .260 | .298 | .328 | .202 | +3.0, p=.18 | +12.6, p<.0001 | −9.6, p<.0001 |
| 8 | pooled | | | | | +6.1, p<.0001 | +11.3, p<.0001 | −5.2, p=.0001 |
| 12 | 42 | .260 | .282 | .308 | .244 | +2.6, p=.21 | +6.4, p=.002 | −3.8, p=.048 |
| 12 | 43 | .260 | .324 | .260 | .308 | −6.4, p=.001 | −4.8, p=.020 | −1.6, p=.46 |
| 12 | pooled | | | | | −1.9, p=.19 | +0.8, p=.62 | −2.7, p=.048 |

The pooled tests hold the checkpoints fixed and test only item-level noise. They do not account for variation between training seeds, and two seeds cannot estimate that variation. A repeat evaluation of seed-42 B step 8 scored .328 against the original .348: 102 tasks flipped (56 to 46), p=.37. That is the same size as the difference between B's step-8 checkpoints at the two seeds (122 flips, −2.0), so B at step 8 reproduces across seeds within evaluation noise. Seed-42 B vs A at step 8 has 110 discordant tasks split 78 to 32, well outside that noise. Repeats of A at steps 4 and 8 and B at step 4 are still running and will be added here.

## Other benchmarks, seed 43

Δ vs REF in points, with the same tests and conventions as the interim comment. Starred cells have p<.05.

| Step | Arm | GPQA-D | MMLU-Pro | Math500 | AIME24 | OT-TBLite |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | A | +4.4 | +0.7 ★ | −0.8 | −1.7 | 0.0 |
| 4 | B | +5.9 ★ | missing | −1.6 | +0.3 | +1.0 |
| 8 | A | +1.2 | missing | −0.8 | −4.3 ★ | −4.0 |
| 8 | B | +9.6 ★ | missing | −0.6 | −2.3 | +1.0 |
| 8 | C | +5.1 ★ | +0.4 | 0.0 | −1.0 | −5.0 |
| 12 | A | −0.3 | −1.1 ★ | −2.8 ★ | −2.3 | −8.0 ★ |
| 12 | B | +5.6 ★ | −1.1 ★ | −5.8 ★ | −2.3 | 0.0 |
| 12 | C | +5.9 ★ | −1.1 ★ | −2.8 ★ | 0.0 | −7.0 ★ |

On OT-TBLite, B stays within 2 points of REF at both seeds through step 8, while A and C fall 4 to 5 points by step 8. At step 12 it leads A by 8 points at seed 43 (p=.057) and by 1 point at seed 42. With 100 tasks, no OT-TBLite difference between arms is significant on its own. In B's step-12 OT-TBLite run, 13 trials across 10 tasks ended in Daytona sandbox validation errors before Harbor's error gate stopped the job. They count as failed trials, so that score is a lower bound.

## Did the two seeds draw different pivots?

The data-sampling seed changes which pivots B sees, and the two draws share 16 of 612 SWE pivots. Their difficulty is the same. The mean K = 16 pass count of the drawn SWE pivots is 5.22 at seed 42 and 5.26 at seed 43 (chi-square p=.69). For a sample of the Terminal pivots it is 4.00 and 4.04 (Mann-Whitney p=.93). Neither draw contains a SWE-bench Verified repository. The SWE draw was replayed from the sampler and matched the rollout payloads exactly (116 of 116 at the right step). The smaller step-8 gain at seed 43 is not explained by easier or harder pivots.

## Conclusions

- **Selection matters.** B beats C at step 8 at both seeds, by 10.0 and 12.6 points. C is at or below REF at every seed-42 checkpoint and at seed-43 step 8. This is the clearest result of the experiment.
- **Selected pivots help SWE-bench Verified at step 8.** B is above REF by 8.8 and 6.8 points, and above A by 9.2 and 3.0. The first decision rule from the plan, B above A by more than two paired standard errors with no reasoning loss, holds pooled and at seed 42, but not at seed 43 alone.
- **Reasoning benchmarks are not hurt at step 8.** GPQA-Diamond is up for every arm at both seeds. Math500 and MMLU-Pro stay within about a point of REF through step 8. The one significant step-8 loss is A's AIME24 at seed 43, −4.3 points.
- **Every arm drifts by step 12.** Math500 falls 2 to 8 points and MMLU-Pro about 1 to 3 points in all six step-12 runs. SWE-bench rankings at step 12 flip between seeds. The arm that loses most Math500 is the one with the highest policy entropy at step 12, A at seed 42 and B at seed 43.

## Next

- Add the remaining repeat evaluations to the noise estimate above.
- Run past step 8 only with a change that holds the policy near the reference: a stronger KL coefficient, a lower learning rate, no entropy bonus, or a length penalty. The optional B-10 and B-30 arms were not run.

Data: the final collection and plots, with series a, b, c, a-seed43, b-seed43, c-seed43, were produced with `experiments/post_training/pivotrl/mixed_rlvr_analysis.py` from #10411 (`collect`, then `plot --shared-items` and `test`).

🤖 Repeat evaluations, to separate evaluation noise from training-seed variation on SWE-bench Verified. We re-ran SWE-bench Verified on the seed-42 A and B checkpoints at steps 4 and 8. Each repeat used the same checkpoint, harness and strict scoring as the original run. Everything else in the final comment above stands.

| Checkpoint | Original | Repeat | Discordant tasks | Δ | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A step 4 | .288 | .262 | 77 (45 / 32) | −2.6 | .17 |
| A step 8 | .256 | .242 | 83 (45 / 38) | −1.4 | .51 |
| B step 4 | .348 | .340 | 114 (59 / 55) | −0.8 | .78 |
| B step 8 | .348 | .328 | 102 (56 / 46) | −2.0 | .37 |

Rerunning a fixed checkpoint flips 77 to 114 of the 500 tasks and moves the score by up to 2.6 points. Each eval run has a noise standard deviation of roughly 1.4 points. All four repeats came in slightly lower than the originals, by 1.7 points on average. None of the four differences is significant, but the shared direction could come from heavier cluster load during the repeats.

Seed-42 and seed-43 checkpoints of the same arm and step disagree on 91 to 133 tasks. That is somewhat more than the repeats, so the training seed adds variance beyond evaluation noise, mostly at B step 4 (133 discordant, −5.0, p=.037).

B's advantage over A survives re-evaluation:

| Step | B − A, original runs | B − A, repeat runs |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | +6.0 (66 / 36), p=.004 | +7.8 (67 / 28), p<.001 |
| 8 | +9.2 (78 / 32), p<.0001 | +8.6 (76 / 33), p<.0001 |

At seed 42, B's lead over A is a property of the checkpoints and not of one lucky eval run. The seed-43 gaps are smaller, −0.4 at step 4 and +3.0 at step 8. That shortfall comes from training-seed variation, not from evaluation noise. The step-8 conclusion is unchanged: B beats A at both seeds, by an uncertain margin of about 3 to 9 points.

topics.title: [post-training] Axolotl SFT launcher on Iris for the Phase 0 bases
topics.body:
Stage 0 trains the three non-Grug bases through the pinned [`marin-community/axolotl`](https://github.com/marin-community/axolotl) fork used by #6839 and #7427. Marin had no launcher for this work, so submission required a manual handoff, as in #7098. An Axolotl SFT step under `experiments/post_training/` now submits it through Iris.

`AxolotlSpec` requires the pinned base checkpoint and revision, CL12 data manifest, explicit chat template or the tokenizer's builtin template, optimizer settings, and batch geometry. It has no silent defaults. `axolotl_config` builds the fork's training YAML. Setting `tokenizer_save_jinja_files: false` enables the fork's `template_integrity` guard; the pod entrypoint checks again after training that the saved checkpoint embeds the configured template. This prevents the template omission behind the 0%-SWE-bench result in #6839 from silently exporting a checkpoint.

The Iris entrypoint clones the fork at revision `a208d550` with the feature set described in MARIN_FORK.md, installs it, trains, and writes a run manifest with the fork revision, transformers pin, data path, optimizer, and batch geometry.

Transformers `==5.12.1` ships `qwen3_5_moe` and `nemotron_h`, so neither requires a fork change. A CPU test checks that contract against the installed transformers. The fork has no `integrations/expert_parallel`; `AxolotlSpec` rejects `expert_parallel=True` at construction and points to the fork worktree path. Expert parallelism requires a fork PR first.

The Nemotron base repository has no chat template: `tokenizer_config.json` has no `chat_template`, and there is no `chat_template.jinja`. Its runs therefore require an explicit template, which the config builder enforces. The published family template is the intended source under the train-equals-serve rule.

The #6839 masking canary runs for each template against the real tokenizers. It incrementally renders a conversation with reasoning and a tool call, then checks that the supervised region covers assistant turns only (`train_on_inputs=false`), partitions the render, and excludes system, user, and tool-response tokens. The Nemotron canary uses an explicit template because its base has none. A launch command provides the 20-step tiny-model smoke for cluster-only execution.

Part of the Phase 0/1a work for the OPD-SFT controls experiment.

---
[Original description](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10490#issuecomment-6342339617) <!-- marin-prose-cleanup -->
