topics.title: levanter/zephyr: S3 writes to CoreWeave can hang forever (no finite botocore timeout, never requeued)
topics.body:
🤖 _Filed by an agent after hitting this twice while building a Levanter store on CoreWeave._

## Summary

Levanter cache/ledger commits and Zephyr's execution-dir cleanup issue `fsspec`/`s3fs` writes to S3 with **no finite botocore connect/read timeout**. When a request to an S3-compatible endpoint wedges (e.g. a `CompleteMultipartUpload` that never returns, or a recursive `rm`), the call **hangs forever**. Because Zephyr's heartbeat runs on a separate thread, the coordinator keeps seeing the worker as alive (`0 dead`) and **never requeues the shard**, so the whole job stalls indefinitely with no auto-recovery.

This is the same class as #6487 (s3fs/aiobotocore default to *no* timeout), but on the **write/finalize** paths that don't go through `rigging`'s timeout-injecting `open_url`/`url_to_fs`.

## Where it was observed

Building the datakit `(cluster × quality)` Levanter store on `cw-us-east-02a`, reading inputs from R2 and writing the store to CoreWeave object storage (`s3://marin-us-east-02a`, endpoint `cwlota.com`, virtual-hosted). 100,810 shards, ~10.4T tokens. Two distinct indefinite hangs:

### 1. Worker finalization — wedged `CompleteMultipartUpload`
A large shard finished its row processing and hung while closing its per-bucket cache writers. `py-spy dump` showed the **identical** frame across many samples over >6 minutes, RSS flat (~1.35 GB), no OOM/crash:

```
_join_filter_stream_shard (experiments/datakit/store/datakit_store.py)   # ExitStack closing writers
  SerialCacheWriter.__exit__ (levanter/store/cache.py:801)
    _serialize_and_commit (levanter/store/cache.py:615)
      _serialize_json_and_commit (levanter/store/cache.py:890)
        fsspec close -> s3fs _upload_chunk -> commit (s3fs/core.py)       # CompleteMultipartUpload
          asyncio sync -> wait                                            # blocked forever
```
Killing the shard subprocess forced a fresh retry that completed immediately — i.e. it was a single stuck commit on a wedged connection, not a data/compute problem.

### 2. Driver finalization — wedged recursive `rm`
After the map finished, the driver hung in Zephyr's exec-dir cleanup:

```
build_clustered_store -> ZephyrContext.execute
  _cleanup_execution (zephyr/execution.py:148)   # fs.rm(exec_dir, recursive=True)
    fsspec sync -> wait                            # blocked; exec_dir object count flat (~100,831) for minutes
```

## Root cause

`s3fs`/`aiobotocore` default to **no** connect/read timeout. Levanter's cache writers (`TreeStore`/`SerialCacheWriter` ledger commits) write through plain `fsspec` rather than `rigging`'s timeout-injecting helpers, and if the process `FSSPEC_S3` has no `config_kwargs` timeouts, a stuck request never errors and never retries. Zephyr's per-worker heartbeat is a separate thread, so a worker that is *alive but wedged on I/O* keeps heartbeating — the coordinator reports `N in-flight, 0 dead` and never requeues.

## Impact

Any Levanter **store or checkpoint** write to CoreWeave object storage (or any S3-compatible endpoint that occasionally wedges a multipart commit) can hang a job **indefinitely** with no recovery — particularly painful at scale where the probability of at least one wedged connection approaches 1.

## Workaround (used to finish the run; not a fix)

- Set finite timeouts on the default s3 stack via `FSSPEC_S3` `config_kwargs`, e.g. `{"connect_timeout":30,"read_timeout":120,"retries":{"max_attempts":5,"mode":"standard"}}` (plus the `addressing_style: virtual` that CoreWeave requires).
- Manually `kill` the wedged shard subprocess to force a Zephyr retry; for the driver cleanup hang, re-run with `--aggregate-only` (skips the zephyr pass + its cleanup) which finishes from the durable sidecars.

## Suggested fix directions (intentionally not implemented in this issue)

- Give Levanter's cache writers finite botocore timeouts — route their fsspec/tensorstore-adjacent writes through `rigging`'s timeout-injecting filesystem, or construct the s3 filesystem with `config_kwargs` timeouts.
- Ensure Zephyr's `_cleanup_execution` (and any result/coordination I/O) uses finite timeouts.
- Consider making Zephyr's heartbeat/liveness detect a *stuck* task (no forward progress for N minutes), not just process liveness, so an alive-but-wedged worker is requeued.
- Have the cluster-injected `FSSPEC_S3` include finite timeouts by default.

## References
- #6487 — same no-timeout class on the read/upload path.
- #6677 — rigging: preserve `FSSPEC_S3` `config_kwargs` (addressing_style) in the S3 timeout-defaults injection.
- #6676 — levanter: tensorstore virtual-hosted S3 for CoreWeave.

comments.body:
🤖 Still live on current `main`, on a write path the existing timeout injection does not cover: zephyr's scatter/shuffle write, not a Levanter cache writer.

Datakit `normalized/dolma4pdfs` normalize on cw-rno2a (writing `s3://marin-us-east-02a`, `cwlota.com`). The map stage froze at 38942/38944 for ~5h — `2 in-flight, 0 queued, 1024/1024 workers alive, 0 dead`, no errors or requeues. `py-spy dump` of the wedged `zephyr.shard_subprocess`, stable across samples, ~22s CPU over ~10h wall (idle):

```
close (zephyr/shuffle.py:636)
  _write_scatter (zephyr/shuffle.py:730)
    _write_stage_output (zephyr/stage_io.py:240)
      flush/close (fsspec/spec.py) -> _upload_chunk -> upload_part (s3fs/core.py:2459)
        sync -> wait (fsspec/asyn.py:91 -> threading.py)   # blocked forever
```

Why it is unfixed on this path: `rigging/filesystem/factory.py` injects `connect_timeout`/`read_timeout`/`retries`, but only for filesystems built via its `url_to_fs`/`open_url`. The zephyr scatter write uses a bare s3fs from the ambient `FSSPEC_S3`, and the cluster-injected `FSSPEC_S3` still carries no timeouts — the live cw-rno2a task-env is `{"endpoint_url":"http://cwlota.com","client_kwargs":{"region_name":"auto"},"config_kwargs":{"s3":{"addressing_style":"virtual"}}}`. Both remaining fix directions from the report still apply here: default finite timeouts in the cluster `FSSPEC_S3`, and routing zephyr's shuffle/result I/O through the timeout-injecting filesystem.

Recovery without a re-drive: `iris job kick --state preempted <worker-task>` on the wedged workers forces the attempt terminal, the coordinator requeues those shards, fresh workers complete them, and the stage advanced (now in stage1-Reduce). Cleaner than manually killing the subprocess.

🤖

# Research

Iris generates cluster `FSSPEC_S3` with endpoint, region, and addressing settings only; the finite 30/120-second timeout and five-attempt defaults are added only by rigging filesystem entry points. Raw fsspec consumers such as Levanter checkpoint metadata and temp-directory uploads bypass those entry points, so a wedged S3 request can remain live while the worker heartbeat continues.

**Relevant code**
- [`s3_compat.py#L39-L50`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/filesystem/s3_compat.py#L39-L50) - ambient config omits timeouts
- [`factory.py#L38-L63`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/filesystem/factory.py#L38-L63) - wrapper-only timeout defaults
- [`controller.py#L739-L761`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/controller.py#L739-L761) - task environment injection
- [`cloud_utils.py#L136-L163`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/utils/cloud_utils.py#L136-L163) - raw fsspec upload
- [`checkpoint.py#L1116-L1122`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py#L1116-L1122) - raw checkpoint filesystem

# Proposed Fix

`IrisProvider._s3_task_env()` → `fsspec_s3_conf()` → `fsspec.get_fs_token_paths()` currently constructs an S3 filesystem without finite botocore bounds. Add the shared timeout/retry defaults to `fsspec_s3_conf()` while preserving endpoint-specific addressing; generated CoreWeave task environments will then fail wedged requests into the existing task retry path, and explicit caller-supplied `FSSPEC_S3` remains untouched.

🤖 Implemented in #7547. Generated CoreWeave `FSSPEC_S3` now carries `connect_timeout=30`, `read_timeout=120`, and five standard retries, so raw fsspec consumers use finite request bounds while virtual-host addressing and explicit caller configuration remain intact. The 471 rigging tests, 36 focused Iris/CoreWeave tests, all-files lint/type checks, hosted unit and integration suites, CoreWeave/GCP smokes, CodeQL, and docs checks pass.

🤖 Reopening. #7547 is live in the task environment and the same hang still occurs.

Job `/rav/datakit-normalize-all-pending-20260730-rno2a`, child `zephyr-normalize-334637d5-p0-a0`, on cw-rno2a, writing `s3://marin-us-east-02a` through `http://cwlota.com`. Stage 0 froze at `8163/8196 complete, 33 in-flight, 0 queued, 1024/1024 workers alive, 0 dead; items=172.90M` and stayed there for more than 13 hours. Coordinator lines sampled at 07:00, 07:30, 08:00, 09:00, 12:00, and 18:00 UTC are the same. Exactly 33 workers still log, one per in-flight shard. Each holds a distinct `UploadId` at a low `PartNumber` (parts 2, 3, and 4 on the three I inspected).

The `FSSPEC_S3` change from #7547 did reach the process. `/proc/<pid>/environ` in the wedged pod contains `read_timeout`, `connect_timeout`, `max_attempts`, `addressing_style`, and `endpoint_url`. The upload hung anyway. The missing config was one cause, and not the only one.

Three measurements from the wedged shard subprocess (PID 2985, shard 3984, up 13h14m) show why nothing can end the wait.

TCP: fd 13 maps to socket inode 292120618, `10.168.219.199:64008 -> 10.0.1.172:80`, `state=ESTABLISHED tx_queue=0 rx_queue=0 retransmits=0 tm->when=00:00000000`. The request went out in full and the peer acknowledged it. No response byte, FIN, or RST arrived, and no TCP timer is armed.

asyncio: the loop thread sits in `epoll_wait(epfd=4, maxevents=2, timeout=-1)`, sampled four times across 25 minutes, always -1. In `BaseEventLoop._run_once`, a `None` selector timeout requires an empty `self._scheduled`, so no `call_later` handle exists and no read timeout is armed for this request. The loop watches fd 13 for `EPOLLIN|EPOLLERR|EPOLLHUP`. It recorded 0 voluntary context switches across 50 seconds.

Caller: `fsspec.asyn.sync` has local `timeout=None` and loops `Event.wait(1)` with no exit.

`py-spy dump --locals` of the main thread, the same across three dumps 38 seconds apart except the poll waiter lock address:

```
sync (fsspec/asyn.py:91)
    timeout: None
    args:   (<S3FileSystem>, "upload_part", {})
    kwargs: {"Bucket": "marin-us-east-02a", "PartNumber": 2,
             "UploadId": "883c5a93-861e-44d5-8f0b-257f4b4cfbae", ...}
    result: [None]
_upload_chunk (s3fs/core.py:2484)  final: False   min_chunk: 52428800
flush (fsspec/spec.py:2080)
write (fsspec/spec.py:2039)        out: 3713055
_flush (zephyr/shuffle.py:575)     target: 6309   offset: 104444980
close (zephyr/shuffle.py:634)      close_flushes: 4629
```

The process is not stopped, and no profiler is involved. `TracerPid` is 0 on the process and on all 266 threads, every thread is in state `S`, `SigPnd` and `ShdPnd` are 0, and the main thread makes exactly 50 voluntary context switches per 50 seconds. The freeze also predates the first profile by 12.5 hours.

A larger `read_timeout` will not help here, because the value never becomes a live timer on the response wait. A fix needs a total request deadline: an aiohttp `ClientTimeout(total=...)` on the s3fs session, or a finite `timeout` passed into `fsspec.asyn.sync` from zephyr's scatter write path.

`iris job kick --state preempted <worker-task>` still recovers a wedged worker without a re-drive. The 33 tasks in this run are untouched, in case anyone wants to inspect them first.

🤖 Correcting the mechanism I gave above. The observations stand; the explanation was wrong, and the real cause is narrower.

I claimed `sock_read` only limits the gap between bytes after a response starts, so nothing bounds the wait for the first response byte. That is not true. Against a peer that accepts a request and stays silent, `sock_read` fires at exactly its configured value — with a 1 KB body and with a 52 MB body fully drained, on a fresh connection and on a reused keep-alive connection. Same `aiohttp 3.14.1` / `aiobotocore 2.26.0` / `s3fs 2026.1.0` as the task image. I also rebuilt the filesystem through `rigging.filesystem.url_to_fs` inside a live worker of that job and confirmed `read_timeout=120` is applied, so the config did reach the client.

The actual cause is the `Expect: 100-continue` handshake. botocore sets that header on every `UploadPart`. aiohttp waits for the interim response **before** writing the body, and no scalar bound covers that wait, because no read is in flight for `sock_read` to arm against.

Same peer, same session, only the header varying:

```
no Expect header        -> ReadTimeoutError at 8.02s
Expect: 100-continue    -> still waiting at 30s, body bytes sent = 0
Expect + total=10       -> ReadTimeoutError at 10.37s
```

That accounts for the production evidence I posted, including the parts my earlier explanation left loose:

- the body is never written, so server-side `ListParts` showed the blocked part missing for all 32 open uploads
- only headers were sent and acknowledged, so `tx_queue=0` and `rx_queue=0`
- the expect100 wait sits on a bare future, so `_scheduled` is empty and the loop parks in `epoll_wait(timeout=-1)`
- 13 hours elapsed with `read_timeout=120` correctly applied

Method note for whoever picks this up: my first four probes called `AIOHTTPSession.send()` with a bare `AWSRequest`, which does not carry the `Expect` header that botocore adds for S3 operations. They exercised a different code path than production and produced a confident wrong answer in both directions. Reproducing through the real client path — `url_to_fs` to s3fs to `fsspec.asyn.sync` on the fsspec IO loop — is what surfaced it.

The conclusion is unchanged: a larger `read_timeout` cannot fix this, and a whole-request deadline can. #7807 adds `total=600` via `http_session_cls` and carries a regression test that withholds `100 Continue` and asserts the body is still unsent.

The CoreWeave side of this is also sharper than I first described. Their endpoint accepted request headers for 32 concurrent uploads inside a 36-second window across 26 nodes and sent no `100 Continue`, no error, no FIN, and no RST. They did not receive the bodies, contrary to what I wrote earlier.

topics.title: evaluating whether a model spends the right amount of thinking
topics.body:
# Proposal: `think-budget-calibration`: evaluating whether a model spends the right amount of thinking

**Related:** #7090 (Epic: new evals for Marin — wish-list)

## 1. Summary

An eval suite that measures **compute allocation quality**, not accuracy: does the model spend tokens in proportion to (A) how hard the item is, and (B) whether it has any realistic chance of solving it at all?

Models are scored against an **oracle allocator** that knows, per item, the minimum budget at which *that model* succeeds. Headline metric is the fraction of the oracle-vs-uniform gap recovered at equal total budget, decomposed into three named failure terms.

| ID | Task | Measures | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **TBC-1** | Effort–Difficulty Calibration | Does token spend track model-relative difficulty? | generation |
| **TBC-2** | Futility Detection | Does it stop early on items it cannot solve at any budget? | generation |
| **TBC-3** | Budget Self-Report Probe | Logprob-only forced choice over difficulty buckets | logprob, in-loop |

## 2. Prior work

- **OptimalThinkingBench** (arXiv 2508.13141): OverthinkingBench + UnderthinkingBench with thinking-adjusted accuracy. No model out of 33 evaluated thinking and non-thinking models is optimal on both halves. Needs an LLM judge.
- **AbstentionBench** (arXiv 2506.09038): 20 datasets of unanswerable/underspecified items. Reasoning fine-tuning degrades abstention ~24%; raising the thinking budget makes it worse.
- **TRIAGE** (arXiv 2605.13414): closest neighbour. task pool + self-calibrated budget, model commits to an ordered plan, scored against a knapsack oracle. Names the right object: abstention in AbstentionBench is a property of the *question*, but what matters is the *model–task–budget triple*.
- **TALE / L1 / SelfBudgeter**: budget-following as a control problem, not a measurement one.

All of the above evaluate frontier models, one task at a time, and mostly presuppose that the model can follow a budget instruction.

## 3. What this suite lets us test

1. **Emergence during pretraining.** Run TBC-3 across an open scaling ladder and within-run checkpoint sequences: does difficulty-awareness appear before, with, or after the ability to solve the item? This needs published intermediate checkpoints across a FLOP range, which most projects do not have.
2. **Allocation quality without budget-following.** Measure natural token spend and score it against the oracle at the same total. Requires no instruction-following, so it works on SFT-only checkpoints and on base models with few-shot CoT.
3. **Real difficulty estimation vs. surface-cue regression.** Matched pairs, equal token count and unequal solution depth, separate "spends more on hard problems" from "spends more on long prompts".
4. **The futility threshold, as a curve.** Procedural tool-required items (exact 40x40-digit multiplication, character indexing over 4k strings) parameterised by digit count give a per-model boundary for "no realistic chance with what I have", rather than a binary answerable/unanswerable label. Judge-free.
5. **Which of three failure modes a checkpoint has.** Overthinking, futility waste, and starvation are separately reported rather than collapsed into one efficiency scalar.
6. **Whether budget-following and calibration dissociate.** Declared vs. actual spend is measured separately from allocation quality, so a model can be good at one and bad at the other.

## 4. Design

**Ground truth.** For model `M`, item `i`, over budget grid `G = {64, 256, 1024, 4096}`:

```
b*_i = min { b ∈ G : M answers i correctly under budget b }   (∞ if never)
S    = { i : b*_i < ∞ }
```

`b*` is a property of the (model, item) pair, so it is recomputed per checkpoint. Report alongside intrinsic difficulty `d_i` (generator parameter, or MATH level): tracking `d_i` is a population prior; tracking `b*_i` beyond `d_i` is self-knowledge.

**Regime.** Primary is *emergent* — no budget instruction, record natural spend `a_i`, set `B = Σ a_i`, score against the oracle at that same `B`. Advisory and enforced regimes (model declares its own per-item budgets, non-binding then binding) are secondary; expect weak compliance on non-RL-trained checkpoints and report it separately from calibration.

**Item pools** (~200 each): `trivial` (overthinking probe), `ladder` (procedural, parametric difficulty), `math-levels` (external validity), `surface-control` (matched pairs — equal token count, unequal solution depth). Futility items: underspecified variants, false premise, and the tool-required sweep.

**TBC-3** is generation-free — score bucket logprobs on a fixed continuation (`Difficulty for me: {EASY|MEDIUM|HARD|IMPOSSIBLE}`) using the existing `choice_logprob` path. Metric: ρ against `b*_i`, plus AUROC of `P(IMPOSSIBLE)` against `1[b*_i = ∞]`. Verbalised self-report is a known-weak signal, but it is nearly free and the *trajectory* across checkpoints is meaningful even when the absolute level is not.

**Generator.** Reuse #7090's difficulty ladder (multi-axis vector, D1–D5 presets, procedural instances with provably correct answers). It already produces known ordinal difficulty plus programmatic grading — the expensive part. Futility items are the same generator with a premise deleted or the digit count pushed past threshold. Recommend it lives in #7090 and is imported here.

## 5. Metrics

**Headline — `η_alloc`** at total budget `B`:

```
V_oracle  = max #items solvable within B   (0-1 knapsack over S, weights b*_i)
V_uniform = |{ i : b*_i ≤ B/n }|
η_alloc   = (V_model − V_uniform) / (V_oracle − V_uniform)
```

Uniform, not random, is the right reference: the alternative to good allocation isn't random selection; it's spending the same everywhere, which is what models actually do. Also report normalized regret `(V_oracle − V_model)/V_oracle`, stable when `V_oracle ≈ V_uniform`.

**Decomposition of the gap** — same separate-the-failure-modes move as dual grading in #7090:

- **Overthinking tax** `Σ_{i∈S, correct} max(0, a_i − b*_i)` — tokens past the point of success
- **Futility waste** `Σ_{b*_i = ∞} a_i` — tokens no budget would have saved
- **Starvation loss** `|{ i∈S : a_i < b*_i }|` — items abandoned below threshold

**Supporting:** partial ρ(`a_i`, `b*_i`) controlling for `d_i`; **surface-control delta** (ρ within matched pairs only — a large drop means the model is reading prompt features, not estimating difficulty); futility detection and waste rates (adopt TRIAGE's definitions for comparability); raw accuracy always reported alongside, since `η_alloc` alone would reward answering everything in 10 tokens.

## 6. Making the sweep affordable

Naive cost is `|G| × n` full generations per checkpoint. Instead: generate one greedy trace per item at `B_max`, then for each `b ∈ G` truncate the thinking, append `\n</think>\nFinal answer:`, and generate ≤32 tokens from the cached prefix. Cost drops from `Σ_b b` to `B_max + |G|·32`.

This is s1's budget-forcing used as a measurement device, and it biases low — a truncated trace underestimates a model that natively knew it had budget `b`. **Phase 1 gate:** re-generate 50 items natively at each `b`; if rank correlation with truncation-derived `b*` is below ~0.8, drop the trick and coarsen the grid instead.

Greedy decoding throughout (`do_sample=False`), consistent with #6235. Exception: `k=4` at `t=0.7` on futility items, where a single greedy failure is weak evidence for `b*_i = ∞`.

## 7. Plan

- **Phase 0** — TBC-3 as an lm-eval-harness task on an in-house base and SFT checkpoint pair. Logprob only, no GPU. Validates harness, generator, metrics at zero generation cost.
- **Phase 1** — full emergent-regime pipeline on two external ~1–2B models that fit a free-tier T4: one hybrid-thinking model (gives thinking/non-thinking arms from one checkpoint) and one reasoning-distilled model. Validates the truncation trick; produces first `η_alloc` and decomposition.
- **Phase 2** — in-house checkpoints via the existing vLLM path. With no thinking mode available, this measures natural CoT spend under few-shot prompting — an under-reported regime.
- **Phase 3** — TBC-3 across the scaling ladder and within-run checkpoints. Plot ρ and solve rate against FLOPs on one axis. This is the part that is a paper, not a dashboard number.

## 8. Open questions

1. Is compute-priced evaluation in scope for the dashboard, or better as a standalone artifact that imports checkpoints?
2. Is there appetite for running TBC-3 across the scaling ladder? Highest-value experiment here, and the one needing maintainer compute rather than contributor compute.
3. Is a thinking-mode or RL-trained checkpoint on the roadmap? If so, the budget-following regimes become far more informative and should be designed against that target now.

comments.body: @penfever Can you look at these issue

Some details that might enrich the plan.

- The task choice might affect the budget style. If the pattern is generalizable across different tasks (or task groups), maybe starting with task with shorter budgets is a better idea (an extreme example is SWE vs simpleQA).

- How is Pt 4 in Section 3 being tested here?

- Would the budget setting limits the task choice (e.g. math reasoning), and is this preference expected?

- If budget-controlled training strategy is included in the checkpoints, the model choice should include this into consideration if accessible (even though they are beyond the budget choice).

@Nativeatom 

**1. Task choice affecting budget style:**
Agree on starting short, disagree on assuming generalization. TRIAGE found triage quality doesn't transfer across benchmarks, so cross-family transfer should be a reported result, not a design assumption. v0 stays single-turn with ≤1k-token horizons; a second family gets added only once within-family η is stable, and transfer is measured explicitly. SWE-style agentic tasks are out of scope for v0 regardless — the budget object there is turns × tokens, not tokens, so `b*` isn't the same quantity.

**2. How Pt 4 is tested.**
The concrete test: sweep the generator's difficulty parameter n (digit count), and at each n record solve rate, mean tokens spent, and abstain rate. That gives two thresholds — `n_cap` where accuracy hits zero, and `n_behav` where spend drops or abstention rises. The metric is the **lag** `n_behav − n_cap`; a calibrated model has lag ≈ 0, and the known failure is `n_behav` sitting far past `n_cap`. Futility waste then gets restricted to `n > n_cap` rather than computed over a hand-labelled set. 

**3. Does the budget setting constrain task choice.**
Yes — it needs programmatic grading, single-turn, and an answer that's still verifiable after truncation, which pushes toward math/code/procedural. Same bias exists in UnderthinkingBench and TALE. It's expected but the domain isn't the axis that matters; "thinking pays" vs "thinking doesn't pay" is, and the `trivial` pool covers the second. Real limitation to state plainly: no free-form or long-form generation in v0, so nothing here speaks to calibration where quality isn't binary.

**4. Budget-controlled training as a covariate.**
Agree. A length-RL'd model can post good η_alloc because its spend was shaped in training, not because it estimates difficulty — so provenance has to be recorded and results stratified by it (no length control / prompt-budget SFT / length-RL). Worth including one length-controlled checkpoint deliberately, as an upper-reference arm rather than a comparison point. Sharper consequence for §3.1: if length shaping enters partway through a training run, the emergence curve across that run's checkpoints is contaminated — those sweeps need checkpoints from before the stage, or the stage boundary marked on the plot.

I like the model-relative framing here, but I think these points need to be resolved before implementation:

1. How does Phase 0 get the `b*_i` labels without running generations? TBC-3 is scored against `b*_i`, but those labels only exist after evaluating each item over the budget grid. Should TBC-3 move after the first generation sweep, or should Phase 0 use the generator’s intrinsic difficulty `d_i` as its target?

2. How should the oracle handle non-monotonic results across budgets? A model may succeed at 256 tokens and fail at 1024, so retaining only the minimum successful budget loses information and makes the uniform baseline unreliable. Could the design retain the observed result or success probability for every `(item, budget)` pair and compute the oracle from that curve? Items with no success should be described as “unsolved within the tested grid,” rather than impossible.

3. What exactly counts as natural thinking spend `a_i`? This needs a fixed rule for models without `<think>` delimiters, responses that hit the maximum output length, and responses that produce an answer without explicit reasoning. Without that definition, the total budget `B` is not reproducible across models or checkpoints.

4. Where will the initial task pool come from? #7090 is a wishlist and does not currently provide the referenced D1–D5 generator. Could the v0 scope define one concrete task family, generator parameters and seeds, programmatic grader, item count, and matched-pair construction? That would make the first implementation and its acceptance criteria clear.

@mrinal-bespoke thanks for the questions. All of them are relevant and below are the detailed responses to each of them: 

## 1. Phase 0 circularity

TBC-3 has two targets conflated into one task, so I will split them like: 

- **TBC-3a — intrinsic.** Target is the generator's difficulty parameter `d_i`, known at item-construction time. Generation-free, no sweep, runs in-loop. Claim: *the model has learned the population difficulty prior.*
- **TBC-3b — model-relative.** Target is the model's own success curve. Requires the sweep, so it runs after the first generation pass. Claim: *the model knows what is hard for itself.* The `P(IMPOSSIBLE)` AUROC metric also lives here, since it needs the sweep too.

Phase 0 therefore reports 3a only, and is honest about being a plumbing-and-prior check rather than a self-knowledge result. The interesting quantity — partial ρ against the success curve controlling for `d_i` — is a Phase 1 deliverable.

Consequence for the scaling-ladder experiment: 3a runs across the full ladder cheaply; 3b needs a sweep per checkpoint, so it runs on a subsample of 8–12 checkpoints spanning the FLOP range. Worth stating that the emergence plot has two curves at different resolutions rather than one.

## 2. Non-monotonicity

Agreed, and scalar `b*_i` should go. Replace it with the full curve.

For each item and each grid point, estimate `s_i(b) ∈ [0,1]` from `k` samples and retain every `(i, b)` pair. The oracle then becomes a **multiple-choice knapsack**: each item selects exactly one `b ∈ G ∪ {0}` at cost `b` and value `s_i(b)`, maximising `Σ s_i(b_i)` subject to `Σ b_i ≤ B`. Exact DP over budget discretised at the grid's gcd — no monotonicity assumption anywhere, and it's cheaper than the 0-1 formulation it replaces. `V_uniform = Σ s_i(B/n)` snapped to the nearest grid point.

Terminology fixed as you suggest: `U_G` = **unsolved within the tested grid at k samples**, with `G` and `k` stated in every table. No impossibility claim.

`b*_i` survives only as a derived reporting convenience, `argmin{b : s_i(b) ≥ 0.5}`, never as the object the oracle is computed from.

## 3. Defining `a_i`

- `a_i` = generated tokens from end of prompt to the first token of the extracted answer span, **excluding** the answer span, counted in the evaluated model's own tokenizer.
- **With `<think>` delimiters:** tokens inside the delimiters. Both figures are logged; they should agree, and a disagreement means the answer-extraction regex is wrong.
- **No explicit reasoning** (answer emitted immediately): `a_i = 0`. This is a valid measurement and the correct behaviour on trivial items, not a degenerate case.
- **Hit the cap without a parseable answer:** `a_i = cap`, `s_i(b) = 0` for that pair, flagged as truncated. **Truncation rate is reported; if it exceeds 10% at `B_max` the cap is too low and `B_max` must be raised before the run counts.**
- **Post-answer continuation:** excluded from `a_i`, logged separately as trailing tokens so total serving cost is still recoverable.
- Answer extraction is one regex per task family, owned by the grader.

Cross-model comparability: token counts are in each model's own tokenizer, so absolute `B` is not comparable across models. Within-model curves use raw tokens; cross-model comparisons normalise by that model's median spend on the trivial pool.

## 4. v0 task pool

Correct, and thanks for catching it — the D1–D5 generator was something I proposed in the wishlist thread, not something that exists. Dropping the dependency; v0 defines its own family standalone. If the proxy-benchmark generator does land later it can be upstreamed, but nothing here should block on it.

**Family: `mulcarry`** — exact integer multiplication with controlled carry structure. Chosen because one generator covers every mechanism the design needs.

- **Parameters:** `(n_digits, carry_density, seed)`. Operands are sampled to hit a target carry density at fixed digit count.
- **Why this family:** surface length is exactly `n_digits`, so difficulty and prompt length are decoupled by construction — matched pairs are trivial to build rather than curated. CoT genuinely pays (long multiplication is unreachable at 64 tokens, reachable at 1024), so the budget response is informative. Grading is exact integer comparison. And the futility sweep is the same knob pushed further, so the threshold curve needs no separate item source.
- **Grader:** strip non-digits from the extracted span, compare as integers.
- **Seeding:** items are a deterministic function of `(family, n_digits, carry_density, index)` under one published master seed; the generator reproduces the item set byte-identically.

| Pool | Parameters | Items |
|---|---|---|
| `trivial` | `n_digits ∈ {1,2}`, low carry | 60 |
| `ladder` | `n_digits ∈ {2..6} × carry_density ∈ {0.1,0.5,0.9}` | 300 |
| `surface-control` | fixed `n_digits`, `carry_density` 0.1 vs 0.9, paired | 60 pairs |
| `futility-sweep` | `n_digits ∈ {8,12,16,24,32,40}` | 150 |

~630 items. With `|G| = 4` and the truncation trick that's roughly 1.4M generated tokens per checkpoint — around 13h on a free-tier T4 at 1.5B, so a reduced smoke config (`ladder` seeds cut to 10, `|G| = 3`, ~350 items) is the default for iteration and the full config is a single overnight run.

MATH-by-level stays in the design as external validity but is explicitly **out of v0 scope**, since it brings a difficulty label we don't control and a grader we'd have to trust.

**v0 acceptance criteria:**

1. Generator reproduces the item set byte-identically from the published seed.
2. Grader agrees with hand-checking on 50 sampled traces, zero false accepts.
3. Non-monotonicity rate reported, with truncation-derived and natively-generated curves compared on a 50-item subsample.
4. `η_alloc` plus the three-term decomposition computed end-to-end on one sub-2B model.
5. Surface-control delta reported — if global ρ survives but within-pair ρ collapses, the eval is measuring prompt length and v0 has failed its own check.

topics.title: [finelog] Record container state before Harbor task execution
topics.body:
Capture and retain the exact prepared container state in Finelog after all setup and agent dependency installation and before the first agent action. Include the inner agent environment after setup installs dependencies; an outer image digest or project `uv.lock` does not describe packages installed later inside a nested container. Finelog is the durable record; collection must happen at the Iris/Harbor runtime boundary that can inspect the environment.

In the identity-SFT campaign, Harbor ran `uv tool install mini-swe-agent==2.1.0 --with mcp==2.3.0` in an inner Docker container. The outer Harbor lock pinned LiteLLM 1.92.0, but did not constrain this separate environment. Historical `vendor/harbor/src/harbor/agents/installed/base.py::_exec` attached captured stdout/stderr as logging `extra` fields on the message `Command outputs captured`; `trial/trial.py::_init_logger` used a default file formatter that omitted those fields. Retained logs and trial archives therefore do not establish the installed inner LiteLLM version. This prevented attributing exposure to a reported compromised package; it is not proof of installation or exfiltration. Related: #10262 (dependency drift and missing agent output), #9816 (sandbox isolation).

Done when:

- Before task execution, a durable snapshot records immutable image identity, build/source provenance, runtime/container identity, setup commands and outcomes, and resolved dependency inventories for every agent environment prepared by that boundary. Preserve lockfiles where present, exact installed versions and available package artifact hashes/origins; explicitly record missing provenance.
- Capture both initial container state and the post-install state handed to agent execution, including OS packages, Python tool environments and other agent package managers. Record runtime mounts, privilege, network settings and environment variable names without credential values. Use immutable filesystem/layer identity plus a content manifest for setup-time changes so package lists alone are not represented as exact filesystem state.
- Finelog records link snapshots and installer stdout/stderr to cluster, job, task attempt, Harbor trial and timestamps. Large artifacts may live in durable object storage with checksums and queryable Finelog references; the record survives container deletion and retries do not overwrite it.
- Successful installer output is retained, not just a message saying it was captured. Retain completed setup commands, installer output and available partial state when setup fails. Redact credentials from every retained artifact, including output, lockfiles and provenance URLs. Describe mounts without copying mounted datasets or secrets; mark all exclusions so the record does not imply a fully reconstructable filesystem. Collection must not import newly installed packages to inspect them.
- Harbor does not begin agent task execution until snapshot persistence succeeds; failures have a visible setup error.
- An integration test installs a dependency differing from the outer lock, deletes the nested container, and reconstructs the actual version and container identity from retained evidence. Cover setup failure, capture failure, retry separation and secret redaction.

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Marin's pinned Harbor driver delegates trial preparation to Harbor, so the Iris task sees the outer process while `Trial._prepare()` creates and installs into the inner agent environment before `_run()`. The installed-agent helper truncates command output and attaches it to logging `extra`; the trial logger does not persist those fields, and neither boundary records the prepared container state. Finelog's `Table.write()` is buffered and may drop rows, so its `flush()` cannot enforce the requested pre-execution persistence gate. No open PR found for #10481 or this root cause.

**Relevant code**
- [`trial.py#L222-L229`](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/14777c013bee9d75821bc19dd2f35824bc9f3e96/src/harbor/trial/trial.py#L222-L229) — preparation before agent run
- [`base.py#L304-L369`](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/14777c013bee9d75821bc19dd2f35824bc9f3e96/src/harbor/agents/installed/base.py#L304-L369) — installer output capture
- [`base.py#L694-L823`](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/14777c013bee9d75821bc19dd2f35824bc9f3e96/src/harbor/environments/base.py#L694-L823) — environment contract lacks inspection
- [`log_client.py#L278-L330`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finelog/src/finelog/client/log_client.py#L278-L330) — buffered write and flush
- [`stats_service.rs#L131-L163`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finelog/rust/src/server/stats_service.rs#L131-L163) — acknowledged durable write

# Proposed Fix

## Design

Add a Harbor trial setup recorder at the boundary that owns the leaf agent environment. `Trial._prepare()` records an **initial** state immediately after environment start and a **prepared** state after healthcheck, uploads, and `agent.setup()`, before any agent task action. On setup failure it records completed commands, their output, and the available partial state before finalizing the trial. A snapshot failure raises a typed setup error, so `_run()` is never entered. Add an inspection contract to `BaseEnvironment`; implement it for Docker (Linux and Windows) and Daytona direct/DinD, including the inner `main` container in DinD. An environment that cannot supply the required identity and inventory fails setup visibly.

Each state record identifies the actual container/sandbox and immutable image or root filesystem digest, Harbor and build source revision, build inputs, timestamp, runtime mounts (paths and mode only), privilege/network settings, and environment variable **names**. Collect OS, `uv`/`pip`, Node, Cargo, and other agent package-manager inventories, including every Python tool environment, with installed versions, available artifact hashes/origins, and sanitized lockfiles. Inspect distribution metadata and package-manager output without importing installed packages. Pair the base filesystem/layer identity with a hashed manifest of setup-time changes in the writable layer. Exclude mounted datasets, secret paths, and other uninspected roots explicitly; never describe an excluded filesystem as reconstructable. Provider-specific inspection must report unavailable fields rather than substitute the outer image or lock.

Record environment build commands and all setup-phase `environment.exec` calls at their common boundary, including successful stdout/stderr, exit status, and timing. Redact before any Finelog, artifact, logger, `config.json`, or exception write: use known injected secret values and encoded forms, credential-bearing URL parts and auth fields, plus explicit secret-path exclusions. Keep raw output transient in memory; reject persistence if sanitization or inventory validation fails. This also requires replacing the installed-agent helper's truncated `extra`-only output path for setup commands.

Write immutable artifacts under `output_dir/harbor_evidence/<job>/<iris-attempt>/<trial>/<digest>`, with SHA-256 checksums. Keep this prefix outside trial directories: [Marin deletes unscored trial directories on retry](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py#L157-L169). Add queryable Finelog snapshot and setup-command rows keyed by cluster, Iris task ID/attempt, Harbor job/trial, phase, and capture timestamp; rows carry artifact URI, checksum, status, and exclusions. Upload and verify artifacts first, then use a synchronous Finelog write whose successful response means the row is durable. Do not use `Table.write()`/`flush()` for this gate: that API marks dropped rows processed. Give the Finelog namespace and artifact store matching forensic retention, and use unique attempt identities so retries never overwrite evidence. Marin passes the Iris/cluster identity into Harbor and advances its Harbor pin after the Harbor changes land.

## Delivery and tests

1. Add a strict acknowledged Finelog writer and the snapshot/command schemas, with a test that rejects dropped or failed writes.
2. Add Harbor provider inspection and setup recording, including sanitized build and installer output and partial failure records.
3. Wire the Marin driver identity and pin, then run a local Docker integration test: install an inner dependency at a version different from the outer lock, delete the container, and recover its exact version and container identity from Finelog plus checked artifacts. Cover setup failure, capture/write failure blocking execution, retry separation, and secrets in stdout, lockfiles, URLs, and existing trial artifacts. Exercise Daytona direct/DinD provider contracts in their dedicated integration environment.

## Open questions

- Can Daytona direct expose an immutable leaf filesystem/image identity and a complete writable-layer change list? If not, which provider capability must be added before enabling the gate there?
- What retention window should the new Finelog namespace and referenced artifacts share? The current issue specifies durability across deletion and retries but no time bound.

topics.title: [pulumi] Import Github into Pulumi
topics.body:
* Import existing non-secrets into Pulumi
* Regenerate secrets and store them in into Secret Manager, then link them to Github with Pulumi

comments.body:
🤖 **Analysis — not opening a PR.** This is multi-step infra work that needs live GitHub org-admin + GCP Secret Manager access, `pulumi import` against live state, and (item 2) production secret rotation. That is destructive and owner-driven, outside what an agent should execute blindly. Handing off a proposed approach for review.

# Research

The `github` Pulumi project today records Actions **secrets** only, as read-only external lookups (`.get()` — the stack cannot create, update, or rotate them). No non-secret resources (variables/environments/repo settings) are managed, and no secret is sourced from Secret Manager; `source_ref` values are recovery metadata only, never dereferenced. So both issue items are net-new.

The manifest already carries the disposition metadata that scopes this work:
- `move-to-variable` (item 1): `GCP_PROJECT_ID` (org + repo), `IRIS_CI_GCP_SSH_KEY_PUB`, `NIGHTSHIFT_APP_ID`.
- `gcp-secret://…` already pinned to a Secret Manager version (item 2 candidates): `DISCORD_WEBHOOK_CODE_REVIEW`, `DISCORD_WEBHOOK_INTERNAL_DISCUSS`, `HF_TOKEN`, `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN`.
- `replace-with-oidc` (out of scope here, but blocks rotating those): `IRIS_CI_GCP_SA_KEY`, `IRIS_CI_GCP_SSH_KEY`, `MARIN_CD_CLOUD_RUN_SA_KEY`.

**Relevant code**
- [`github/__main__.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi/github/__main__.py) — stack entry; only registers credentials.
- [`resources.py#L66-L90`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi/src/iac/github/resources.py#L66-L90) — read-only `ActionsSecret.get()`; no variable resources.
- [`Pulumi.marin-community.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi/github/Pulumi.marin-community.yaml) — dispositions per credential.
- [`github/README.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi/github/README.md) — states variables/environments/settings "can be added here as normally managed Pulumi resources."

# Proposed Approach

**Item 1 — non-secrets (non-destructive, safe to land first).**
1. Add `variable`-scope support to the manifest schema (`credentials.py`) or a parallel `variables` block, and emit `github.ActionsVariable` / `ActionsOrganizationVariable` as *managed* (not `.get()`) resources in `resources.py`.
2. Seed declarations from the four `move-to-variable` credentials plus any other non-secret org/repo settings we choose to adopt.
3. `pulumi import` the existing live variables so the first `pulumi up` is a no-op, then have the audit assert no drift.
This produces real code and can be a reviewed PR; running the import needs a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with org admin, so an owner runs that step.

**Item 2 — secrets via Secret Manager (destructive, owner-driven).**
1. For each `gcp-secret://` credential, add a GCP Secret Manager version read and switch its resource from `.get()` to a managed `github.ActionsSecret` whose `plaintext_value` comes from that version — Pulumi then owns create/update.
2. Rotation itself (generate new value → new SM version → `pulumi up`) is a live, irreversible op on CI credentials; sequence it per-secret with the owner, not in a blind PR.
3. Resolve `replace-with-oidc` credentials separately — those should move to OIDC, not be re-stored as secrets.

**Suggested split:** land item 1 (variable adoption + import scaffolding) as its own reviewed change; track item 2's rotation per-secret behind owner execution. Relates to #7213, #7262 (IaC user permissions/grants).

If you want, I can draft the item-1 code (schema `variable` scope, managed variable resources, an import helper + audit drift check) as a PR for you to run the live `pulumi import` against — say the word and I'll scope it to the four `move-to-variable` entries. I won't touch secret rotation.

topics.title: [grug] Hero vibe-check samples pre-switch checkpoints with the current model config
topics.body:
The hero completions sampler stamps every discovered checkpoint with the current `HERO_MODEL_CONFIG`, so after the 16K context switch (#9615) a rebuilt or re-released sample store would sample checkpoints from before step 257553 with `qk_mult` 1.48 instead of the 1.3 they trained with. Nothing flags the mismatch, because `model` is excluded from `sample_id`.

Requests already in the store are safe: `SampleStore.save_request` writes a request only once, and the stored requests for steps 246000, 252000, and 257553 record `qk_mult` 1.3 and `max_seq_len` 4096. The risk appears only when `spec.release` is bumped (the documented backfill knob) or the store root changes.

`sampling_model()` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/ops/vibe_check/config.py` should choose the model per checkpoint. `hero_checkpoint_paths` already reads each ancestor run's W&B config and could carry its `model` along; alternatively the context history could record `qk_mult` per phase.

Found in the independent review of the 16K deploy PR.

topics.title: [levanter] Add opt-in MXFP8 routed experts to the ragged EP backend
topics.body:
Add `ExpertPrecision.MXFP8`, which runs the six routed-expert GEMMs of the `ragged_all_to_all` MoE backend in MXFP8 on fused grouped-GEMM kernels from `nvidia-cudnn-frontend` 1.31.0, a new Linux-only dependency of levanter's `gpu` extra. It is off by default. The EP hero run (`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep`) opts in with `GrugModelConfig.expert_precision` or `--expert-precision mxfp8` in `launch_diagnostics.py`. Parameters keep their dtype and layout, so checkpoints restore under either precision.

MXFP8 stores E4M3 values with one power-of-two E8M0 scale per 32 elements, which Blackwell tensor cores apply inside the MMA at twice the bf16 rate. A GEMM needs its scale blocks along the axis it contracts over, so an activation is quantized along features for the forward and data-gradient GEMMs and along tokens for the weight gradients. Four kernels cover one SwiGLU expert MLP: the gate/up GEMM with a SwiGLU epilogue that quantizes its output along both axes, a plain grouped GEMM, the down-projection data gradient (the unified dGLU kernel with `act_func="dswiglu"` and `deterministic=True`, which also returns the per-row routing-weight gradient), and the grouped weight gradient. `levanter.grug._moe.mxfp8.adapter` wraps them as JAX calls through `cutlass_kernel_cache`, as the existing bf16 QuACK kernels are, and `triton_quant.py` builds both MXFP8 copies of an activation and their swizzled scales in one pass, bitwise equal to the pure-JAX reference in `quantize.py` (0.80 ms against 5.14 ms for the XLA composition at the shape below).

One change the package lacks needs an override: `mxfp8/kernels/swiglu_forward_only.py` subclasses the dedicated SwiGLU kernel and copies its `__init__`, `__call__` and `kernel` from 1.31.0 to add a compile-time `forward_only` option, marked "Modified by Marin". With it set, the kernel skips the pre-activation and token-quantized outputs, which only a backward pass reads; the expert MLP uses it for a forward pass whose backward recomputes it. That file is 1,945 of the 5,437 added lines, and the pin is exact because it copies private methods. `uv.lock` gains only the package itself: `nvidia-cutlass-dsl` 4.6.2 and `apache-tvm-ffi` were already locked. `cutlass_call` gains an optional `input_output_aliases` argument, which the dGLU call uses to accumulate into a zeroed buffer; existing callers are unchanged.

An MXFP8 request raises, rather than running bf16 experts in its place, on any other backend, without an expert axis of size two or more, for non-SiLU experts or non-bf16 tokens, off SM100, and when the kernels or Triton do not import. Dropless eval swaps in a local (non-EP) backend, which has only bf16 experts, so it also resets the precision to bf16. 1.31.0 is the first release whose weight-gradient kernel acquires its online TMA descriptors before using them; without that, CUDA-graph replays read a stale descriptor when XLA gives both weight-gradient calls the same workspace and returned a partly NaN gradient. A replay test fails with the acquire removed and passes with it. The hero keeps XLA GPU command buffers off for every precision because of #5675.

The fused kernels need each expert's rows to start on a 256-row boundary. `_expert_granular_a2a_params` takes a receiver alignment, which the expert MLP declares: 256 for MXFP8 and 1 for the bf16 MLPs. The dispatch all-to-all writes each expert's rows from an aligned start, and the return all-to-all reads from the same starts. A chunk's receiver buffer grows from its capacity C to round_up(C + 255 * Echunk, 256) rows, where Echunk is the chunk's expert count and 255 is the most padding one expert can need. Token dropping still counts against C. The quantizer reads only each expert's received rows and treats every other row as zero, so unwritten rows between experts never reach a GEMM. With alignment 1 the bf16 ragged MoE's value-and-gradient program has the same jaxpr hash as before, on CPU and on a B200.

The table compares the expert MLP alone, with quantization and without the transport, on one B200. The shape is one sequential expert chunk of the EP hero run on one GPU: Echunk = 3 experts, C = 302,336 rows (303,104 aligned), hidden size H and expert width I both 3072. The baseline is the bf16 QuACK expert MLP. These runs used the legacy dSwiGLU backward kernel; the dGLU kernel used now measured about 0.1 ms slower per call.

| Program | MXFP8 | bf16 QuACK |
|---|---|---|
| Forward and backward with the forward recomputed (remat), as the hero runs it | 31.9 ms, 13.47 GiB peak | 51.0 ms, 15.89 GiB peak |
| Forward and backward | 25.7 ms, 15.32 GiB | 40.1 ms, 14.16 GiB |
| Forward only | 7.1 ms, 4.63 GiB | 12.7 ms, 5.35 GiB |

Without remat, the MXFP8 peak falls in the dSwiGLU backward step, where the saved bf16 pre-activation and both FP8 copies of its gradient are live at once. Under remat the forward stores no residuals, and the recomputed forward's FP8 copies are smaller than QuACK's bf16 activations.

Each kernel output is within 1e-3 (GEMMs) or 2e-3 (quantized outputs, weight gradients) relative Frobenius error of f32 matmuls on the dequantized operands it consumed, and an expert without rows gets an exactly zero weight gradient. End to end on Gaussian data, MXFP8 outputs and all gradients are off by 6.4-6.8% from an f32 reference in relative Frobenius norm, which includes MXFP8 rounding of every operand; bf16 QuACK is off by 0.2-0.3%. Reruns are bitwise identical. On 8 B200s, with the stock jax-cuda13-pjrt build and XLA's default NCCL ragged all-to-all instead of the hero's device-initiated kernel, 16 experts over 8 GPUs match an f32 dense reference within 0.1 (10%) relative error per token shard and per expert, for balanced routing and for skewed routing with 1,131 dropped token-expert assignments, and NaN-filled and zero-filled transport buffers give bitwise identical MXFP8 results; that ran on an earlier revision of this branch. The existing bf16 `test_ragged_moe_reads_no_unwritten_transport_rows_on_gpu` fails the same way on main on those 8 GPUs, with 1,330 of 9,216 elements differing between its NaN- and zero-filled runs; the bf16 program it tests is unchanged here. The GPU tests skip without an SM100 GPU; the single-GPU ones passed on a Modal B200 at this revision.

Not measured yet: the full hero step on GB200, a run at 16 or more nodes, and training quality against bf16. From their share of model FLOPs and an assumed 75% of peak for the QuACK kernels, the expert GEMMs are an estimated 21% of the 13.8 s hero step; this is not a profile. If the remat row's 1.6x speedup holds there, steps would be about 8% shorter.

Part of #6699.

comments.body: 🤖 @mcwitt @dlwh @ClassicLarry could you review? This adds opt-in MXFP8 routed experts to the ragged EP backend (#6699) on `nvidia-cudnn-frontend` 1.31.0's fused kernels. On one B200 at the hero expert chunk under remat, the expert MLP is 1.6x faster than bf16 QuACK (31.9 vs 51.0 ms) with a lower peak (13.5 vs 15.9 GiB); it is off by default and the bf16 program is unchanged. topics.title: [taskforge] Add the GLM chat client, agent loop and call recording
topics.body:
Every later Taskforge stage calls GLM-5.3 through this layer: proposal and triage make structured calls, the build stage runs agent sessions, and validation runs graded RolloutEngine trials. `llm` gains a `ModelClient.complete` that takes request fields such as `tools`, the tool loop `run_agent` with RolloutEngine's shell tool and Parallel's web tools, the RolloutEngine model `GlmRolloutModel`, an on-disk call cache, and an `LLM_CALL` ledger span for every call, failed calls included. Call recording needs the ledger's record and span types, so `ledger/records.py` lands here.

`LLMPolicy` now defaults to GLM-5.3's published sampling (temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95). Callers that build `LLMPolicy()` without a temperature, such as `generate_tasks.py` on main, move from 0.7 to 1.0.

`GlmRolloutModel` runs rollouts under RolloutEngine's messages trace, because a validation trial is graded and never trained on. Each turn is one streamed chat-completions call. The turn carries the reply and the call's usage with empty token ids and no logprobs, and the engine charges that usage against the attempt's token budget, which Taskforge leaves unset. A request that carries token ids (a `ModelRequest.continuation` or pinned prompt ids) raises `RolloutContractError` before any call. Rollout turns and agent turns send a `prompt_cache_key` built from the workpiece, round and step, so the router keeps one conversation on the node that holds its prefix in cache.

The client bounds connect and write separately from the read timeout and expires idle pooled connections after 30 s. A stalled read replaces the connection pool, at most once per 30 s, so the retry cannot reuse a dead connection. The old pool closes when the last request streaming on it ends.

This is the first PR of the Taskforge stack and is based on main. #10292 adds the JSONL and Finelog ledger writers on top of it. The rollout model's RolloutEngine tests need `spec.draft` and land with the spec package in #10294.

topics.title: [loom] Add the claude profile and enable the claude.ai connector
topics.body:
Turn on Loom's claude.ai connector on loom.oa.dev and add the `claude` launch profile that connector launches use by default. The connector is a Streamable HTTP MCP endpoint at https://loom.oa.dev/mcp, and Loom is its OAuth authorization server. Open-Athena members sign in with GitHub, as in the web UI, and keep access only while their organization lease keeps renewing.

The profile is named for where the work comes from, not the agent. It inherits the interactive default, so it runs Codex with the default model and repository access. Its instructions treat context wrapped from a claude.ai chat or browser page as data, not instructions. They also require a pull request labeled `agent-generated` that the agent does not merge, and they put every created URL in the final status and result, because the person reads the outcome in claude.ai.

After deploy, a Loom administrator registers claude.ai once with `loom oauth-client add`, and an organization admin adds the custom connector in claude.ai. The README section gives both steps. Claude.ai calls `/mcp`, `/oauth/*` and `/.well-known/oauth-*` from Anthropic's servers, so those paths must stay publicly reachable.

Deploy this only after marin-community/loom#404 is on Loom's default branch. An older Loom build rejects the unknown `connector.enabled` setting, so activation would fail.

topics.title: Vendor Harbor with an isolated runtime and local Marin dependencies
topics.body:
Move Harbor's evaluation runtime into `vendor/harbor` with its own uv project and lock. Editable local Rigging and FineStore sources allow dependency updates to land together. Marin invokes Harbor through a subprocess; ordinary workspace environments do not install it.

Import the runtime from Harbor revision `9d099696a567f489a111dc7e3c61183c98f007f0`. Retain agents, environment providers, verification, archives, telemetry, and acquisition of prebuilt task datasets. The Tau3 relay resides with runtime agents. Remove benchmark generators and their development tooling, inputs, locks, and tests, along with the website, results viewer, benchmark publishing, hosted result sharing, and unused registry snapshot. Prebuilt datasets remain available through Hugging Face, the Harbor registry, and local task trees.

All Harbor launches execute the checked-out source. Historical cohort metadata continues to validate saved records. Evaluation provenance records a combined source digest for Harbor, its Marin driver, and local Rigging and FineStore dependencies alongside the Harbor lock digest. CI checks the independent lock for freshness.

Preserve packaged runtime assets in Iris bundles and exclude vendored unit tests by default.

Related incident: [TPU CI runner deletion](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/793).

topics.title: infra - all post-training experiments should be runnable from the Marin repo
topics.body:
Our post-training work is run from a variety of forked repositories: MarinSkyRL, evaluations from evalchemy & harbor. This ~works, but the handoff between stages is by hand and non-obvious - making it easy to accidentally introduce errors -- and it makes it hard for us to track versions and test appropriately.

We propose adding all of our current forked repositories as dependencies of the Marin repo, and driving experiments "from Marin". This will allow us to describe complete pipelines as a single experiment, and build out appropriate testing and performance analysis for our complete set of workflows, as well as provide an easier way to manage and deploy consistent versions across projects. For instance, launching experiments from Marin will allow us to unify the various "run something on Iris|Slurm|Together" instead of duplicating it across projects.

Note this is _not_ a proposal to rewrite existing forked code, but instead to _integrate_ that code more tightly into our workflows. Things this will not do:

* Prevent users from running experiments independently from other repos
* Vendoring all code directly into the Marin repo
* Developing our own replacement code for upstream libraries

Instead this should be considered as trying to take the existing dependencies and model pipeline steps as e.g Marin's `ArtifactSteps` or similar. For example, let's say that we're currently using Llama-Factory for model fine-tuning on GPUs. We could write this as something like:

```
@dataclass
class SftConfig:
  model: ArtifactStep[LevanterCheckpoint]
  datasets: dict[str, ArtifactStep[TokenizedCache]], 
  resources: ResourceConfig

def run_llama_factory(...):
  # launch iris job (or slurm if needed)
  
def sft(config: SftConfig):
  return ArtifactStep(
     run_cmd=run_llama_factory,
     build_config=lambda: config,
  )
```

While encoding experiments as an artifact step is nice, this isn't a hard requirement: experiments should also be runnable via e.g. `uv run {llama-factory|skyrl|xyz}` as if we were working in the original repo.

topics.title: [post-training] PivotRL on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507: long-SWE single-turn
topics.body:
TL;DR:

Done (stopped at step 10 after a step-11 CUDA OOM). SWE-bench Verified rose from 4.6% (base) to 15.6% at step 10 (+11.1 pts paired, 59 gained / 4 lost, p < 0.001), and AIME24 held at 0.917. Held-out pivot accuracy rose from 0.175 to 0.374 (Grug: 0.285 to 0.390). Details: see the results comment.

Recipe:

Rerun of the 2026-10-14 Grug single-turn long-SWE PivotRL recipe on `Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507` (revision `144afc2f`). Pivots were re-selected from Qwen's own K=16 pass rates (`0 < passed_nemo < 16`; 22,209 rows from 221 of 286 candidate chunks). Recipe: GRPO, lr 4e-6, KL 0.01, 64 prompts x 16 samples, 8,192 generated tokens, 12 steps planned (stopped at 10).

Evaluation goal:

Measure whether PivotRL on Qwen improves SWE-bench Verified, and whether it erodes math the way the Grug runs did. Grug AIME24 fell from 0.830 (SFT) to 0.803 by step 2 and to 0.76-0.77 by step 10.

Evaluation results:

| Step | AIME24 | SWE-bench Verified |
|---|---|---|
| 0 (base) | 0.917 | 0.046 (23/500) |
| 5 | 0.917 | 0.070 (35/500) |
| 10 | 0.917 | 0.156 (78/500) |

Both evals use the October 5 verified policy, the same one as the Grug checkpoints. The mini-swe-agent harness suits Qwen poorly: base Qwen often submits within 20 steps and misses tool calls. Compare Qwen checkpoints with each other, not with Grug's absolute SWE-bench scores.

Run links:

* W&B (Qwen): https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/marin-community/pivot-rl/runs/duu3twcu
* W&B (Grug baseline): https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/marin-community/pivot-rl/runs/lxm4qlxv
* Related: #10214

Decision log:

* Stopped at step 10 after a CUDA OOM at step 11; no resume.
* AIME24 is the fast regression canary: it was the earliest downstream drop in the Grug runs.

<details><summary>Original description</summary>

```markdown
## TL;DR

Running. Held-out pivot next-action accuracy rose from 0.175 to 0.283 by step 5 (Grug: 0.285 to 0.380). Downstream evals are in progress.

## Description

Rerun of the 2026-10-14 Grug single-turn long-SWE PivotRL recipe on `Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507` (revision `144afc2f`). Pivots were re-selected from Qwen's own K=16 pass rates (`0 < passed_nemo < 16`; 22,209 rows from 221 of 286 candidate chunks). Recipe: GRPO, lr 4e-6, KL 0.01, 64 prompts x 16 samples, 8,192 generated tokens, 12 steps.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Measure whether PivotRL on Qwen improves SWE-bench Verified, and whether it erodes math the way the Grug runs did. Grug AIME24 fell from 0.830 (SFT) to 0.803 by step 2 and to 0.76-0.77 by step 10.

## Status

| Step | AIME24 | SWE-bench Verified |
|---|---|---|
| 0 (base) | running | 7/120 resolved (partial) |
| 5 | running | 9/118 resolved (partial) |
| 10 | pending | pending |
| 12 | pending | pending |

Both evals use the October 5 verified policy, the same one as the Grug checkpoints. The mini-swe-agent harness suits Qwen poorly: base Qwen often submits within 20 steps and misses tool calls. Compare Qwen checkpoints with each other, not with Grug's absolute SWE-bench scores.

## Links

* W&B (Qwen): https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/marin-community/pivot-rl/runs/duu3twcu
* W&B (Grug baseline): https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/marin-community/pivot-rl/runs/lxm4qlxv
* Related: #10214

## Decision Log

* AIME24 is the fast regression canary: it was the earliest downstream drop in the Grug runs.

## Conclusion

```

</details>

🤖 Held-out pivot next-action accuracy rose from 0.175 to 0.283 by step 5, but downstream transfer is still unknown. The SWE-bench Verified counts (base 7/120; step 5 9/118) are partial, and AIME24 is running. This is an active evaluation rather than an isolated code fix.

Plan:
1. Finish the October 5-policy AIME24 and SWE-bench Verified evaluations for base and step 5, then evaluate steps 10 and 12. Record checkpoint IDs, complete denominators, failed trials, retries, and run links.
2. Compare Qwen checkpoints on the same SWE tasks with paired outcomes and uncertainty; compare AIME24 against base with identical sampling. Keep the comparison within Qwen because the mini-swe-agent harness behaves differently on Grug.
3. Publish the completed step table and decide whether any SWE gain survives paired analysis without an AIME24 decline. If it does not, record the negative result and scope a separate recipe-change experiment before further training.

🤖 **Final results.** Training was stopped at step 10 (W&B `duu3twcu`).

| Step | AIME24 (avg@10) | SWE-bench Verified | Paired vs base (SWE-bench) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 (base Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507) | 0.917 ± 0.007 | 0.046 (23/500) | — |
| 5 | 0.917 ± 0.008 | 0.070 (35/500) | +2.4 pts on 499 tasks (21 gained, 9 lost), p = 0.04 |
| 10 | 0.917 ± 0.007 | **0.156 (78/500)** | **+11.1 pts** on 496 tasks (59 gained, 4 lost), p < 0.001 |

The p-values come from an exact binomial test on the tasks whose outcome changed.

**Takeaways**
- SWE-bench Verified went from 4.6% to 15.6% (3.4×) in 10 steps.
- AIME24 did not move. In the Grug-SFT runs on the same recipe, AIME24 had already dropped from 0.83 to 0.80 by step 2–5.
- Much of the gain is likely format repair rather than new skill. The base model submits early, and about 2/3 of its trajectories hit at least one "No tool calls found" error.

**Training dynamics vs Grug (`lxm4qlxv`), same recipe**

| | Qwen start → step 10 | Grug start → step 10 |
|---|---|---|
| Held-out pivot accuracy | 0.175 → 0.374 | 0.285 → 0.390 |
| Train reward | 0.28 → 0.70 | 0.44 → 0.63 |
| Policy entropy | 0.565 → 0.389 | 0.448 → 0.157 |
| KL | 0 → 0.107 (sharp rise after step 8) | 0 → 0.011 |
| Tokens per response | ~1,000 → 546 (halved at step 9) | ~260 |

- Qwen's pass@16 held at about 0.92, while Grug's pass@8 fell from 0.89 to 0.70.

**Stopped at step 10:** step 11 hit a CUDA OOM in policy `ppo_train`. One actor was using 66.5 GB, plus 12.6 GB from a second process, likely the colocated reference model. Checkpoints exist for steps 5 and 10, with HF exports under `export/global_step_{5,10}/policy`.

**Eval infra notes**
- **AIME24 and preemption:** AIME24 (Evalchemy) needed about six resubmits because preemptions on cw-us-east-02a removed the inference endpoint (404), and Evalchemy has `max_task_failures=0`. Fixed by raising the outage grace to 40 min (iris22 workspace commit `c7118ec10b`).
- **Host memory on cw-rno2a:** with DP8, the 61 GB checkpoint OOMs a 256g host; it needs `--memory 768g`.
- **Cross-cluster export barrier:** the export-barrier job couldn't see a us-east export from rno2a. Worked around with a pre-verified export marker.
- **SWE-bench:** Harbor resumed cleanly across preemptions.

🤖 Correction after tracing the current checkpoint path: the long-lived `GlobalAsyncCheckpointManager` keeps the completed TensorStore commit futures in `_commit_futures`; `wait_until_finished()` joins but does not clear them, and the writes allow indefinite source-buffer references. This mechanism predates #8609 and plausibly retains one staged checkpoint share per writer rank. PR #8599 contained a reviewed post-join cleanup for these futures, but that part did not land with #8609. The pinned-host BFC pool in #8609 remains an additional allocator-level floor that clearing the manager cannot purge. Updated evidence and safe cleanup boundaries: https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/227

topics.title: [iris] Deliver application secrets through files
topics.body:
Deliver application secrets through per-attempt VM tmpfs files and Pod-owned Kubernetes Secrets. Rigging provides named file-first lookup with environment fallback and shared native HF and AWS file discovery. Submissions automatically include the client's current mounted bundle and available HF/W&B/CoreWeave credentials from files or environment fallback. Explicit entries override inherited defaults. Other credentials use the secrets map or CLI `--secret NAME SOURCE`.

The submitting client resolves inheritance for ordinary child jobs, Fray actors and Zephyr workers. `SecretBehavior.ISOLATE` and sandboxes send only explicit secrets. The controller receives the resolved map for dispatch and retries. Remove cluster default application credentials and operator environment injection. Ordinary `env_vars` retain environment delivery.

CoreWeave tasks require the submitter's own storage keys, delivered through the same bundle with native AWS file discovery. Their output uploader receives only a native AWS file containing the submitted storage keys. Operator storage keys remain restricted to infrastructure Pods. Development callers of `configure_coreweave_s3()` must supply native AWS credential configuration explicitly; it no longer exports credential values into the process environment. Controller signing credentials remain controller-only. Submitted values still travel through authenticated job RPCs and remain in database/checkpoint state; display APIs redact every secret-map value.

Apply the IaC namespace Role/RoleBinding for per-attempt Secrets before deploying the Kubernetes controller. The `cw-us-west-04a` stack must first import CI's bootstrapped `task-secret-role` and `task-secret-binding` resources into Pulumi state, following the linked deployment guide. Update submitters and runtime images together, and roll GCP workers for new attempts to use files. Existing containers retain their original delivery. No new HF/W&B cloud resources or grants are required. See the [secret-delivery guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/weaver/rigging-secret-management/lib/iris/docs/secrets.md) for configuration, deployment and rotation.

Rollout incident: [CoreWeave submission failures during secret-file cutover](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/838).

Incomplete coverage fails scoring while leaving completed training and export reusable.

CPU checks cover artifact cache reuse, export preservation after scoring failure and recovery across two independently built scoring attempts. Fresh qualification of the assembled GPU path is still required; the two-to-four-hour loop remains a target to measure.

The Evalchemy fork ignored that directory, and the vendored copy (#10288) does not. The new regression tests import the checkers, so vendor/evalchemy/.gitignore now ignores it. Without the rule, a checkout that has run the tests gets different Evalchemy source hashes, and its Iris job submissions fail because the bundle exceeds the 25 MiB limit.

On the audit's model panel (16 configurations, 228 complete runs, 78,432 constraint verdicts), upstream's checkers change 257 strict verdicts relative to the vendored copy's, 227 of them in ratio:overlap, and move each configuration's greedy strict prompt-level score by at most one prompt (0.33 points).
