topics.title: [precision] QAT during SFT to ship a 4-bit-deployable EOY model
topics.body:
## TL;DR

Proposal to run **quantization-aware training during SFT / post-training** so we can ship a **natively 4-bit inference checkpoint** of our end-of-year models — the pattern Kimi K3 (MXFP4 weights + MXFP8 activations, "QAT from the SFT stage onward"), Kimi K2-Thinking (INT4 W4A16, "lossless" at ~2x decode), and Gemma-3 QAT (int4 + distillation) all use. The concrete near-term target is the checkpoint we're publishing to Hugging Face (Snowball / 67B-A2B, #7366) and the post-trained EOY MoE (#6705 / #7170); the goal is ~2x faster, ~4x smaller inference at near-BF16 quality. This issue covers **QAT-for-deployment**; making the *pretraining* matmuls run in FP4 for a training speedup is the separate, complementary native-FP4-pretraining issue #7403. Both split out of the umbrella plan #7402.

## Scope: QAT-for-deployment, not training speedup

Two things get conflated under "4-bit." This issue is only the second:

- **(A) Native low-precision training** *(sibling issue)* — the pretraining GEMMs execute in FP4 for a real ~2x speedup on Blackwell. A pretraining-cost optimization.
- **(B) QAT-for-deployment** *(this issue)* — master weights stay bf16, compute stays bf16, but **fake-quant (quantize→dequantize) ops + a straight-through estimator** are inserted during fine-tuning so the model *learns to be robust to a later low-bit deployment*. **No training speedup** — it buys inference accuracy that plain post-training quantization (PTQ) would lose.

They are independent and can both ship. This one is lower-risk and directly serves inference/serving and the HF release.

## Where Marin is today

- **Post-training runs PyTorch/CUDA**, not JAX: MarinSkyRL fork (GRPO/RLVR) and the Axolotl SFT backend fork (#6839) — the latter already carries a torchao QAT callback we don't use. Pretraining is JAX/Levanter; the framework boundary matters here because the mature FP4 QAT tooling (torchao/Axolotl) is PyTorch.
- Native in-repo SFT is Levanter-native and consolidating on a shared `sft_step` launcher (#7231, #7250, both merged) with HF↔Levanter conversion (#7337); chat-template/tool-mask correctness tracked under #7045.
- We are actively standing up the first published Marin MoE: **publish Snowball to HF** (#7366), with the first-class GrugMoE HF snapshot/loading landed in #7227 and export decoupling in #6752 — this is the checkpoint a QAT pass would produce a 4-bit variant of.
- On-policy distillation exists as a post-training mechanism (#5853, MVP in #5939), and the OPD teacher-serving RFC (#7236) already reasons about **quantization perturbing distillation targets** — directly relevant below.
- Quantization substrate is all training-side FP8/MXFP8 (#7282, #7079, #620); **no QAT-for-deployment anywhere yet.**

## What "QAT during SFT" means, and the QAT-vs-QAD distinction that matters for MoE

Keep bf16 master weights; in the SFT/post-training forward pass, fake-quantize the target tensors to the deployment grid (quantize→dequantize) so the model sees quantization noise; backprop with a straight-through estimator (rounding treated as identity) updating the bf16 masters. After training, a `convert` step packs the real low-bit checkpoint. The served weights are then natively low-bit.

The single most important finding for a **MoE that goes through SFT+RL**: plain QAT (fake-quant + task cross-entropy) can **regress below even PTQ**, because CE loss can look fine while the output distribution has drifted from the bf16 model. The fix is **QAD — quantization-aware *distillation***: replace/augment the loss with KL to the full-precision checkpoint's output distribution (teacher = the un-quantized model). Reported example (NVFP4, Nemotron MoE): PTQ AIME25 85.0, plain QAT 83.3 (worse!), **QAD 87.9** vs BF16 89.1. For an SFT-only target, QAT ≈ QAD; for our SFT+RL MoE, **use QAD**. This dovetails with our existing distillation work (#5853) and the quantized-teacher reasoning in #7236.

## Format choice

| Scheme | What | When to pick |
|---|---|---|
| **INT4 W4A16, group 32** | 4-bit weights, bf16 activations, runs on bf16 tensor cores | Kimi K2-Thinking / SGLang-slime pattern. Simplest, best train↔infer consistency, ~2x decode (bandwidth-bound), plain QAT often suffices. **Recommended default.** |
| **MXFP4 wt + MXFP8 act** | 4-bit weights + 8-bit activations, OCP MX (block 32) | Kimi K3 pattern; "broad hardware compatibility" (Hopper + Blackwell + AMD). Quantized activations add risk. |
| **NVFP4 W4A4, group 16** | 4-bit weights + activations, Blackwell-only | Max compute throughput, but activation quant needs distillation to recover; Blackwell-only serving. |

For a large MoE where decode is weight-bandwidth-bound, **W4A16 gives most of the win with the least risk**. Escalate to activation quantization only if we need the compute throughput on Blackwell serving, and pair it with QAD.

## What to quantize

Routed-expert MLP GEMMs are 90%+ of MoE params → quantize **only the routed-expert up/gate/down weights**; keep **attention (Q/K/V/O), the router/gating linear, shared/always-on experts, embeddings, LM head, and norms in BF16**. Every surveyed model does a version of this (gpt-oss: only MoE weights to MXFP4; K2-Thinking: "the MoE components"; Nemotron: last ~15% + attention + latent projections in BF16). The router especially must stay high precision — routing errors compound through expert selection.

## Recipe (concrete, from Gemma-3 / slime / NVIDIA QAD)

- **BF16 master weights + STE**; fake-quant only in the forward.
- **Full-precision warmup, then enable fake-quant** (torchao default ~1000 steps; exposed as `fake_quant_after_n_steps`) so weights stabilize before quant noise. (Kimi K3 instead runs QAT for the whole SFT.)
- **Small budget vs pretraining:** Gemma-3 used ~5000 steps; NVIDIA QAD token budgets ~0.3–3B (scaling with size; ~2.5B for a 30B-A3B MoE). Hundreds of millions to a few billion tokens.
- **Conservative LR 1e-6 → 1e-5**, at or below the original post-training LR (higher destabilizes). Distillation temperature T=1.
- **For RL rollouts:** enforce train↔infer consistency (fake-quant grid == inference grid) and consider a router-replay so expert selection matches the inference engine — Marin already has router-replay/TIS work in this area, and reuse of Grug MoE kernels in the PyTorch SkyRL trainer is tracked in #7164.
- **Evaluate with KL-to-BF16-teacher, not just task accuracy** — CE can look fine while the distribution drifts (the QAD central caution).

## Tooling: the PyTorch path, and the MoE gap

- **torchao QAT + Axolotl `qat:`** is the turnkey path and slots into our existing Axolotl SFT fork (#6839): config keys `activation_dtype` (int8/int4/float8/nvfp4), `weight_dtype` (int4/fp8/nvfp4), `group_size` (32; **16 for NVFP4**), `fake_quant_after_n_steps`; flow is `axolotl train` (torchao `QATConfig(step="prepare")`) → `axolotl quantize` (`step="convert"`). Published Blackwell NVFP4 QAT recovery: ~63–72% of degradation for Gemma3-12B/27B.
- **The gap:** torchao's mainline `FakeQuantizedLinear` targets 2D `nn.Linear`; grouped-expert 3D weight stacks / grouped-GEMM MoE are **not first-class for QAT**, and Axolotl's MoE-MXFP4 request (axolotl-ai-cloud#3333) is a closed proposal with no implementation. Kimi's own stack used a custom `_FakeInt4QuantizationSTE` inside Megatron/TransformerEngine plus `int4_block_quantize`/`pack_int4_to_int32` for export. **Expect to write MoE-expert fake-quant** rather than getting it free — verify against the installed torchao version first.
- If we want QAT inside the JAX/Levanter loop instead, note **qwix** (JAX-native QAT) supports int4/int8/fp8 but **not FP4**; a JAX MXFP4/NVFP4 fake-quant is a custom_vjp+STE build (a few hundred LOC). Since our post-training is already PyTorch, the torchao/Axolotl path is the natural fit.

## Proposed plan

- **Phase 0 — format + loss decision.** W4A16-INT4 (recommended default) vs MXFP4-W/MXFP8-A vs NVFP4-W4A4, from the serving-hardware constraint; and QAT vs QAD (QAD if the target went through RL). Decide serving target with the vLLM-fork/upstream work (#7367, #6869/#6870).
- **Phase 1 — pilot on Snowball (67B-A2B, #7366).** MoE-expert-only W4A16 QAT fine-tune with a full-precision warmup, on the PyTorch/Axolotl path; produce a packed 4-bit checkpoint, serve on the vLLM fork, measure decode speedup and accuracy vs bf16 and vs naive PTQ. This validates the MoE fake-quant plumbing on a real, already-being-published model.
- **Phase 2 — EOY post-trained MoE (#6705 / #7170).** Apply the chosen scheme (QAD if SFT+RL) as the finishing stage of post-training; ship the 4-bit checkpoint alongside the bf16 one.

## Definition of Done

- Phase 0 decisions recorded: target format (W4A16 / MXFP4-W-MXFP8-A / NVFP4) and QAT-vs-QAD, with rationale.
- MoE-expert fake-quant works in our post-training stack (torchao/Axolotl path, with custom MoE handling as needed); a natively-4-bit checkpoint of Snowball (#7366) is produced.
- Served on our vLLM fork with measured decode speedup (target ~2x vs bf16) and an accuracy-recovery number vs naive PTQ, evaluated with KL-to-BF16-teacher plus task accuracy.
- Recommendation back on #7402 on the scheme for the EOY post-trained model.

## Risks & open questions

- **Plain QAT can underperform PTQ for SFT+RL / MoE models** → default to QAD (KL to bf16 teacher) for post-RL targets; ties into #5853 / #7236.
- MoE-expert QAT is not first-class in torchao/Axolotl → budget for custom fake-quant on grouped/3D expert weights.
- Kimi K3's exact quant scope, warmup, and step budget are **undisclosed** — treat "MXFP4-W/MXFP8-A from SFT" as the target, not a reproducible recipe.
- The fake-quant grid must bit-match the deployment quantizer (torchao / our vLLM-fork kernels) or QAT trains against the wrong noise; also required for RL rollout stability.
- Serving a quantized Grug checkpoint depends on the vLLM-fork / upstream support (#7367, #6869/#6870) and export correctness (#7146).

## Prior work / related Marin issues

Umbrella plan: **#7402** (QAT & FP4 plan — parent). Sibling: **#7403** (native FP4 pretraining — regime A).

SFT infrastructure: #7045 (SFT-with-confidence umbrella), #6839 (Axolotl SFT fork — the QAT host), #7231 / #7250 (shared `sft_step`, merged), #7337 (hf→levanter), #7088 (DenseMixer router gradient for MoE SFT), #7086 / #7087 (packed-SFT masking), #7098 (post-training runnable from repo).
Post-training program: #6705 (10T post-training hero run), #7170 (first post-trained Marin MoE, 2T cut), #7074 (post-training token budget), #6053 (EOY post-training plan), #6496 (post-training data manager).
RL / SkyRL stack: #6682 (JAX backend to SkyRL), #7164 (reuse Grug MoE kernels in PyTorch SkyRL trainer), #6341 (RL feature checklist — notes quantized/AWQ teacher), #6162 (RL framework guide).
Distillation (for QAD): #5853 (on-policy distillation), #7236 (RFC: quantized-teacher serving — quantization vs distillation targets), #5939 (sampled-token OPD MVP), #6535 (self-verified distillation).
Quantized inference / serving: #7367 (upstream Grug to vLLM/HF), #6869 / #6870 (GrugMoE GPU inference), #7097 (one vLLM fork), #6136 (FP8 decode-corruption bug), #6500 (serving infra).
Publishing checkpoints: #7366 (publish Snowball to HF — Phase-1 target), #7227 (GrugMoE HF snapshot/loading, merged), #6752 (export_hf ArtifactStep), #7146 (HF RoPE export bug).
Quantization substrate (regime A, related): #7282 (MXFP8 on GB200), #620 (archived INT8/AQT).

## External references

Kimi K3 (https://www.kimi.com/blog/kimi-k3); Kimi K2-Thinking (https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K2-Thinking) + LMSYS INT4-QAT reproduction (https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-01-26-int4-qat/); Gemma-3 QAT (https://developers.googleblog.com/en/gemma-3-quantized-aware-trained-state-of-the-art-ai-to-consumer-gpus/); NVFP4 QAD (arXiv 2601.20088); gpt-oss MXFP4 (arXiv 2508.10925); torchao QAT (https://docs.pytorch.org/ao/stable/workflows/qat.html); Axolotl QAT (https://docs.axolotl.ai/docs/qat.html) + quantize (https://docs.axolotl.ai/docs/quantize.html); Axolotl MoE-MXFP4 request (https://github.com/axolotl-ai-cloud/axolotl/issues/3333); qwix (https://github.com/google/qwix).

comments.body:
🤖 **Scope: design/research proposal, not a PR.** This is a 3-phase QAT-for-deployment program (Phase 1 is a pilot fine-tune + serving run on Snowball), gated on Phase-0 decisions and net well over 100 lines across the PyTorch post-training stack. Following the fix-issue policy for large/design work, I did not open a PR. Below is a codebase-grounding pass so a human can act on the plan; the design in the issue body stands on its own.

# Codebase grounding

The mature QAT tooling (torchao/Axolotl) and the referenced SkyRL/Axolotl forks live **outside this repo** — a sweep of `main` found no `axolotl`, `torchao`, `qat`, `fake_quant`, or `qwix` anywhere. That is consistent with the issue (post-training is a separate PyTorch fork), but it means **none of the QAT plumbing lands in marin/main today.** The only quantization substrate here is training-time, JAX-side, and explicitly *not* for deployment.

**Relevant code (verified on `main`)**
- [`haliax/quantization.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/haliax/src/haliax/quantization.py) — `Fp8DotGeneralOp` (L154), `Int8DotGeneralOp` (L237, wraps AQT), `QuantizationConfig` (L263). Training-time only.
- [`haliax/docs/fp8.md` L45-46](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/haliax/docs/fp8.md#L45) — states this is "not designed to quantize a model to FP8 for deployment." Confirms the "no QAT-for-deployment yet" claim.
- [`experiments/sft/launcher.py` L315](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/sft/launcher.py#L315) — `sft_step` (the merged shared SFT launcher, #7231/#7250). Levanter-native; the proposed QAT path is PyTorch/Axolotl, i.e. a *different* backend.
- [`levanter/models/snowball.py` L131](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/snowball.py#L131) — `SnowballConfig`, the 67B-A2B GrugMoE (Phase-1 target, #7366).
- [`levanter/main/export_lm_to_hf.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/main/export_lm_to_hf.py) — HF export; produces bf16 checkpoints, no low-bit packing.

# Two things worth resolving before Phase 1

1. **Framework boundary is the real gating fact.** The QAT recipe is PyTorch (torchao/Axolotl fork), but Snowball is defined and exported Levanter-side (`snowball.py`, `export_lm_to_hf.py`). The Phase-1 dependency chain is: Levanter bf16 → HF export (#7366) → load into the PyTorch/Axolotl fork → QAT fine-tune → pack → serve on the vLLM fork (#7367). Recommend making "HF-exported Snowball loads cleanly into the Axolotl fork" an explicit Phase-1 prerequisite, since the RoPE-export bug (#7146) sits directly on that path.
2. **`qwix` has no FP4 and is absent here.** The issue already notes qwix lacks FP4; combined with post-training being PyTorch, the JAX/Levanter QAT option is effectively off the table for the recommended W4A16/MXFP4 targets. Suggest Phase 0 explicitly closes the JAX path so no effort is spent there.

# Smallest first actionable slice

Everything else depends on MoE-expert fake-quant existing (torchao targets 2D `nn.Linear`; grouped-expert 3D stacks are not first-class). The lowest-risk, most decoupled first PR is **a standalone MoE-expert W4A16 fake-quant (quant→dequant + STE) op with a numerical test** — round-trip error bound on a grouped-expert weight tensor, grid bit-matching the vLLM-fork kernel — before any training-loop wiring. That validates the one piece the issue flags as "expect to write yourself," is unit-testable without a training run, and de-risks Phase 1.

This needs a human owner for the Phase-0 format/loss decision (W4A16-INT4 default vs MXFP4/NVFP4; QAT vs QAD) — those are serving-hardware calls (#7367, #6869/#6870), not something to infer.
our friends at Bonsai (@opooladz et al) can do 1-bit or ternary for us!

topics.title: Switch QB implementation to approximate quantile within global batch
topics.body: The current QB implementation follows exactly the blogpost, which calculates quantiles in local batch, then average across replicas. but K3 paper actually approximates global batch quantiles using bucket based all reduce. for aux loss based moe, QWEN https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.11873 has shown that global batch aux loss is significantly better than local batch aux loss. my small experiments also show perplexity win from global batch aux loss. I believe that global batch QB will have similar gains over local batch implementation.

topics.title: [grafana] Add a run-scoped training dashboard
topics.body:
Marin now exposes Finelog, live Iris state, W&B metrics, Kubernetes node metrics, DCGM GPU telemetry, and Telltale training progress through the Grafana bridge. The training dashboard still does not treat one run as a coherent unit: operators must assemble training, worker, and accelerator panels manually, and run selection does not define behavior at high cardinality. This is the run-scoped follow-up to #2830, which was closed as stale before the current Grafana and Finelog path landed.

Done when:

- An operator can find a run by exact ID or server-side prefix search without loading every run ID into a client-side selector.
- One run view combines loss, throughput, optimizer progress, phase, worker health, CPU and memory use, and available GPU or TPU telemetry.
- Panels preserve root run, Iris job, task, worker, role, rank, and restart-attempt identity so outliers can be traced to a worker.
- The view links to Iris tasks, W&B, logs, and related evaluation records when those sources exist.
- A user can enable or disable the supported stall and resource alerts for a run, and each alert carries the selected run identity.
- A benchmark or load test verifies run search and initial dashboard queries against at least 100,000 distinct run IDs.
- Grafana remains the operational time-series and alert surface; Evaldash remains the evaluation-record, sample, grading, and trajectory surface.

Part of #5198. Supports #6598 and #7098. Builds on #7296, #7322, #7336, and #7692.

comments.body:
🤖 **Scope:** New dashboard + server-side run search at 100k scale + per-run alerts + load test. This is a feature/design task, not a <100-line fix, so this comment is a root-cause map and proposed approach for review before implementation begins, not a PR.

# Research

The bridge already exposes everything a run view needs (telltale loss/throughput/phase/step, iris task state and per-task resources, k8s/DCGM node telemetry, W&B, GitHub) through the raw-SQL `/finelog/{cluster}/query` proxy. The gap is that the training dashboard has no run identity: it has only a `cluster` datasource variable, every run overlays into one `COALESCE(run, job_id, 'unknown')` series, and there is no run selector, no per-run panel set, no identity breakdown (task/worker/rank/attempt), and no per-run alert. There is also no benchmark for run search or initial-load queries at high cardinality.

**Relevant code**
- [`dashboards/training.json#L17-L101`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/grafana/dashboards/training.json#L17-L101) — only `cluster` var; loss/throughput grouped by `COALESCE(run, job_id)`, no run filter
- [`src/server.py#L564`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/grafana/src/server.py#L564) — generic `/finelog/{cluster}/query` raw-SQL route (backs any panel/variable query)
- [`lib/rigging/src/rigging/telltale.py#L205-L231`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/telltale.py#L205-L231) — `TelltaleMetric`: `run`, `job_id`, `task_index`, `attempt`, `worker`, `region`, `process_index` already flattened to top-level columns
- [`src/training_stalls.py#L90-L120`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/grafana/src/training_stalls.py#L90-L120) — existing bounded stall alert; template for a run-scoped alert
- [`tests/test_provisioning.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/grafana/tests/test_provisioning.py) — dashboard/alert validation pattern to extend

# Proposed approach

**1. Run search variable (server-side, no client-side load of all IDs).** Add a `run` template variable of type `query` (not `datasource`) that hits `/finelog/{cluster}/query` with a prefix-bounded, `LIMIT`ed SQL, e.g.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT COALESCE(run, job_id) AS run
FROM "telltale"
WHERE COALESCE(run, job_id) LIKE '${run_prefix}%'
  AND ts >= {{from}} AND ts < {{to}}
ORDER BY 1 LIMIT 200
```

Pair it with a free-text `run_prefix` variable so the prefix is pushed into finelog and only matches return. Selection stays O(prefix matches), never O(all runs). The `name`-clustered telltale namespace prunes row groups, so this stays cheap.

**2. One run view.** New `dashboards/training_run.json` (uid `marin-training-run`), every panel filtered by `WHERE COALESCE(run, job_id) = '$run'`:
- loss, throughput, optimizer/step progress, `levanter_phase` — from `telltale`
- worker health + pending/running + CPU/mem — from `iris.task_state` / `iris.task` on `root_job_id = '$run'`
- GPU/TPU telemetry — from the k8s/DCGM sources, filtered to the run's nodes
- an identity table selecting `run, job_id, task_index, attempt, worker, role, region, process_index` so outliers trace to a worker
- text/links panel to Iris task, W&B run, logs, and eval records (Evaldash stays the eval surface; Grafana stays time-series + alerts)

**3. Per-run alerts.** Extend the stall/resource alert (`training_stalls.py` pattern) so the rule is templated on the selected run and each alert row carries full run identity (root run, job, task, worker, rank, attempt). Wire via a new `/finelog/{hub}/alerts/...` endpoint plus a `provisioning/alerting/rules.yaml` entry; operators enable/disable per run.

**4. Load test at 100k run IDs.** A test in `infra/grafana/tests/` that seeds ≥100,000 distinct run IDs into a finelog fixture and asserts the prefix-search query and the run view's initial queries return within a bounded row cap and latency. This is the one place a real test earns its keep — it fails if search degrades to a full scan.

Open questions before implementation:
- Canonical run key: `run` (W&B id) vs `job_id` (Iris root) — coalesce order, and whether non-Levanter jobs should appear.
- Should the run view replace or sit alongside the current `training.json` fleet overview?
- Alert enable/disable granularity: per-run rule instances vs one rule filtered by an active-run set.

With the run-key convention and alert model confirmed, this splits into: (a) run search variable + run view dashboard, (b) per-run alert, (c) 100k load test.

topics.title: [grug] weight_decay is configured but never applied in the Grug MoE optimizer
topics.body:
`experiments/grug/moe/launch_cw_scale.py` sets `weight_decay=0.1`, but `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py` never reads the field. `GrugMoeMuonHConfig.build()` chains its AdamH, expert-AdamH and Adam transforms with no decay term, and `inject_hyperparams` only schedules the learning rates. Runs therefore train with zero weight decay while advertising 0.1.

This is long-standing rather than new, which means every recorded Grug MoE measurement ran without weight decay. The numbers are internally consistent; the configuration is what misleads.

Two ways out, and they are not equivalent. Implementing decay changes optimizer semantics and invalidates comparisons against everything measured so far, so it needs its own matched A/B. Removing the setting and documenting the zero-decay recipe changes no behavior and makes the config honest.

Found by the automated review on #7780. The two hero templates that inherited the setting by copying drop it there; this issue covers the base template.

`weight_decay_modules` and `default_weight_decay_mask` are set alongside it and are worth checking for the same problem.

Restore the checkpoint's stored router bias for inference and export, matching training-time evaluation. Pending quantile-balancing estimates belong to the next training update; applying them during inference previously selected a different model from the same checkpoint.

topics.title: [SkyRL] RunAI S3 weight loading exhausts retries before training
topics.body:
A five-update OPD training smoke on `cw-rno2a` failed before any optimizer update because the rollout engine could not load policy weights through RunAI's S3 streamer. The initial engine-gang initialization and all five retries failed, including attempts on different workers.

Reproduce (observed setup; underlying storage/network trigger remains unknown):
1. Start a SkyRL Megatron run with `generator.model_loading: stream`, a policy `source_uri` in CoreWeave S3, and vLLM's `runai_streamer` loader with `distributed: true`.
2. Load `open-athena/Marin-Snowball-67B-A2B-v0.1` at revision `adc0078a19a4383bc998fcdb43867b3360baf5f3` (39 safetensors shards, about 134 GB). The allocation was 7 nodes × 8 H100 GPUs: 32 learner GPUs, 8 rollout GPUs, and 8 GPUs for each of two teachers. The rollout engine used TP=1, DP=8, EP=8.
3. Observe S3 throughput errors followed by a file-access error and engine initialization failure. Training never begins.

Expected: policy loading completes, or the failure provides enough context to diagnose the storage/network problem without repeating the entire unsuccessful engine initialization six times.

Relevant log excerpts on 2026-10-22:
```text
18:12:21.621 [s3/client/client.cc:307] Failed to download s3 object:
Http connection channel shut down due to failure to meet throughput minimum
(aws-c-http: AWS_ERROR_HTTP_CHANNEL_THROUGHPUT_FAILURE)
18:13:48 ValueError: Could not receive runai_response from libstreamer due to: b'File access error'
RuntimeError: Engine core initialization failed. See root cause above.
```
The driver exited with code 1 at 18:36:32 UTC, after 0/5 optimizer updates. Later attempts failed while reading different weight shards, including `model-00033-of-00039.safetensors` and `model-00034-of-00039.safetensors`.

The stack runs through `GrugMoe.load_weights` → `runai_safetensors_weights_iterator` → `SafetensorsStreamer.get_tensors` → `DistributedStreamer.prefill` → `request_ready_chunks` → `runai_response`. Runtime vLLM: `0.0.0.dev20260929+marin.39e62869693c`; Marin source checkout: `d9d49f2c656cbb72af3148de09a90b27af2dfc3b`.

Loader selection: [main_base.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d9d49f2c656cbb72af3148de09a90b27af2dfc3b/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/entrypoints/main_base.py#L168). The environment-contract default for `RUNAI_STREAMER_S3_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` is `10000`; the effective value was not separately captured, and its role in the failure is unproven.

Internal execution record: Iris coordinator `/benfeuer/checkpoints-benfeuer-opd-identity-mixed-plumbing-2026.10.22.2-coordinator-7fe83d15`; [W&B run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/opd-identity-patch/runs/3bakylkb). The local experiment entrypoint was `python -m experiments.post_training.opd_identity.launch --arm mixed --stage plumbing --version 2026.10.22.2 --run`; that experiment module is not upstream yet.

A recovery using `generator.model_loading: stage_local` successfully staged the complete policy on all seven nodes, loaded rollout weights with `load_format=auto` in about eight seconds per rank, and completed all five optimizer updates. [Recovery W&B run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/opd-identity-patch/runs/6cj79wk9) is finished at step 5; the distributed checkpoint was saved. The recovery also explicitly forwarded rotated CoreWeave credentials, so this is not a controlled isolation of the original cause. HF-format export also completed, and the exported checkpoint loaded successfully for direct inference tests. This differs from #9035, which concerns passing RunAI-only options to a different loader.

The effective S3 timeout, per-node throughput, and whether the same object-store fault affected each attempt are unknown.

**Relevant code**

topics.title: [iris] Capability-URL round trips into cw-us-east-02a take 6–10 s under load (cw-rno2a: 0.15–0.5 s through the same gateway)
topics.body:
**Symptom.** Generation jobs in cw-us-east-02a each serve an OpenAI-compatible proxy as an Iris link endpoint (`/glm-harbor/<run>-<id>`). Agents call it through its capability URL (`https://iris.oa.dev/proxy/t/...`) once per agent step. On 2026-10-20 at about 04:50Z, a `GET /v1/models` on such an endpoint took 6–10 s through the capability URL. The same request sent directly to the endpoint's registered address from inside its container took under 10 ms. At the same time, capability URLs for endpoints in cw-rno2a (vLLM servers) answered the same request in 0.15–0.5 s from the same client. About 900 concurrent agent trials sat behind cw-us-east-02a endpoints then: 28 jobs × 32 trials, 56 registered endpoints. That was roughly double the load before about 03:10Z.

**Measurements**

| | result |
|---|---|
| `GET /v1/models` via capability URL, cw-us-east-02a endpoint (4 endpoints, 3–6 calls each) | 5.9–10.5 s; connect 0.01 s; nearly all of it is time to first byte |
| same endpoint, direct to its registered address from its own container | 0.000–0.009 s |
| `GET /v1/models` via capability URL, cw-rno2a endpoint, same client, same minute | 0.15–0.49 s |
| per agent step, gap from model reply to the next request (job request logs) | p50 0.4–1.3 s before ~03:05Z; 23–28 s after ~03:40Z |
| model backend latency per request, measured at the proxy (same window) | unchanged: p50 0.8 → 1.0 s, 6.7 → 6.9 ms per output token |

**Ruled out**
- The proxy process: it answers directly in under 10 ms, uses 5–7% of a core, and the containers have no CPU limit.
- The model backend: its latency and per-token speed are unchanged.
- The sandboxes (Daytona): command execution takes 20–80 ms per call, CPU speed is normal, host load is 22–37 on 64 cores.
- Client-side connection setup: connect time is 0.01 s, and the delay is all time to first byte.

**Not available.** There are no gateway or endpoint-relay metrics from before the slowdown. Load dependence is inferred from timing: the gap rose from about 03:10Z and leveled off by 03:40Z, as about 450 more trials started behind cw-us-east-02a endpoints. It has not been measured directly.

**Ask**
1. Gateway and endpoint-relay metrics for cw-us-east-02a from 2026-10-20 00:00Z onward: request rate, latency, queue depth and in-flight connections, compared with cw-rno2a.
2. Is there a per-cluster limit on proxied endpoint traffic (connection pool, worker count, a single relay stream to the cluster) that about 900 concurrent clients would saturate? If so, can it be raised, or should high-request-rate clients use another path?

🤖 The earlier answer was too categorical. I found **no explicit per-cluster request or active-connection cap in the checked-in Iris proxy or ingress configuration**, and the parent does not send a cluster's traffic through one relay stream. There is still shared capacity: each CoreWeave cluster has [one controller pod](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/controller.py#L249), each relayed request gets a [target decision from the public parent's private Python listener](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/rust/src/lib.rs#L540), and the requests traverse the child's Traefik ingress. Any of those stages can saturate without an explicit limit. We have not established a threshold at 900 trials; the child proxy's measured mean in-flight request count was 339–374 in the cited later windows, and trials are not simultaneous HTTP requests.

I also need to correct my earlier connection-pool claim. [PR #9480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9480), merged September 27, changed the Rust upstream client to retain up to **256 idle connections per host for 90 seconds**. That is an idle-reuse ceiling, not a cap on active connections. I have not verified which controller image was deployed during the incident. The checked-in Traefik route has an IP allowlist, with no request-limit middleware configured; the live Traefik settings remain unverified because the earlier Kubernetes read was denied.

The existing [Finelog comparison](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10318#issuecomment-6283946880) shows added time between the parent and child proxies for the POST workload, but its counters cannot distinguish the parent's decision, connection setup, and the child's ingress. So adding timings is useful, but it is not the only action: check the deployed image and live Traefik/controller resources, then run the same GET/POST mix at roughly 450 and 900 trials while timing the public route and the parent-to-child route separately. Change whichever stage shows the added wait, then verify the latency and error rate under the same load. Until an authenticated alternative is validated, off-cluster Daytona agents should use the capability URL; in-cluster clients can use their registered endpoint address. I corrected the [incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/795) to remove the stale zero-idle-connection claim.

topics.title: [observability] Make workload metrics durable and joinable
topics.body:
Marin has several operational metric paths, but coverage and identity differ by subsystem. Levanter and native vLLM publish Prometheus-compatible metrics through Telltale. Iris writes task, worker, state, event, and provisioning rows. Zephyr writes stage and shard rows directly. SkyRL and several evaluation and service paths have no equivalent producer.

The rows cannot always be joined. Zephyr stats omit Iris job, task, attempt, and worker identity. Kubernetes task rows name the pod but not its node, so they cannot be joined to node-level DCGM readings. The accelerator fields on `iris.task` are not populated. Arbitrary Iris tasks do not start durable Telltale forwarding by default.

In scope: Iris control-plane and workload metrics, Levanter training, native vLLM and evaluation serving, Zephyr pipelines, and Marin RL/SkyRL. Model-quality metrics remain in W&B and evaluation records remain in Evaldash. Logs, traces, profiles, and Finelog deployment work are separate branches of #5198.

Done when:

- A checked-in producer matrix lists each in-scope process, its metric families, identity fields, cadence, Finelog namespace, and Grafana or alert consumer.
- Workload rows carry an unambiguous cluster, root job, task, attempt, worker or node, process or rank, and role where those fields apply. Service rows carry cluster, component, instance, and version identity.
- Metric names, units, types, reset behavior, cadence, and label-cardinality limits are documented and tested.
- Every in-scope workload reports readiness or phase, progress or completed work, failures or retries, latency, and saturation when the signal exists.
- Zephyr metrics can be filtered to one execution and joined to its Iris job.
- Iris task metrics can be joined to node-level GPU telemetry, and the existing accelerator fields are populated or removed in favor of the canonical source.
- A bounded smoke for each producer queries its rows from Finelog after the process exits and verifies the expected identity and metric families without parsing logs.
- #7795 can build one run view from these identities, and #6598 can aggregate resource usage without subsystem-specific name parsing.

Part of #5198. #7798 is the first producer-specific child.

comments.body: 🤖 This issue is the operational metrics contract branch of #5198. #7798 covers SkyRL worker telemetry, and #7681 covers Levanter rank-level straggler reporting. #7795 and #6598 are the first consumers of the shared identities.

🤖 **Analysis — not opening a PR.** This is a cross-subsystem epic (a producer matrix plus identity/schema work across Iris, Levanter, vLLM, Zephyr, and SkyRL, with 8 acceptance bullets). Well past the ~100-line self-contained bug bar, so posting root-cause + a proposed decomposition for a human to review before implementation.

# Research

The forwarding path already exists and stamps full Iris identity; the gaps are (a) directly-written stat rows that omit that identity and (b) unpopulated/unjoinable fields.

- Telltale metrics already carry `job_id, task_index, attempt, worker, region, process_index`, stamped authoritatively at scrape time and written to the `telltale` namespace — so Levanter/vLLM rows are already joinable to Iris. [`rigging/telltale.py#L186-L231`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/telltale.py#L186-L231), [`iris/runtime/telltale.py#L31-L62`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/runtime/telltale.py#L31-L62)
- `iris.task` rows have `task_id, attempt_id, worker_id` but **no `root_job_id`**, and `accelerator_util_pct`/`accelerator_mem_bytes` are nullable and (per issue) unpopulated. No node id, so no join to node-level DCGM. [`iris/cluster/stats/tables.py#L146-L166`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/stats/tables.py#L146-L166)
- `zephyr.stage`/`zephyr.worker` rows carry only `execution_id` — no Iris `job/task/attempt/worker`, so they cannot be filtered to one execution's Iris job. [`zephyr/stats.py#L71-L115`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/stats.py#L71-L115)
- Pod name is captured (`TaskStatus.container_id`) and `attempt_uid` reaches `TaskEventRow`, but neither pod name nor node reaches `iris.task`. [`job.proto#L215`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/job.proto#L215), [`reconcile/commit.py#L253-L273`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reconcile/commit.py#L253-L273)
- SkyRL has no Finelog producer — tracked separately as the first producer child #7798.
- Prior design context: [`.agents/projects/2026-07-24_grafana_unified_jobs_and_finelog_federation.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/projects/2026-07-24_grafana_unified_jobs_and_finelog_federation.md) (cluster stamping, `iris.task_state` emission), and the alert contract joining telltale to `iris.task_state` via `(cluster, root_job_id)` in [`docs/ops/training-stall-alert-contract.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/docs/ops/training-stall-alert-contract.md).

# Proposed decomposition

The epic mixes documentation (producer matrix), schema changes (Iris/Zephyr identity), and per-producer smokes. It should land as separate PRs, each independently reviewable and testable. Suggested children under this issue:

1. **Producer matrix doc** — checked-in table: each in-scope process → metric families, identity fields, cadence, Finelog namespace, Grafana/alert consumer. Pure docs; establishes the contract the schema PRs implement against.
2. **Iris `iris.task` identity + accelerator fields** — add `root_job_id` (derivable from the `task_id` path via `Namespace.from_job_id`), add `pod_name`/`node`, and either populate the accelerator fields from the worker usage sample or remove them in favor of the canonical DCGM/node source. Enables the `iris.task` ↔ node-DCGM join. Test: emit a task attempt, query the row from Finelog, assert `root_job_id` and node/pod are non-null.
3. **Zephyr → Iris linkage** — thread `job_id/task_id/attempt_id/worker_id` (available in the runner's Iris job context) onto `zephyr.stage` and `zephyr.worker`. Test: run a small pipeline under Iris, assert both namespaces filter to one execution and join to its `iris.task`.
4. **Per-producer durability smokes** — one bounded smoke per producer that queries its rows from Finelog *after the process exits* and asserts identity + expected metric families, no log parsing. Reuses the pattern the telltale forwarder already implies.
5. **Metric-name/label registry** — document and test names, units, types, reset behavior, cadence, and label-cardinality limits (guards SkyRL/#7798 and future producers).

Ordering: (1) first to fix the contract, then (2)/(3) in parallel, then (4)/(5). Each is <200 LOC and independently mergeable.

Open questions for a human before implementation:
- Populate the accelerator fields on `iris.task` from the worker heartbeat (`IrisWorkerStat.gpu_util_pct`/`hbm_used_bytes` already exist per worker), or **remove** them and always read from node-level DCGM? The issue lists both as acceptable — pick one.
- Node identity for the DCGM join: add `node` to `iris.task` (worker-emitted), or join `iris.task.worker_id` → `iris.worker` → node? The latter avoids schema churn if `iris.worker` can carry node.

Happy to take child #1 (producer matrix) or #2 (Iris identity) as the first concrete PR once the two questions above are settled.

🤖 Update: first telemetry review units

- [marin#7839](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7839) merged the bounded Rigging-to-Finelog foundation.
- [marin#7863](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7863) combines canonical Iris identity and export health, NVIDIA/NCCL probes, the Finelog benchmark record, and centralized vLLM queries and dashboard. Its reported checks are green; the GCP smoke remains in progress.
- [Evalchemy#57](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/pull/57), [Harbor#58](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/58), and [MarinSkyRL#263](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/263) are open and green. Evalchemy and Harbor join Marin-owned vLLM telemetry through `serving_job_id`; SkyRL keeps Ray, vLLM, DCGM, and hardware metric ownership unchanged while adding RL critical-path signals.
- No standalone feeder or upstream vLLM PR is planned.

Next: review the four open units. Deeper Levanter, Marin RL, and Zephyr instrumentation, probe rollout, alerts, and additional drilldowns remain follow-up work after these contracts land.

topics.title: [loom] Add a Claude plugin for handing work to Loom
topics.body:
Add a Claude plugin under `infra/loom/claude-plugin` that hands code changes in marin-community repositories to Loom through the claude.ai connector. Its use-loom skill launches a session whose goal holds the person's request verbatim, acceptance criteria, where to look, and the landing rule. It wraps pasted or page context as untrusted data, replies with the session link, and answers follow-ups with the connector's get, messages, status, list, send, interrupt and archive tools. A `/loom <request>` command hands the rest of a message to Loom.

claude.ai organization sync reads only private or internal repositories, and this one is public, so the plugin is published by uploading a zip or by listing it in a private marketplace repository. Making the plugin available does not add the connector. An organization Owner adds it separately with the stack-declared public OAuth client `claude-ai`. The README also covers connecting Claude Code as the `claude-code` client.

This stays a draft until #10533 declares those clients and marin-community/loom#405 lands the Loom support they need.

topics.title: [levanter] Honor dtype overrides for BF16 safetensors
topics.body:
Apply `dtype_override` to BF16 tensors when streaming safetensors. NumPy's floating predicate excludes BF16, so requesting FP32 left those weights in BF16, including through `HFCheckpointConverter.load_pretrained(dtype=...)`. Integer tensors retain their source dtype.

The intended FP32 Levanter reference run in #10213 loaded BF16 weights, so it compared Levanter BF16 against HF FP32. Its measurements remain valid for that comparison.

Fixes #10266

topics.title: Vendor Evalchemy with an isolated evaluation runtime
topics.body:
Vendor Evalchemy under `vendor/evalchemy` with all 42 benchmark dataset
generators, active graders and resume support. Remove benchmark pages,
database tracking, reporting, original model providers, standalone rollout
drivers and unused evaluator configurations. Keep the prompt processing and
scoring code used by Marin.

Evalchemy has its own `uv.lock` and environment outside the root workspace's
dependency resolution. Marin invokes its CLI in a child process. FineStore and
Rigging resolve from checkout-local sources so changes can land atomically.
Replace the active fork pin and refresh machinery, and retire the fork's
nightly dashboard lane while preserving its history.

Fetch larger canonical benchmark datasets from full Hugging Face commit SHAs.
Stage shared copies under repository/revision/file keys using the configured
scratch storage, with leases and completion markers. Standalone runs can use
the native HF cache without origin probes or an explicit local/object-store
destination. Direct HTTP files use the same staging mechanism with an explicit
publisher version; downloads stream without additional content hashing. The
NUPA-Loose and NUPA5K-Loose benchmarks also read from the shared cache. Preserve
dataset ordering, prompts, benchmark test cases and sample identities; keep tiny
datasets and custom snapshots bundled. The default Iris bundle is 14.4 MiB,
within the deployed 25 MiB limit.

Immutable evaluation caches track evaluator inputs, portable configuration
and the dependency lock. Evaluation records retain broader adapter and
local-library provenance. Dated `eval-policy-*` configurations that select
external Evalchemy commits fail before writing configs or starting jobs.
Historical policies and grader replay scripts require the corresponding
pre-vendoring Marin checkout.

The copy has its own `uv.lock`, sits outside the root workspace, and gets its own CI lane. The fork-ferry and `config/external/evalchemy` machinery is removed. The vendoring itself fits the repository: Marin still reaches Evalchemy only through the `client.py` CLI boundary. The integration changes around it need work before merge. They are the new runtime identity, an unrelated broker startup change, and a bundle-cap raise that is no longer needed.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph launcher["experiments/evaluation launch"]
    resolve["_resolve_definitions"]:::changed -->|"evalchemy_runtime_descriptor"| ident["EvaluationIdentity / pipeline cache_key"]:::changed
  end
  subgraph child["Evalchemy child job (same Iris bundle)"]
    uvrun["uv run --project vendor/evalchemy --frozen"]:::changed --> cli["evalchemy CLI"]:::added

  classDef changed fill:#fde7c8,stroke:#e8710a,stroke-width:2px
  classDef added fill:#d7f0dd,stroke:#1e8e3e,stroke-width:2px
```

**Before.** `EvalchemyRuntimeConfig.requirement` held a `git+…@<commit>` requirement, and the child ran it through `uvx --from` with CPU-torch wheel URLs and `s3fs`/`gcsfs` added via `--with`. That requirement string was both the record's `eval_runtime` and, for pipeline launches, part of the run-id cache key. It changed only when someone bumped the pin. Verified eval-policy cohorts selected their own Evalchemy commit through `RUNTIME_COMMITS`.

**Design.** The child now runs `cd $IRIS_WORKDIR; UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=$IRIS_WORKDIR/vendor/evalchemy/.venv uv run --project vendor/evalchemy --frozen --no-default-groups --extra …` with `setup_scripts=[]`. The torch pin and the cloud filesystems move into the vendored `pyproject.toml`. `evalchemy_runtime_source_hash()` hashes `vendor/evalchemy/eval`, `evalchemy_config`, `lib/finestore/src`, `lib/rigging/src`, both locks/manifests, and Marin's own `client.py`, `runner.py`, and `runtime.py`. Verified `eval-policy-*` versions that include Evalchemy now raise and point to a pre-vendoring checkout. Separately, `_start_brokered_inference` now blocks in `_wait_for_broker_workers` until every requested worker's current task attempt has registered. Iris raises `MAX_BUNDLE_SIZE_BYTES` to 50 MiB. The merge of main brings in the new default bundle exclusions (`tests/` and `docs/` at any depth), and with them the vendored tree fits under the deployed limit.

**Evidence and limits.** I ran the changed root tests locally (`tests/evals/test_evalchemy_config.py`, `tests/evals/test_inference_proxy.py`, `tests/evaluation/test_eval_policy_launch.py`, `experiments/evaluation/test_launch.py`) plus `lib/iris/tests/cluster/client/test_bundle.py`, and all passed. `create_workspace_zip('.')` at this head is 22.3 MiB, under the 25 MiB cap that deployed controllers enforce. All 1,072 tracked `vendor/evalchemy` files outside the top-level `tests/` ship in the bundle; I found no runtime file that main's any-depth `tests/` and `docs/` exclusions drop. So the earlier inline controller-rollout concern on `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/bundle.py:33` no longer applies at this head. Nothing in the PR shows an Evalchemy job running on Iris with the new child command.

**Findings**

- **1. Should fix:** `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/runtime.py:15` The source hash covers `lib/rigging/src`, `lib/finestore/src`, and Marin's `runner.py`/`client.py`/`runtime.py`. `experiments/evaluation/launch.py:378` puts that descriptor into the run-id cache key whenever `cache_key` is set, which is every immutable `eval_step` in `experiments/evaluation/pipeline.py:106`. As a result, a pipeline whose eval step is relaunched after any unrelated rigging or finestore commit (28 in the last month) gets new run IDs. It then re-executes evaluations that already finished and abandons their partial archives, which is the reuse that `test_relaunch_reuses_completed_steps_and_preserves_partial_archive` protects for the CLI. Under the old pin, identity changed only on a deliberate bump. Key the cache on the evaluator inputs only (`vendor/evalchemy/{eval,packages,pyproject.toml,uv.lock}`) and keep the wider hash as provenance. Also hash the git-tracked file set that the bundle actually ships. The current `rglob` with a hand-written skip list includes untracked files, so two checkouts of the same commit can record different `eval_runtime` values. `rigging.cache.directory_content_hash` already exists for this, and #10287 uses it.
- **2. Should fix:** `lib/marin/src/marin/inference/iris.py:750` `_wait_for_broker_workers` makes brokered startup wait for all `instances` workers. Before, startup proceeded once one worker registered (`_registered_worker_metadata`). With `instances=8`, a single worker that cannot be placed holds the evaluation for up to `_ENDPOINT_PLACEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (4 h) and then fails the whole startup, even though seven servers are ready. One worker job that exhausts its retries fails the startup the same way. This is unrelated to vendoring and has no stated motivating incident. Move it to its own PR. If the actual problem is stale registrations, keep the current-attempt check but require at least one current registration, and let later workers join the broker as they register.

It needs a rebase onto main's exclusions before it merges, and the combined bundle needs a size check against the 25 MiB deployed cap: this PR alone leaves 2.7 MiB of headroom.

topics.title: [taskforge] Grade decision-model tasks on the host
topics.body:
Grade decision-model tasks on the host. The owner is undecided on this kind of task, so this PR is kept separate from the rest of the stack; its upstream counterpart is #10280.

Verification is now one of five kinds (`answer_in_box`, `decision_model`, `code`, `llm_as_judge`, `composite`), and a composite is a weighted list of at least two other kinds. A `DecisionGrader` is its own grader type, not an LLM judge: the authoring model writes a rubric and a gold reference, and a decision model of fixed strength reads one state, by default the visible output of the solver's final turn, and answers one comparative question on five levels. Grading stays out of the rollout: a trial runs with the grader swapped to `NoGrader`, and the host grades the trial's final conversation afterwards. A read that fails transiently is read once more on the same conversation, and the solver's rollout is never re-run. `ClefDecisionClient` sends the reads to Clef behind the Orion gateway, using the request schema and state budget copied from clefclient into `taskforge.llm.clef`.

TaskSpec has no decision grader type until #10280 lands, so a TaskSpec carries the grader as a `NoGrader` whose contract holds it.

Builds on #10301 and is the last PR of the stack. Its five commits are the restack's own, cherry-picked unchanged; the stack sync adds the decision port and the decision parts of the spec and validation ports. The tree under `lib/taskforge` and the experiment matches the restack head (`taskforge/capability-restack` 87ffb54b02). The taskforge suite passes 814 tests here (78 more than #10301).

topics.title: Cluster observability
topics.body:
Forward-looking issue: stand up cluster observability for our (TPU, GPU) fleets.

Back in my (now distant) Hadoop days, having a good cluster-wide observability made a big difference in terms of managing frequent failures that occur at large scale. This will matter even more for us in the GPU land. Noting that CoreWeave ships with Grafana out of the box.

Goals for the platform:
* Bird's-eye view - health, utilization, availability, capacity
* Hardware/fabric health - there will be many hardware issues, we should be able to discover and track them. This includes observability but also both active and passive health checks
* Topology-aware rollups
* Drill-down: profiles / logs / traces - from cluster → job → task → node → hardware event → log span.
* Bad-node lifecycle - detect → quarantine → drain → return. A workflow, not just a metric.
* Alerting
* Agent-first by design - structured/queryable APIs/DBs, stable IDs etc.

Some general notes:
* I'm intentionally not trying to advocate for any specific vendor
* It may be tempting to squeeze this into Iris, but IMHO we should resist that temptation, and build it above Iris

FYI @marin-community/r-3

@hammer nice, we should definitely chat to Philip! Preferably in person :)

Using this issue to come up to speed on the latest developments in the observability market and [OpenObserve](https://github.com/openobserve/openobserve) seems like the self-hosted option with the architecture our team is most likely to select (i.e. Parquet on object storage). On the research front [Flare](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05413) seems worth a closer read. I think it's the evolution of the XPUTimer debugging tool mentioned in the [LING MoE paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.05139v2)?
@hammer in terms of specific tech/vendors, I have done very little research on this issue. I spend a brief moment on Grafana in CoreWeave. A thorough research is definitely warranted here!

I agree better observability would be good, and splitting it from Iris is the right call. (We can certainly add the hooks in Iris as needed).

topics.title: [grug] Take ring_filtered's slot-weight gradient through a gather
topics.body:
Replace a slow scatter-add in the backward pass of the ring_filtered MoE backend (#9880) with a gather. On MI350X the scatter-add cost 31 ms per June Snowball training step.

Before ring_filtered sends tokens to the expert shards, it fills a send buffer with one slot per kept (token, expert assignment) pair. It looks up each slot's combine weight with `combine_weights_local[safe_source]`. JAX differentiates that indexed read as a scatter-add: every slot adds its gradient back into the [tokens, top-k] weight array. On MI350X, a bfloat16 scatter-add uses atomic adds, which slow down sharply as more writes hit the same memory. At 65536 tokens per GPU it takes 31 ms per step, but at half as many tokens it takes only 7 ms.

The scatter is unnecessary because the mapping is one-to-one: every kept pair has exactly one send slot. A custom VJP uses the reverse map from each pair to its slot and gathers the pair's gradient from that slot. Pairs without a slot, which are padding tokens and pairs the sender drops for capacity, point at a sentinel slot and keep a zero gradient, as before.

Step times on June Snowball (EP8, batch 128 per node, save_moe, PGLE). These numbers combine this change with the AMD cross-entropy backward block (#10341):

| Setup | Before (s/step) | After (s/step) | Step time change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One 8x MI350X node | 2.906 (15.56% MFU) | 2.805 (16.12% MFU) | -3.5% |
| One 8x MI355X node | 2.523 | 2.448 | -3.0% |
| Two 8x MI355X nodes (EP8 x DP2, batch 256) | 3.198 | 3.106 | -2.9% |

Measured alone on a one-GPU stand-in for one EP8 rank, this change reduces step time by 1.3%. Losses are unchanged, and the ring_filtered tests pass on MI350X.

This branch is stacked on #9880; merge that first. Part of #9812.

topics.title: SREbots -- agent ops workflows
topics.body:
Investigate having asynchronous "ops" agents which scan our Iris cluster(s) for various types of activity:

  * security anomalies - new users or jobs appearing, GCP resource or permission changes
  * performance anomalies - JAX jobs which are running slower than expected, data loading warnings
  * stability - check cluster health statistics, controller responsiveness, triage slowdowns
  * failures - activate in response to health alerts, triage, attempt to fix, escalate
  * cleanup - identify patterns in human/agent processes, codify them into runbooks or skills

Where should these live? Likely independent of our Iris controller to have a separate failure domain, perhaps as Github actions, or on a dedicated agent service like github.com/rjpower/weaver? They will require sensitive permissions, so alternatively a GCP VM & locked down agent controls would be valuable.

comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue + actionability check
- [x] Survey existing ops/agent infra (skills, GitHub Actions, Iris health code)
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no open PR/issue on SREbots)
- [x] Post analysis + proposed approach (design issue → no PR per agent scope rules)

This is a design/research issue (new cross-cutting infra, no concrete bug or definition of done), so per the agent workflow I'm posting analysis for a human to steer, not a PR.

# Research

We already have most of the building blocks for SREbots — they just aren't pointed at the live cluster yet. Two patterns exist today:

1. **Scheduled Claude agents via GitHub Actions cron** (`.github/workflows/ops-*.yaml`) that shell into `infra/scripts/nightshift_*.py` and spawn Claude Code. These run on `ubuntu-latest` with no cluster credentials — they only touch the repo (cleanup, doc-drift, CI-health).
2. **Failure-triggered triage agents** (`.github/actions/claude-triage`) fired by the canary ferries on failure — these already do collect → diagnose → file-issue → Slack.

What's missing is exactly what this issue asks for: a *proactive, periodic* agent with read access to cluster state. None exists; grep finds no "SREbot"/"ops agent" loop. ("weaver" in our ops logs is the external issue tracker, not an agent service.)

**Relevant code**
- [`.github/workflows/ops-nightshift-cleanup.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.github/workflows/ops-nightshift-cleanup.yaml) + [`infra/scripts/nightshift_cleanup.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/scripts/nightshift_cleanup.py) - cron→Claude pattern to copy
- [`.github/actions/claude-triage`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/main/.github/actions/claude-triage) - collect→diagnose→file-issue→Slack, already built
- [`.agents/agents/ops-steward.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/agents/ops-steward.md) - read-only ops persona to base scan agents on
- [`lib/iris/OPS.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/OPS.md) - diagnostic commands + SQL the agent would run
- [`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller) - `worker_health.py`, `audit_logging.py`, `pruner.py` (health/audit signals to scan)

Existing postmortems in [`.agents/ops/`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/main/.agents/ops) are the concrete anomaly classes to detect (stuck `WAITING_FOR_RESOURCES` backlog, zombie/recycled-IP workers, scheduler-thread freezes, orphaned slices, taint timeouts).

# Proposed approach

The hosting question is the crux. Recommendation, in order:

**Where they run — split by failure domain and privilege:**
- **Phase 1 (low-risk, no new infra):** read-only scanners as GitHub Actions cron, same shape as nightshift. Auth to the cluster via the controller's RPC endpoint using a **read-only/observer credential**, not GCP admin. Out-of-band from the Iris controller → separate failure domain, which is the stated requirement. Output = ops-log file + `/file-issue` + Slack on high severity. Strictly no mutations.
- **Phase 2 (privileged actions):** anything needing GCP resource/permission visibility or remediation moves to a **dedicated locked-down GCP VM** with a narrowly-scoped service account and an allowlist of commands — not GitHub-hosted runners, which shouldn't hold standing cluster-admin secrets. This is where a `rjpower/weaver`-style hosted agent would slot in if we want a persistent service rather than cron.

**The five categories map to different triggers, so don't build one mega-bot:**
- security / GCP-permission drift → privileged (Phase 2), read GCP audit logs
- performance (slow JAX, data-loading warnings) → cron scan of finelog/W&B (Phase 1)
- stability (controller responsiveness, health stats) → cron scan of controller RPC (Phase 1)
- failures → **reuse the existing `claude-triage` action**, just add health-alert triggers alongside canary-failure triggers
- cleanup → already partly covered by nightshift; extend to codify recurring `.agents/ops/` patterns into runbooks/skills

**Suggested first slice (smallest useful, fully Phase-1):** `ops-sre-scan.yaml` (cron, e.g. every 4h) → `infra/scripts/sre_scan.py` → Claude with the `ops-steward` persona running the read-only diagnostics in `OPS.md`, emitting a finding only when a threshold trips (stuck-QR count, dead-worker count, reconcile latency). File an issue / Slack ping per finding; never mutate. This validates the credential boundary and output plumbing before we grant any write/GCP scope.

Open questions for a human before implementation:
1. Is a read-only controller/observer credential available, or does scanning require minting one?
2. Phase-2 host preference: dedicated GCP VM vs. an external agent service (weaver)?
3. Should failures route through the existing `claude-triage` action, or a separate SRE path?

Happy to turn the Phase-1 slice into a concrete PR (workflow + script + skill) once the credential and hosting questions are settled.

🤖 Grafana already hands critical alerts to idempotent Loom operator runs through `infra/grafana/src/loom_alerts.py`; this is the first working service-agent path.

#7800 defines the deterministic failure evidence Evaldash must expose. Once that contract is stable, an incomplete or infrastructure-failed evaluation can be the second producer for the same incident handoff. Diagnosis should remain read-only by default, cite the run records and artifacts used, and require explicit approval for remediation. No separate shared-agent issue is needed before this second producer is implemented.

🤖 `prefill` here is a task-level choice to continue an unfinished assistant message, not a choice about vLLM's internal prefill scheduling. A task can end with assistant text such as `{"value":` or a partial tool call. The runtime needs to know that this text is the prefix of the answer, rather than a completed turn in the conversation history; the final message's role alone does not say which one it is.

For this harness, we render that final message with `continue_final_message=True` and `add_generation_prompt=False`, then give the resulting token IDs to vLLM for generation. The generated suffix stays raw text, including reasoning or tool delimiters, so the task can grade the actual continuation. Ordinary chat rendering starts a new assistant turn, and parsed reasoning/tool-call responses can lose the syntax these tasks are checking. vLLM still decides how to execute the prompt's prefill and decode.

topics.title: [skyrl] Record Grug router telemetry in Megatron training and enforce R1
topics.body:
Record Grug router telemetry during Megatron training and enforce router level R1, for the interference experiment's routing-drift and collision-mass metrics.

With `trainer.router_telemetry.enabled`, the training wrapper observes every router forward. It masks rows to supervised response tokens, using the layout router replay already uses: packing or left unpadding, sequence-major rows, then the sequence-parallel slice. It skips recompute forwards. Load counts are keyed by (layer, global expert).

Collision mass is each expert's routed-gradient sum of squares, read from `main_grad` by post-accumulation hooks before any reduce-scatter. It is split per micro-batch by the micro-batch's response-token task mix, so a mixed θ_XR step yields per-task rows. Expert indices carry the EP rank offset, and Megatron's grouped-GEMM parameter names are parsed. Counts and mass reduce across the data, tensor and expert groups.

Every rank enters every collective, so PP > 1 cannot deadlock. The last pipeline stage writes per-step metrics and a JSONL sidecar under the export path. Its record covers every stage's layers. Context parallelism and virtual pipelines raise.

R1 is enforced for Grug only, until the per-architecture bias knob exists. Each optimizer step asserts that the expert-bias buffers are unchanged, and a nonzero aux-loss coefficient is rejected. `router_policy.json` is derived from the live model: whether router weights require grad, whether a guarded bias exists, and mcore's resolved aux-loss coefficient.

Both GPU gates passed on a CoreWeave H100 node (`/benfeuer/wp3-router-telemetry-gate-11`):
- One `ppo_train` step on tiny Grug at PP=2 writes a sidecar covering all 8 layers, with per-task collision rows for a mixed batch.
- The observed load counts on the HF model equal an independent `torch.topk` over the router weights and a nonzero bias.

CPU tests cover load statistics, collision attribution, the response-token mask, and the bias guard.

Part of the Phase 0/1a work for the OPD-SFT controls experiment (CL7, CL4 assertion, CL5 assertion).

topics.title: Marin Eval Policy (2026-10-16)
topics.body:
## Overview

This document is an attempt to formalize Marin’s policy towards what constitutes reportable, public-facing, canonical eval results for Marin models as well as the baselines we compare against.

Why do we need this document? With the first “snowball” release of a 67B A2B MoE, Marin is entering a regime where we regularly compare Marin models to existing open and closed-source models. Because Marin’s unique claim is that we are open development, we will need to hold ourselves to a high standard of transparency on how we report eval scores of Marin models and what claims we make about Marin model capabilities based on those scores.

What is in scope? This document is intended to act as a living snapshot, trustworthy for any given period in time, as to the what and the how of Marin’s canonical set of evals, a set of standards to which we will aspire to hold ourselves. By "the what", we mean “which evals did we run, with what consistent set of hyperparameters and experimental constraints”. By "the how", we mean “where is the self-contained codebase that is both necessary and sufficient to reproduce our eval results independently”.

## Previous version notes

* Released Sept 24, 2026: 18 non-agentic benchmarks, 8 Harbor agentic benchmarks, and 4 reserved out-of-distribution benchmarks.

## Complete eval list, with hyperparameters
